Where Archivio di Stato di Modena, Carteggio Principi Esteri, 1623, b. 2/2, 2, 10; DECODE R1142. Catalogue item 160. The cipher A graphic substitution alphabet; the closing says it is the old cipher of the two sisters, and a new one is enclosed. How it was deciphered Not here: the decipherment is printed in MDE IV (1878) supplement no. 45, the closing in MDE III (1877) no. 54 and the plain body in Berzeviczy (1914) no. LVI. They were matched to the photographs. What it says Andriolo is to be brought to Hungary at the king’s expense; the editor ties it to the Djem affair. Still open The printed Virtus , Fortis and M. ; which cipher “the old cipher” was. Catalogue item 160 grouped five letters of Beatrice d’Aragona, Queen of Hungary, to Ferrara; since 14 October 2026 each cipher, and the plain letter, has its own page: the 1482 letters , 8 March 1486 , 2 May 1486 and the plain letter of 1505 . This letter’s alphabet looks different from the 1482 one, and it announces a change of cipher, so it stands alone.

MDE IV (1878), p. 367, supplement no. 45: the printed decipherment of the cipher passages, with the unexplained Virtus , Fortis and M. in the text. A crop of the public-domain edition, not an archive photograph. Image: Magyar Diplomácziai Emlékek IV (1878), p. 367, via MTAK REAL-EOD. The first written page contains cipher passages about bringing Andriolo to Hungary, paying his expenses and honoring the king’s promises. They appear in MDE IV, supplement no. 45 . The editor associates the negotiation with the Djem/Cem affair; that identification is the editor’s. The intervening plain pages concern Ippolito’s appointment to Esztergom and opposition from Cardinal Ascanio. Berzeviczy printed them in 1914, explicitly omitting material already published in MDE III p. 67 and IV p. 367. The final paragraph of the physical letter matches MDE III no. 54: Con la cyfra havemo antiquamente con Vostra Signoria … ne li mandamo qui alligata un altra nova She is using the old cipher and sending a new one for subsequent correspondence. The printed no. 54 is therefore the closing part of this letter and adds no further ciphertext to the set. The related same-date letter printed as no. 53 should not be substituted for this manuscript. Limit: the 1878 decipherment keeps Virtus , Fortis and repeated M. in awkward positions. They are on the printed page and are not OCR errors. Their role in the cipher is not established. They are not deleted here as supposed nulls, and the printed text is not claimed to be flawless.

Buda, 8 March 1486 Beatrice of Aragon to her sister Eleonora of Ferrara: the cipher passages concern bringing Andriolo to Hungary, paying his travel and honouring the king's promises (the 1878 editor ties the negotiation to the Djem affair); the plain body is on Ippolito d'Este's appointment to Esztergom and Cardinal Ascanio's opposition, and the closing says the letter uses the old cipher and encloses a new one. Et nui, el secundo di poi la cruda nova dela morte dela felice memoria del Signore Cardinale, comune fratello, la cui anima Dio habia, havendolo optenuto per esso nostro nepote, ne scripsimo ala Maesta del Signore Re, nostro comune patre et Signore, che, poi che Sua Maesta non possea proponere a dicta dignita persona che piu li obtinesse del figliolo de Vostra Signoria, perche ali figlioli legitimi, como sono li Illustrissimi Signori Don Federico et Don Francesco, non ne porra ragionevole se donasse, ne meno ali figlioli delo Illustrissimo Signore Duca de Calabria, per non ne havere si non dui, havesse facta opera con la Santita del Papa, una cum lo prefato Signore Duca, consorte de Vostra Signoria, del optenere dicto archiepiscopato cum curatore. Et per cio bisogna che esso Signore Duca et Vostra Illustrissima Signoria per tucte quelle vie possibile fara instantia con la Santita prefata che se contente dare el curatore, perche da qua e stato electo esso figliolo de Vostra Signoria; et con la Maesta del Signore Re nostro padre se fara instancia che habia da procurata per esso figliolo de Vostra Signoria, poi che non lo pote cercase per figlioli legitimi, perche ali naturali, quando ce posse lo desiderio de Sua Maesta, nostro marito et li Baroni non se ne contentariano. Et tanto piu bisogna che esso Signore Duca et Vostra Signoria se aiutano, perche lo Reverendissimo Signore Cardinale Ascanio, multi di avante che dicto Bertholomeo arrivasse qua, mandao uno suo ambassatore qua ad nostro marito et ad nui ad cercare dicto archiepiscopato. Et essendoli stato referito et resposto che del dicto archiepiscopato era stato facto exito, et donatolo ad uno figliolo de Vostra Illustrissima Signoria et nostro nepote, credemo fara tucti quilli obstaculi [che] porra [fare] per impedire questa electione; perche dicto ambassatore dixe che lui se persuadeva che la Maesta del Signore Re, nostro comune padre, et lo Signore Duca vostro consorte, per rispecto de esso cardinale Ascanio, cedevano, perche non vorriano preponere uno puctino ad Sua Signoria, per la auctorita che havea in corte de Roma; et ancora che de questa lo havessemo facto fare certa che questo non stava ala Maesta del Signore Re nostro padre et ad vostro consorte, ma stava ad nostro marito et ad nui, et che per cio non bisognava pensarence, et quando ben da loro se cedesse, el che non credevamo, nui non se ne haveriamo contentata. Ne lo regno de Hungaria consenteria che tale archiepiscopato, ne altro qualesevole benefitio, se habia da dare ad Cardinali, perche non deliberano ponere tale consuetudine in quisto Regno, dove non e stata mai. Et allegando esso ambassatore lo Cardinale de Agria et la bona memoria del Cardinale, nostro comune fratello, li declaraimo che quando fo donato lo episcopato de Agria a lo Cardinale, non era si non simplice monaco et servitore de nostro marito, et havea da fare la vita sua in Hungaria; et similiter quando fo donato lo archiepiscopato de Strigonio ala dicta bona memoria del Cardinale de Aragonia, non era Cardinale; et ancora che ce fosse fratello, alo quale se li devea havere rispecto, et se ne deveano rompere tucte consuetudine, puro ne fu murmurato. Et per questo simo certi, per essereli stata aperta la mente del Signore Re nostro marito et nostra, et che qua non pote havere ne archiepiscopato ne abbatia, dicto Signore Cardinale Ascanio se opponera con omne sforzo che questa cosa non habia ad havere effecto; et quando se videra vinto (perche questo Signore Re nostro consorte avante se delibera lassare el segno che consentire dicto archiepiscopato sia donato ad sua Reverendissima Signoria), cercara de [?farse] bono de quello che non potera vendere, et vorra che lo prefato Signore Duca et Vostra Illustrissima Signoria li farano donatione de qualche bona benefitia in quisto stato o in lo stato de nostro padre. As to the request you have made jointly for the archbishopric of Esztergom for Don Ippolito, son of Your Most Illustrious Ladyship and our nephew, there is no need to enlarge much on it, because through the Magnificent Pesotto Your Most Illustrious Ladyship has been told what we have done; and also now, by letters of the said Bartholomeo, you will learn with what liberality, for love of us, His Majesty has been content that the said archbishopric be conferred and given to Don Ippolito, Your Ladyship's son. And on the second day after the cruel news of the death of the Lord Cardinal of happy memory, our common brother, whose soul God have, having obtained it for our said nephew, we wrote to His Majesty the Lord King, our common father and lord, that since His Majesty could not propose for the said dignity anyone who would obtain it more than Your Ladyship's son — because it could not reasonably be given to the legitimate sons, such as the Most Illustrious Lords Don Federico and Don Francesco, nor still less to the sons of the Most Illustrious Lord Duke of Calabria, since he has only two — he should work with His Holiness the Pope, together with the said Lord Duke, Your Ladyship's consort, to obtain the said archbishopric with a curator. And therefore the said Lord Duke and Your Most Illustrious Ladyship must press His Holiness by every possible way to consent to grant the curator, because Your Ladyship's son has been elected from here; and His Majesty the Lord King our father will be pressed to procure it for Your Ladyship's son, since he could not seek it for legitimate sons; because for natural sons, even if His Majesty desired it, our husband and the barons would not be content. And all the more must the said Lord Duke and Your Ladyship help yourselves, because the Most Reverend Lord Cardinal Ascanio, many days before the said Bartholomeo arrived here, sent an ambassador of his here to our husband and to us to seek the said archbishopric. And when he was told in answer that the said archbishopric had been disposed of and given to a son of Your Most Illustrious Ladyship and our nephew, we believe he will raise all the obstacles he can to prevent this election; for the said ambassador said that he was persuaded that His Majesty the Lord King, our common father, and the Lord Duke your consort would give way out of regard for Cardinal Ascanio, because they would not wish to put a little boy before His Lordship, given the authority he had at the court of Rome. And although we had made him certain on this that it did not rest with His Majesty the Lord King our father and with your consort, but with our husband and with us, and that therefore there was no need to think of it, and that even if they gave way, which we did not believe, we would not have been content with it. Nor would the kingdom of Hungary consent that such an archbishopric, or any other benefice whatever, should be given to cardinals, because they do not intend to establish such a custom in this kingdom, where it has never been. And when the said ambassador alleged the Cardinal of Eger and the good memory of the Cardinal, our common brother, we declared to him that when the bishopric of Eger was given to the Cardinal, he was nothing but a simple monk and servant of our husband and had to spend his life in Hungary; and likewise when the archbishopric of Esztergom was given to the said Cardinal of Aragon of good memory, he was not a cardinal; and although he was our brother, to whom regard was due, and for whom all customs had to be broken, there was nevertheless murmuring about it. And for this reason we are certain — since the mind of the Lord King our husband and ours has been opened to him, and [he knows] that he can have neither archbishopric nor abbey here — that the said Lord Cardinal Ascanio will oppose with all his strength that this matter should take effect; and when he sees himself beaten (for this Lord King our consort would sooner resolve to give up the sign than consent that the said archbishopric be given to His Most Reverend Lordship), he will try to [?make himself] good with what he cannot sell, and will want the said Lord Duke and Your Most Illustrious Ladyship to make him a gift of some good benefices in that state or in the state of our father. And since, if such a permission were granted him, it would greatly offend the mind of the Lord King our consort — because it would look as if he had had some right in the archbishopric, and was ceding it in order to have their exchange — Your Ladyship must therefore exhort the said Lord Duke on our behalf that, so as not to disturb His Majesty's mind and ours, he refuse any offer the said Lord Cardinal may have put to him; because if His Majesty heard that any benefice was being promised him, we fear he would not give the archbishopric to the said Don Ippolito, son of Your Most Illustrious Ladyship, who must constantly solicit at the court of Rome by every way she can and knows that the son be confirmed with a curator, since he has been elected; and not trouble to do anything else, because in the benefices of this kingdom persons are chosen by the Lord King our consort and confirmed by the Pope. And if at present they wished to introduce novelties through the favours of the cardinals, His Majesty is not one to consent to them, nor would he ever give possession; although we believe all these allegations will cease, because His Holiness would not wish to disturb the ancient customs of this kingdom and of His Majesty. But we have written all of it so that Your Ladyship may be informed of it, and may also believe what the said Bartholomeo now writes to you, who has conducted himself and conducts himself with the greatest modesty and virtue. And certainly Your Most Illustrious Ladyship could not have sent us a man who could have satisfied us more, for we know him, and esteem him no less our servant than yours; and we beg you to hold him as a most dear and trusted servant, for he deserves it. And it has seemed to us right to keep him here until we have an answer from Naples, which we expect from day to day, and once we have it we shall send him to you ..... We were also pleased with the other reports you have set out to His Majesty the Lord King our consort and to us about the business proposed by the Magnificent Virtus Andriolo Fortis M. And they pleased us all the more because we see they are given by persons who wish us every good; and in accordance with the reminder and advice to the said Lord Duke and of Your Ladyship, His Majesty the Lord King our husband is proceeding, and answers His Lordship in very good form, and in particular that he should be pleased [?] to encourage the said Andriolo Fortis to come here, M. Fortis, so as to be able to take such order in this that the said negotiation be put into effect by all means; and so His Majesty M. also writes to the said Andriolo Fortis M. that out of regard for His Majesty he should be pleased to come here; and that, once he has spoken with him, he will send him off, and M. will pay him all the expense of coming and returning Virtus. And therefore Your Most Illustrious Ladyship, for the love you bear us, must exhort and encourage your consort to do everything possible that Virtus Andriolo set out on the road at once and come here M. M. Fortis; who, when he has made an agreement on the said negotiation, will return; and besides his expenses being paid, he may be certain that whatever is promised him by the said Lord King our husband, and agreed with him, will be observed to the letter. And this Your Ladyship can well assure him, as has been answered more fully to the said Bartholomeo. With the cipher we have had of old with Your Ladyship, with which you will have it deciphered; and so that from now on Your Ladyship and your consort may write to His Majesty our husband and to us, we send you, enclosed here, another new one, with which Your Lordships will be able to write; and our husband will do the same, and we too shall write with it to Your Most Illustrious Ladyship, to whom we commend ourselves; and Your Ladyship will be pleased to kiss on our behalf all your most illustrious children, whom we all greet. Given in our castle of Buda, 8 March 1486. To Your Ladyship's autograph letter we shall answer in our own hand on Bartholomeo's return. Your Most Illustrious Ladyship's obedient sister, the Queen of Hungary. To the Most Illustrious and Most Powerful Lady Eleonora of Aragon, Duchess of Ferrara etc., our most honoured sister. Ferrara.

DECODE’s “Mr. Conleys Hand” is a misreading of the docket “mr Cowleys Hand”: a fair copy of two royalist letters from the Queen’s court at Paris, in clear English with 23 code numbers. The clear text was transcribed. The numbers are too few to recover a key from, the Hyde–Barwick key does not fit, and they were not decoded. of by 102:43:97:133:52:180: and concerning 57:102:58:20:30: dispatch back… 23 numbers in five runs: a few names and a place, not decoded Paris → a royalist in Holland · numbers in clear English · 28 December 1652 and 3 May 1653 “Mr. Conleys Hand”: two letters in Abraham Cowley’s hand, Paris 1652–53 from Abraham Cowley British Library, Harley MS 7003 ff. 314r–315r, DECODE R7768 and R7769: a fair copy of two letters from the exiled Queen’s court at Paris, in clear English with a few code numbers. Both letters were transcribed from the DECODE images. The author name on DECODE is a misreading of the docket. The numbers were tested against the one related key in the repository and were not decoded; the letters were not found in the printed Cowley correspondence. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letters Two nearly clear English letters from the Queen’s court at Paris, dated 28 December 1652 and 3 May 1653, to an unidentified royalist in Holland. They cover Bordeaux’s mission to England, the Dutch war, the Fronde and a rumour that the Bordelais would declare a republic. Where British Library, Harley MS 7003 ff. 314r–315r; DECODE R7768 and R7769, listed under author “Mr. Conleys Hand” as a nomenclator with no decipherment. A docket reads “mr Cowleys Hand”, so the original was written by Abraham Cowley. The cipher 23 numbers (20 distinct, 7 to 248) in five runs standing for a place and a few persons. Too few to rebuild a key. How it was tried The Hyde–Barwick key of 1659 gives nonsense. The letters are not among Cowley’s printed letters to Henry Bennet in Miscellanea Aulica (1702). Ciphertext-only solving was not attempted. What it says The 1652 letter says Bordeaux’s sending to England has not yet harmed the royalists in Holland; the 1653 one says the King ought to have gone into Holland in person. Still open The code numbers are undecoded. One hypothesis only: the eight-number place is “Scotland”. A Jermyn or Queen’s cipher of 1652–53 would open them.
conley1652.html#the-documents

Harley MS 7003 f. 314r, letter of 28 December 1652: two of the five code runs inside the clear text. Image: British Library, Harley MS 7003 f. 314r, via DECODE R7768. R7768 images f. 314r and f. 314v. R7769 images f. 314v and f. 315r, so the middle leaf appears on both records (the two files are byte-identical). The first letter runs from f. 314r to the top of f. 314v, and under it another hand has written “mr Cowleys Hand”. DECODE read that note as “Conleys” and made it the author. The second letter starts lower on f. 314v and ends on f. 315r with a postscript. Below that, f. 315r starts an unrelated letter (“My Lo:”) from a royalist waiting at the Hague. It has no numbers on the imaged part. The writer is at the Queen’s court. “She intends to write to you”, and he has promised the recipient money. That fits Jermyn’s household, where Cowley wrote. The recipient is in Holland and short of money, and has a son for whom he has asked a favour of the King and Queen. He is neither Secretary Nicholas nor the Chancellor, since both are named in the third person. He is not identified.
conley1652.html#the-reading

The full text is in targets/conley1652/transcription.txt . Their content: 28 December 1652. The “unlucky and unseasonable sending of Monsieur Bourdeaux into England” has not yet harmed the royalists in Holland. An outright Dutch victory at sea would have been dangerous “to us”. Mazarin has not yet returned to Paris. Cardinal de Retz is in prison. The King will go to the Parlement to register edicts worth seven or eight millions. The army is before Sainte-Menehould. Then comes the cipher: “I wish I could send you any Account of the present estate of 228:196:188 (for it is undoubtedly of great importance if you can procure any assistance to be sent thither against next spring …) but wee know nothing here that you will not be informed of by 102:43:97:133:52:180 and concerning 57:102:58:20:30 dispatch back (who was the person that came lately from 248:88:46:47:96:52:7:57 ) Mr Chanchellour has given an Account of it to Secretary Nicolas.” The letter ends with a promise of money “by the next”. 3 May 1653. The writer still believes the King ought to have gone into Holland in person, although it is now too late. The Court has gone to Fontainebleau. The Count de Brienne reports that “the Bourdelois have resolved to declare themselves a Republique” under English protection; it is certain only that they have sent a person into England. The request for the recipient’s son “receives noe difficulty either with the King or Queen”. Postscript: “You may doe well to write a word to Mr 203 .”
conley1652.html#the-cipher

run context 228:196:188 a country or region: “the present estate of ___ … assistance to be sent thither against next spring” 102:43:97:133:52:180 a person: “informed of by ___” 57:102:58:20:30 a person: “concerning ___ dispatch back” 248:88:46:47:96:52:7:57 a place: “the person that came lately from ___” 203 a person: “write a word to Mr ___” There are 23 numbers, 20 of them distinct, running from 7 to 248. The runs of five, six and eight look like names spelled out letter by letter, and the three-number run and the single 203 look like code words. Three values repeat: 102, 52 and 57. Hypothesis (grade M). The eight-number place is “Scotland” (s c o t l a n d). In the winter of 1652–53 the Glencairn rising was being raised in the Highlands, and the court at Paris was looking for help for it by the spring. That would make 52 = a and 57 = d, and the run 57:102:58:20:30 would begin with d . The other runs share too few letters to test it, so it stays a guess from context.
conley1652.html#what-was-tried

Print. Cowley’s fifteen known letters to Henry Bennet, 30 April 1650 to 13 September 1653, are printed in Miscellanea Aulica (1702). A search of the archive.org full text found neither of these letters. Web searches for their distinctive clear phrases also found nothing. The Clarendon State Papers calendar and Nethercot’s list of Cowley’s letters (1928) were not checked. A related key. The royalist Hyde–Barwick cipher of 1659, which the repository already holds, gives meaningless syllables (“much at vi”, “ma p ka ar s ru”). Ruled out. Ciphertext only. Not attempted: 23 numbers cannot fix a key.

A Jermyn or Queen’s cipher of 1652–53, such as the royalist keys in the Clarendon and Nicholas papers, or the original letters, if they carry a decipherment. Identifying the recipient, a royalist in Holland with a son, would show where to look.

Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 13020 f. 297, via Gallica. The slip is mounted on a leaf numbered 297. It is bound among the letters of December 1659 in a volume of Des Noyers’s letters to Boulliau, after the letter headed Danzig, 20 December 1659. The note itself has no date, place or signature, so “Danzig, December 1659” is its place in the volume, not something it says. The printed edition of 1859 heads the letters of 13, 20 and 27 December 1659 Danzig. Pierre Des Noyers (1608–1693) was secretary to Queen Louise-Marie of Poland; Ismaël Boulliau (1605–1694) was an astronomer and scholar in Paris and Des Noyers’s regular correspondent. The note answers a “petit billet” of Boulliau’s, which is not on the slip. Lines three to five. Above each run of groups the gloss gives the word: mort du Prince despagne , le mariage , la mancini , bien hardie . The marks above 30, 20 and 86 are circumflexes. The groups are two-digit numbers. Some carry a mark written above the number (a small ring, a circumflex, a cross, a bar or an accent). A group may stand for a letter or a syllable (29 la , 42 de , 46 s , 52 le , 69 n , 23 r ) or, with a mark, for a whole word (30+ Reine , 86ˆ Prince , 29+ Roy , 00− France ). The same group can be spelt more than one way: 10° reads e in hardie and ie in bien . The key is a table, key.tsv , that Brice Dudout rebuilt from the cipher and gloss pairs of twelve glossed passages of Français 13020 written between September 1658 and December 1659, this note among them. It holds 88 distinct groups with the values they were glossed with. By his count 450 of 507 group occurrences (88.8%) carry the group’s most frequent value, and 105 of 108 code words (97.2%); 200 shuffled controls stay at 34% or below. This is a key rebuilt from adjacent glossed plaintext, in the project’s terms; the passages are in French (1658) and Italian (1659) and the same table serves both. It is not the sign key of 1656 on f. 315 of the same volume. That key is an alphabet of drawn symbols with a nomenclator of groups 3–39. Tested on the glossed passages it gives no trace of its alphabet and 0 agreements in 41 groups 3–39 (200 permuted controls, mean 0.001): a different table. The 1656 key is not used for this note. What was checked here: every one of the 24 values used for this note is a value that key.tsv holds for its group, and each agrees with the gloss. What was not: the other eleven passages’ transcriptions are not in the repository, so the 88.8% and 97.2% are the contributor’s figures and were not recomputed, and the grades below (certain, probable, restored) come from his leave-one-out run, in which this note is left out of the table.

The note reads as one French sentence, in the spelling of the time. The words that come from the cipher are in italics. J’ay veu vostre petit billet et je croy asseurement que sans la Reine on n’attendroit pas la mort du Prince despagne pour rompre le mariage , et il faut que la Mancini soit bien ardie pour entreprendre ce que vous m’en dittes. In English: I have seen your little note, and I certainly believe that, but for the Queen, they would not wait for the death of the Prince of Spain to break off the marriage; and la Mancini must be very bold to undertake what you tell me of her. The cipher part is 24 groups and 12 words. All 12 are given by the gloss. Measured against the table rebuilt from the other glossed passages, 6 are certain (the value occurs at least twice elsewhere and agrees: la , Reine , Prince , le , la , ardie ), 2 are probable ( despagne , where 40 = g occurs once elsewhere; Mancini , where 77 = ni occurs once elsewhere) and 4 are restored, because the group occurs nowhere else in the volume and its value comes from the gloss alone: mort (30ˆ), du (21°), mariage (20ˆ°) and the b of bien (47). None is unread. The gloss writes hardie ; the cipher spells the word without its h , 33 a 23 r 65 di 10° e . The figure below decodes the 24 groups with the table and sets them in the plain text. Pale values are the probable and restored ones. The sense is the contributor’s reading of the context, and the note does not support it by itself. The Peace of the Pyrenees of 7 November 1659 provided for the marriage of Louis XIV and the Infanta Maria Theresa, and Philip IV’s only living son was then an infant, Philip Prosper (1657–1661), whose death would have made the Infanta heiress. On that reading la Reine is Anne of Austria, the king’s mother, and la Mancini is Marie Mancini, Mazarin’s niece. The note names neither: in the glossed passages of 1658 the same group 30+ stands for the Queen of Poland, the Queen Des Noyers served (so the contributor’s notes say), and which Queen is meant here is a judgment, not a measurement. The page does not test the identification. The reading is complete as far as the gloss goes. It adds little to the history: the note is a private aside in a correspondence that is otherwise printed, and its value is the transcription of the cipher and the gloss together and the table.

The date and place. From the note’s position in the volume, after the letter of 20 December 1659; the slip is undated. The glossator. “Probably Boulliau” is the contributor’s attribution, not checked here against Boulliau’s hand. What is certain from the image is that a second, smaller hand wrote the words above the groups. Four words rest on the gloss alone ( mort , du , mariage , the b of bien ) and two are probable ( despagne , Mancini ). The gloss is the deciphering authority here, so they are accepted; they are not independently confirmed. The small ring. The transcription writes a ring after 10, 21 and 20 ( 10o , 21o , 20^o ). On the image the round sign beside the 2 of 20 looks like the zero itself, written small, with the circumflex as the only mark; the ring after 10 and 21 could likewise be a raised zero or a mark. The table treats the ring as a mark in every passage, and this one slip cannot settle it. The last word. It ends in a flourish and is transcribed dittes ; ditte is possible. It is plain text and does not count. The consistency figures (88.8%, 97.2%, the controls) were not recomputed here. Nobody has checked the transcription against the manuscript but AI agents : the contributor’s agents made it, and this write-up compared it with the full-resolution image, group by group. No palaeographer has seen it, and the reading review recorded in the profile is a model’s. Prior publication. The note is not in the 1859 edition of Des Noyers’s letters, which prints the other glossed passages of 1658–1659 in clear. That is from a search of the Internet Archive’s OCR text here for the note’s words and for Mancini; OCR is noisy, so a miss is not a proof.

The key is Satoshi Tomokiyo's reconstruction of “Cardinal d'Este's Cipher (1584–1586)” on Cryptiana, made from the cardinal's letters to Villeroy in BnF fr. 16041–16042. Colbert 338 is not cited there, and we do not claim the table. What was added here is small: shape names for the signs, fixed on glossed pages of this volume (pp. 435–438, 453–454 and 504); the alpha with a descending tail is f (probable words “differer” and “difficultes”), and the large looped rho is a ; the barred dumbbell is e , where Tomokiyo's table has a null. This is left open ; it touches only lines 1 and 22; after the measurement, the thin c with a barred t was found by reading to be nn (donner, donna, vienne). The nulls are M and Z. Mais je vous prie qu'il ne se saiche de qui que ce soict que tel advis vienne de moi, pour ce que je me trouverois privé a l'advenir de sçavoir de teles nouvelles par la voie de ceulx du pape, lesquels encores … je me meterois en peine. In English: “… that the King of {y} had the pope asked to grant him the title of king; His Holiness, so {…} told me, flatly refused; but word is that after the refusal the said King of {y} turned to the emperor, where he is pressing hard for the title. When I said to those who spoke of it to me that the emperor would not grant such a title on his own authority without calling his electors, who would first have to consent, I was told that when Cosimo, duke of {Florence}, was made grand duke of Tuscany, the emperor alone gave him the title by his full authority, without consulting the electors. I thought I should tell you, so that you may let the King know and he may take the decision he pleases. But I beg you that no one learn from anyone that this advice came from me, for I would be deprived in future of such news, which reaches me through people of the pope's, and I would be in trouble.” The working translation adds a note on the grand-ducal title: it was created by Pius V (bull of 27 August 1569) and confirmed to Francesco de' Medici by the emperor Maximilian II (1575–76), and the argument in the letter points to that imperial recognition. This context was not checked against a source here. The prince who wanted a royal title is not identified : his country is the code sign y , which has no value in the table, and Savoy, Mantua and Ferrara are guesses that were not checked. ferdinand1634.html#letter

In November 1634, two months after the victory at Nördlingen, the imperial court was negotiating with the Elector of Saxony at Pirna; the preliminary peace was signed there on 24 November and became the Peace of Prague in 1635. Maximilian von Trauttmansdorff, high steward to the young King Ferdinand and the emperor’s chief negotiator, kept copies of the king’s letters to him. Among them, in the Trauttmansdorff family archive now at Klášter u Nepomuka, is the copy of a letter of 13 November 1634 written in cipher. Jakub Mírka described it in his 2012 survey of the cipher letters in the noble family archives of SOA Plzeň. It is the only enciphered letter among the copies of Ferdinand’s letters to Trauttmansdorff. A passage in clear at its end says that the king enciphers the letter and sends it by his own messenger, which suggests he thought the matter important. Mírka could not break the key. From the number and form of the signs he judged it a nomenclator with homophones, bigrams and probably code words, and he noted that the cipher alphabet is made up entirely of two- and three-digit numbers. His article reproduces seventeen figures; none of them is this letter.

Cryptoole (HUXXXX-1) and Tomokiyo’s list give Mírka’s description only. The 2012 volume of Západočeské archivy is sold in print, and the archive’s library catalogue holds only its cover and contents page. Ferdinand’s cipher of October 1634. A letter of Ferdinand’s of 28 October 1634 to the Cardinal-Infante, sixteen days earlier, was partly deciphered here ( Ferdinand III and the Cardinal-Infante ). Its cipher is made of graphic signs and three-letter codes, not numbers, so it is not the key to this letter. Ferdinand’s later ciphers. Barbora Šimsová’s 2024 thesis edits Ferdinand’s cipher letters of 1635–1638 to Matthias Gallas, deciphered at the time; their key does not survive, and the thesis does not mention this letter.

Mírka suggests the key may survive in Vienna, in the Trauttmansdorff family archive or the Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv. A numerical nomenclator for Ferdinand’s correspondence of 1634 would let the letter be deciphered as soon as it is seen. A five-page letter wholly in cipher from Gabriel de Gramont, bishop of Tarbes, ambassador to Clement VII, to Anne de Montmorency (BnF fr. 3091 no. 23). George Lasry recovered the key, “Gramont’s cipher (1529)”, in 2023 and deciphered the letter then, unpublished; his table was applied here to a new transcription of 4,002 signs. Clement VII on the general council, a feigned illness to wait for the Admiral Chabot, soothsayers and a dream before Bologna. d r R + W C 4 # L ● T Δ K Lo ʒ r R ● t r e d e c i m e v & a v l t r e v ♡ = le Roy · # = a or m · ♀ on a foot = null Rome → the Court · homophonic substitution cipher (Gramont’s cipher, 1529) · 11 October 1529 Gramont to Montmorency, Rome, 11 October 1529 to Anne de Montmorency Go to the full text ↓ A five-page letter wholly in cipher, written as Clement VII left for Bologna, deciphered here with George Lasry’s 2023 key: the Pope’s dread of a general council, a feigned illness, soothsayers and a dream. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 18 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · George Lasry (key or decipherment used, unpublished earlier solution) known key At a glance Known key applied · complete The letters Four ciphered letters to Anne de Montmorency, 1529–1537, by three French diplomats in Italy: Langeac (Venice, 14 January 1529), Gramont (Rome, 11 October 1529 and 21 July 1530) and Mâcon (Rome, 11 April 1537). Where BnF fr. 3083, fr. 3071 and fr. 3091 (Gallica); the catalogue grouped them asking whether they share a cipher. The cipher They do not: each has its own monoalphabetic key with two to seven homophones for common letters, doubled-letter signs, nulls and a few person codes; Mâcon’s code signs are numerals. How it was read A new transcription of about 9,000 signs from the Gallica scans, decrypted with the keys Lasry reconstructed in 2023 and Tomokiyo published as images. What it says Gramont 1529 reports Clement VII’s dread of a general council and his plan to grant one and stall it; Mâcon reports Paul III offering the Farnese marriage and threatening to declare for the Emperor. Still open Gramont 1530 and Mâcon are not complete; Mâcon’s clear text was transcribed loosely. Credit George Lasry reconstructed the four keys and deciphered the letters in 2023 without publishing them; Satoshi Tomokiyo published the key tables.

The letter is BnF fr. 3091 no. 23, ff. 45r–47v, in the volume of Raince’s papers (Gallica btv1b9060253s, filmed as two-page openings, views 49–52). It came to the project as one of four letters to Montmorency grouped as catalogue item 6, which guessed “four letters by three hands, probably three keys”. Matching each against Tomokiyo’s pages on the ciphers of François I showed four keys, one per letter. Since 14 October 2026 each key has its own page: Langeac at Venice in 1529 ( Avranches’ cipher 1 ), Gramont again in 1530 ( Gramont’s cipher, 1530 ) and the cardinal de Mâcon in 1537, now with his other letters in Mascon’s cipher . Each is a different cipher, with its own page. This letter’s key is Lasry’s “Gramont’s cipher (1529)”, built from the siblings fr. 3040 f. 16 and Clairambault 330 f. 53 and dated 5 November 2023. It is a monoalphabetic substitution with two to seven homophones for the common letters, signs for doubled letters, a handful of nulls, and a few code signs for persons. Tomokiyo notes that the published image carries no plaintext, and none of the letter is transcribed or printed elsewhere that we could find.
gramont1529.html#tarbes

Fr. 3091 f. 45r. After Monseigneur, je voy que tant par mes lettres du treziesme et du septiesme de septembre the letter is cipher for five pages. The heart on line 6 is the sign for the King. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3091 f. 45r, via Gallica btv1b9060253s view 49. The letter runs to 171 lines across ff. 45r–47v, closing A Romme le xi me jour d’octobre over the signature G. de Gramont e. de Tarbe . The year is 1529. The Pope has just left Rome (Clement VII set out for Bologna on 7 October 1529), and Gramont leaves “demain” to join him at Perugia. The letter opens with the bull of the four décimes on the French clergy, raised for the princes’ ransom under the peace of Cambrai, and the prince of Orange is before Florence. In outline, modernised (the full decipherment, page by page, is in the repository): The council. Whatever the Emperor says or does only deepens the Pope’s distrust of that side. What won him to the King was the King’s message about the concile general , “lequel il craignoit sur toutes les choses de ce monde, combien qu’il monstrast … qu’il en ait grande envie”. Pressed, he confessed that he knew the council was being pushed to ruin him, and that he meant to grant it and then “s’arrester sur aucunes particularitez pour le differer, et que le delai lui succedast en rupture”. Into the King’s arms. He would “du tout se jecter entre ses bras et se fier en luy seul”. Because the times do not allow open trust, the King and his ministers may say publicly, whenever it helps, that they have little reason to trust the Pope, so long as the goodwill underneath stays whole. “Avec bonnes parolles vous aurez de luy ce que vous voudrez”. His one aim is to get the Emperor out of Italy. Feigning illness for the Admiral. The Emperor is bound “par ses chappitres”, the treaty of Barcelona, to bring the allies to full restitution or make war on them. Gramont has told Philippe Chabot, the Admiral, then on his embassy to Italy, to come as far forward as he can. The Pope offers to slow his journey, or to “faire le malade” in whatever town he is in, to wait for him. On 10 October he told Gramont he had already begun. Soothsayers and a dream. The Pope, though he should not believe “tout plein de gens qui se meslent de deviner”, greatly fears what they say of him. Several have foretold that he will be deposed or will die within the year, and that it will come “du costé dudict” [the Emperor]. The night before he left Rome he had a dream, which Gramont encloses, “lequel l’a mis en merveilleusement grande fantasie”, because he dreamed it at the kind of hour at which earlier dreams of his had come true. He told it to one man only, and Gramont asks that only the King, Madame and those they choose should know of it. Florence. The prince of Orange wanted to deal with [the Florentines]: restore [the Medici] to the state of Florence “comme il souloit”, in return for Pisa and Livorno being put in [the Emperor’s] hands. That is “chose grandement contraire” to what the Emperor had agreed with the Pope. Gramont’s letter adds detail to the French side of the weeks before the congress of Bologna. The council, Florence and the Venetian and Ferrarese restitutions all serve as bargaining counters in it, and the Pope keeps a private line to France through the ambassador. The enclosed dream is not in the volume.
gramont1529.html#method

No cryptanalysis was needed: the work was transcription and decryption. The key table was checked on the first full line ( d r R + W C 4 # L ● T Δ K Lo ʒ r R ● decodes to tredecime v & avltre v ). Each glyph was then given a one-character ASCII alias and a script turned the alias strings back into letters, so that every decryption can be checked against the transcription and re-run. The five pages were transcribed separately and in parallel, each by a model instance working from the same brief, key and crops, and then joined. The joins fall mid-sentence and agree. Points the transcribers found that the table does not give: In Gramont’s hand the loose ǂǂ for a and the compact # for m cannot be told apart, so # is taken as a or m by context. A is the more frequent. A triangle or ring on a stem over a foot bar looks like ♀ ( o ) but is a null, Lasry’s “4 with a flag”. It occurs about twenty times. Taken as o , it produces doepesche . The heart, which Lasry lists only as a person sign, is always the King (“escript au ♡ et à vous”). Three large signs outside the table stand where the Emperor, the Florentines and the Pope or the Medici are expected. Those identifications come from context and are marked as such.

BnF fr. 3091 no. 23, ff. 45r-47v, Rome, 11 Oct [1529] Gramont writes to Montmorency as Clement VII sets out for Bologna (October 1529): he vouches for the Pope's secret alignment with France; Clement dreads the general council and plans to grant it in principle and then stall it, offers to feign illness on the road to wait for the Admiral Chabot, fears soothsayers who foretell his deposition or death "du costé de" the Emperor, and had a dream before leaving Rome (enclosed). Orange is dealing to restore the Medici in Florence against Pisa and Livorno going to the Emperor. After the opening clear words the letter is wholly in cipher: 33 + 34 + 33 + 32 + 32 + 7 = 171 lines, about 7,000 signs. Key: "Gramont's cipher (1529)", reconstructed by George Lasry in 2023 from fr. 3040 f. 16 (table `img/BnF_fr3040_f16.png`, Tomokiyo's GL.htm). Nobody had published a decipherment. Each page was transcribed glyph by glyph into ASCII aliases (`AGENT_BRIEF.md`, `decode.py`) and decoded. Per-page line tables, doubts and glyph notes are in `f45r_transcription.md` … `f47v_transcription.md`. The alias lines are in `work_*/`, which is not tracked. Confidence runs from about 90 to 95 % per page. Every line gives French, and no line is illegible. ## Year No year on the leaf, but 1529 is certain from the content. The Pope has just left Rome ("la nuit avant qu'il partît de cette ville"): Clement VII left for the Bologna meeting with Charles V on 7 October 1529. Gramont follows him the next day to Perugia. The bull of the four décimes on the French clergy (for the princes' ransom under the peace of Cambrai) went to France in autumn 1529. The prince of Orange is before Florence, where the siege began in October 1529. The obligations "par ses chapitres" are the treaty of Barcelona (June 1529). ## Key notes from the reading (all five transcribers agree) * `#` is **A as often as M**: the loose ǂǂ (A) and the compact # (M) are not distinct in this hand. Context decides. * The ♀-like "triangle or ring on a stem over a foot bar" is a **null** (Lasry's "4 with a flag"), in about 20 places. It is distinct from the true ♀ (O). * The dotted ring ◉ is the V "eye". CON also serves for COM (comme, combien, complexion). ρ-o-ρ = FF. * R (E) and K (V) are easily confused. The 4 of I is sometimes a plain cross, like the + of D. * Code signs not in Lasry's table: the heart (person sign) is **the King** every time ("escript au ♡ et à vous", "le ♡ me commanda"). A cross with a spiral or loop head (Lasry's second "unknown") and a large barred ƒ-like sign stand where **the Emperor** is expected ("du costé dudict —", "fondement avec ledict —"). f. 47r has three more: ⊞, probably the Florentines; ▯ (Lasry's "pencil"), the Pope or the Medici; and a large looped ♀, the Emperor. These identifications come from context and are not readings. ## Prior art still to check Wirtz-Daviau's edition of Chabot's 1529 embassy may print or summarise Gramont's letters of the same weeks, perhaps from a deciphered copy. It has not been seen. No decipherment of this letter is known from Tomokiyo, Lasry, DECODE or the BnF catalogue. ## Reading Modernised spelling and punctuation. Cipher throughout, apart from the clear opening and close. Code signs are in brackets. **f. 45r.** Monseigneur, je voy que tant par mes lettres du treziesme et du septiesme de septembre [que par la] depesche de la bulle des quatre decimes et aultres choses que vous aporte le maistre d'hostel du roi de Navarre, aurez prins seureté que, si j'ai par ci devant escript au [Roy] et à vous la bonne volunté de nostre sainct pere, je l'ai plus faict avecques claire congnoissance d'icelle par effectz que par legiere creance ni aultre volunté extraordinaire qui me meust à ce. Et vous puis dire que, quant plus je vois avant, tant plus je conferme mon oppinion, d'aultant que je cognois ordinairement et à clair que la plus grande envie que nostre [d]ict sainct pere ait est de demourer en vraie amitié et union avecques le [Roy], et que quelque bonne parolle ni demonstration qu'il puisse avoir de [l'Empereur (?)], cela lui croist une diffidance qu'il a conceue, tellement qu'il ne peult se persuader que d'aultre chose que mal et inconvenient lui puissent advenir de ce costé-là, bien qu'il montre que le tout soit au contraire. Et pour le faire fier, n'i a nui (?) d'aucune chose [comme] ce que le [Roy] me commanda lui dire du concile general, lequel il craignoit sur toutes les choses de ce monde, combien qu'il monstrast et monstre à ung chascun qu'il en ait grande envie et qu'il le pourchasse. Et au commancement, et avant qu'il me prestast entiere foi, il m'en voulsist bien faire acroire aultant. Le tout debatu et mes raisons ouïes, il fut contrainct se declarer [... f. 45v] **f. 45v.** [... le pape ... de] confesser qu'il connoissoit très bien que ce que l'on pourchassoit, ledit concile, étoit pour le ruiner ; et qu'il étoit délibéré, en l'accordant en voi[e?], toutefois s'arrêter sur aucunes particularités pour le différer, et que le délai lui succédât en rupture. Et que, puisque je l'assurois de la bonne volonté du [Roi] et de l'amitié qu'il lui portoit, il se vouloit du tout jeter entre ses bras et se fier en lui seul. Et pource que le temps ne porte de mettre défiance, il est content (mais que la volonté demeure toujours entière) que toutes et quantes fois qu'il sera besoin, et [que cela] fera à son profit, ledit sieur, tant par lui que par ses ministres, die et fasse dire avoir peu d'occasion de se fier en lui, et qu'il procède hardiment outre comme il verra être à faire ; car il voit que la complexion des gens à qui l'on a affaire porte cela et plus grande chose. Vous savez, que je vous ai souvent écrit, qu'avec bonnes paroles vous aurez de lui ce que vous voudrez ; et ne craignez point qu'il en veuille faire aucun fondement ni profit avec ledit [signe : l'Empereur ?], car il ne tâche sinon l'en envoyer de l'Italie, quelque chose qui lui doive advenir. Et croyez que Monsieur l'Amiral n'aura pas grande affaire, vu la disposition en quoi je l'ai mis, de le faire consentir ce qui pourroit être fait en faveur du [Roi] pour les alliés et confédérés. Et combien que pour [... f. 46r] **f. 46r.** [... f. 45v] ... [à] lui être [!] obligé par ses chapitres, à ce que vous savez, et qu'il fût contraint, pour observer d'eux (?), de faire venir lesdits alliés à entière restitution ou autrement leur faire la guerre. Il fait bonne mine au commencement, [pour voir] s'il viendra; il a ce que je vous dis. De quoi j'ai averti mondit sieur l'amiral, afin que de longue main il regarde à conduire sa charge et qu'il ne laisse de venir si avant qu'il pourra avec ledit [!] aux autres choses, pensant trouver difficulté en celle-ci. Et davantage je lui ai écrit que, s'il trouvait bon, ce que notre dit saint père m'a dit (?), au cas où il retardât son chemin, ou bien que du tout il fît le malade en quelque ville [où] il était, [il est] prêt à tout faire; et il a déjà commencé à se plaindre, afin que, s'il était besoin, la chose ne semblât si soudaine. Il fait tout le possible, tant de parole que par ses ministres, combien qu'ils soient en petit nombre, en qui il se fie, pour m'entretenir, me priant de le vouloir tenir en la bonne grâce du [♡ = the King?] [sign]. Et si je voyais que ledit sieur eût à traiter quelque chose avec lui où il pût y avoir profit ou dommage pour l'un ou pour l'autre, je me tiendrais sur mes gardes; mais voyant qu'il ne demande aucune chose et que ledit sieur n'a aucune querelle à démêler avec lui [... f. 46v] **f. 46v.** [... de 46r] et que de toutes choses que je lui demande de par ledit sieur, soit qu'il n'y ait aucun profit et qu'aucunefois il y ait dommage, il m'en complaît. Il faut que je vous dise qu'il y va de bon pied; ou autrement ce serait le plus grand sot que je vis oncques, vu qu'il donnerait à toute heure sans espérance de rien avoir. Et combien qu'il soit pape, et qu'il ne doive ajouter foi (comme je crois qu'il ne fait) au dire de tout plein de gens qui se mêlent de deviner, si vous puis-je assurer que, quand ils disent quelque chose de lui, si c'est mal, il le craint grandement. Et il y en a plusieurs qui ont dit qu'il doit être déposé, ou qu'il doit mourir en l'année prochaine, et que le tout lui doit venir du côté dudit [sign: l'Empereur?]. Et croyez qu'il y a une merveilleuse fantaisie; et pour lui en tenir davantage, la nuit avant qu'il partît de cette ville il fit un songe, que je vous envoie, lequel l'a mis en merveilleusement grande fantaisie, d'autant qu'il dit qu'il le songea en [même] heure qu'il a songé d'autres fois plusieurs choses qui lui sont advenues. Et il ne s'est déclaré dudit songe qu'avec grande défiance, de n'en dire aucune chose qu'à un homme seul. À cette cause je vous supplie qu'il [... f. 47r] **f. 47r.** [... que la chose] ne soit publiée, et que vous contentiez que le Roi, Madame et ceux qu'il leur plaira le sachent seulement. Je partirai demain pour m'en aller à Pérouse, là où je le dois trouver, et en chemin je pense avoir nouvelles dudit sieur l'amiral. J'ai fait vos recommandations à notre dit Saint-Père, et lui ai montré vos lettres, parce qu'elles étaient bonnes à ces fins; et croyez qu'il en a eu aussi grand contentement qu'il eut en sa vie de chose, et ne tiendra qu'à vous si vous ne lui faites faire entièrement tout ce qui sera le service du Roi, la conduite et l'augmentation de ses affaires. Et il a été aussi grandement satisfait de ce que je lui ai dit de la part dudit sieur [l'amiral] par le commandement qu'il lui a plu m'en faire par ses dernières lettres. Ne vous ébahissez pas, s'il vous plaît, si d'ici à quelque temps vous n'avez plus souvent de mes nouvelles, car le chemin en sera cause, joint qu'il faut donner avis de tout audit sieur l'amiral, qui vous le fera entendre. J'ai été averti que le prince d'Orange voulait s'entremettre avec les [⊞ = Florentins?] pour remettre le [▯ = Pape / les Médicis?] à l'état de Florence comme il soulait [être], et qu'ils baillassent Pise et Livourne et [les remissent?] entre les mains de [Ꝭ = l'Empereur?], ce qui est chose grandement contraire à ce que ledit [Ꝭ] a capitulé avec le [▯]. **f. 47v.** Et je crois qu'il l'a su, car hier soir il me fit entendre comment il avait commencé à faire le malade en attendant des nouvelles de monsieur l'amiral, et que si, au départ de cette ville, il était en bonne volonté, il était à cette heure en [?] bonne volonté. **Clear close.** Monseigneur, je me recommande bien humblement à vostre bonne grace, et prie Dieu vous donner [en bonne] santé longue vie. A Romme le xi^me jour d'octobre. Vostre humble serviteur, G. de Gramont, e[vesque] de Tarbe. ## Summary (English) Gramont writes as Clement VII sets out for Bologna. He vouches for the Pope's goodwill toward France. What won the Pope over was the King's line on a **general council**. Clement dreads a council above all things while pretending to want one, and he admitted to Gramont that it was being pushed to ruin him. His plan was to grant it in principle and then stall over particulars until the delay ended in a breakdown. He "throws himself into the King's arms". He even allows the King and his ministers to say openly that they cannot trust him, if that helps them with the Emperor, so long as the goodwill underneath stays whole. His one aim is to get the Emperor out of Italy. The Emperor is bound by his treaty articles to force the allies (Venice, Ferrara) to restore what they hold or else make war on them. The Pope is ready to delay on the road, or feign illness, to wait for the **Admiral** (Philippe Chabot de Brion, whose embassy to Italy in 1529 is edited by B. Wirtz-Daviau, *Le voyage et l'ambassade de l'Amiral Chabot de Brion en Italie, 1529*) and to fall in with whatever the Admiral proposes for France's allies. By 10 October he had already begun "faire du mallade". Two pages give the Pope's fear of astrologers and soothsayers, who foretold that he would be deposed or die within the year, "du costé de" [the Emperor]. They also report a **dream** he had the night before leaving Rome, which Gramont encloses and asks be shown only to the King, Madame (Louise of Savoy) and whom they choose. Last comes intelligence that the **prince of Orange** was negotiating to restore [the Medici] in Florence on condition that Pisa and Livorno be put in [the Emperor's] hands, "chose grandement contraire" to what the Emperor had agreed with the Pope at Barcelona. The letter fills out the French side of the weeks before the Bologna congress. It shows the council, Florence and the Venetian/Ferrarese restitutions being used as bargaining counters, and a Pope whose private line to France ran through Gramont. Translation fr3091_no23_gramont_en.md # BnF fr. 3091 no. 23, ff. 45r-47v: Gabriel de Gramont, bishop of Tarbes, Rome, to Montmorency, 11 October [1529]: English translation Translation (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026) of the reading in `fr3091_no23_gramont.md` (section "Reading"), the decryption with Lasry's reconstructed key of the cipher, which fills the whole letter apart from the clear opening and close. Same holes and marks: `[...]` unread or a page join, `(?)` and `[word?]` doubtful (here `[?word]`), `[!]` a sign that does not fit, code signs in brackets with their probable meaning, `[word]` a word supplied. ## Translation **f. 45r.** Monseigneur, I see that, both by my letters of the thirteenth and of the seventh of September [and by the] despatch of the bull of the four tenths and other things which the King of Navarre's maître d'hôtel brings you, you will have been made sure that, if I have heretofore written to the [King] and to you of the good will of Our Holy Father, I have done it more with clear knowledge of it by deeds than by light belief or any other extraordinary wish that moved me to it. And I can tell you that, the further I go, the more I confirm my opinion, inasmuch as I see ordinarily and clearly that the greatest wish our said Holy Father has is to remain in true friendship and union with the [King]; and that whatever good word or show he may have from [?the Emperor], this only increases in him a distrust he has conceived, so that he cannot persuade himself that anything but harm and mischief can come to him from that side, although he shows that it is all the contrary. And to make him trust, nothing [?served] in any thing [like] what the [King] commanded me to tell him of the general council, which he feared above all things in this world, although he showed and shows to everyone that he greatly wishes it and is pursuing it. And at the beginning, before he gave me entire faith, he would have liked to make me believe as much. The whole being debated and my reasons heard, he was forced to declare himself [... f. 45v] **f. 45v.** [... the Pope ... to] confess that he knew very well that what was being pursued, the said council, was to ruin him; and that he had resolved, while granting it in [?principle], nevertheless to stop on some particulars to put it off, and that the delay should end for him in a breakdown. And that, since I assured him of the [King]'s good will and of the friendship he bore him, he wished to throw himself entirely into his arms and trust in him alone. And because the time does not allow showing distrust, he is content (provided that the goodwill always remains whole) that, as often as there is need, and [that it] will be to his profit, the said lord [the King], both himself and through his ministers, should say and have it said that he has little reason to trust him, and that he should proceed boldly onward as he sees fit to do; for he sees that the temper of the people one has to deal with requires that and a greater thing. You know, as I have often written to you, that with good words you will have from him what you wish; and do not fear that he will want to make any foundation or profit of it with the said [sign: ?the Emperor], for he aims at nothing but to send him out of Italy, whatever may befall him. And believe that Monsieur the Admiral will not have much to do, given the disposition in which I have put him, to make him consent to what might be done in favour of the [King] for the allies and confederates. And although for [... f. 46r] **f. 46r.** [... f. 45v] ... [to] be [!] bound by his articles, as you know, and that he were forced, to keep them [?], to make the said allies come to full restitution or else make war on them. He puts a good face on it at the beginning [to see] whether he will come; he has what I tell you. Of which I have advised my said lord the Admiral, so that he may look well ahead to conducting his charge, and that he not fail to come as far as he can with the said [!] in the other matters, thinking to find difficulty in this one. And moreover I have written to him that, if he found it good, what our said Holy Father has told me [?], in case he delayed his journey, or else wholly played the sick man in some town [where] he was, [he is] ready to do everything; and he has already begun to complain, so that, if there were need, the thing should not seem so sudden. He does everything possible, both by word and through his ministers, few as they are, in whom he trusts, to keep in with me, begging me to keep him in the good grace of the [♡ = ?the King] [sign]. And if I saw that the said lord had to negotiate something with him in which there could be profit or damage for the one or the other, I would keep on my guard; but seeing that he asks for nothing, and that the said lord has no quarrel to settle with him [... f. 46v] **f. 46v.** [... from 46r] and that in all things I ask of him on the said lord's behalf, whether there be no profit in them and sometimes there be damage, he gratifies me in them. I must tell you that he goes about it in good faith; or otherwise he would be the greatest fool I ever saw, seeing that he would give at every hour without hope of having anything. And although he is pope, and ought not to give credit (as I believe he does not) to the sayings of a great many people who meddle with divining, yet I can assure you that, when they say something of him, if it is ill, he fears it greatly. And there are several who have said that he must be deposed, or must die in the coming year, and that the whole must come to him from the side of the said [sign: ?the Emperor]. And believe that he has a wondrous fancy about it; and to keep him in it all the more, the night before he left this city he had a dream, which I send you, which has put him into a wondrously great fancy, inasmuch as he says that he dreamed it at the [same] hour at which at other times he has dreamed several things that have befallen him. And he has not spoken of the said dream except with great mistrust, telling nothing of it except to one man alone. For this cause I beg you that it [... f. 47r] **f. 47r.** [... that the thing] be not published, and that you be content that the King, Madame and those whom it pleases them should alone know it. I shall leave tomorrow to go to Perugia, where I am to find him, and on the way I expect to have news of the said lord the Admiral. I have made your commendations to our said Holy Father, and showed him your letters, because they were good for these ends; and believe that he had as great contentment from them as he ever had from anything in his life, and it will only be up to you if you do not have him do entirely all that will be for the King's service, the conduct and the furtherance of his affairs. And he was also greatly satisfied with what I told him on behalf of the said lord [the Admiral], by the command he was pleased to give me of it in his last letters. Do not be astonished, if you please, if for some time from now you do not have news of me more often, for the road will be the cause of it, besides which all must be advised to the said lord the Admiral, who will let you know it. I have been informed that the Prince of Orange wished to act as go-between with the [⊞ = ?the Florentines] to restore the [▯ = ?the Pope / the Medici] to the state of Florence as he used [to be], and that they should hand over Pisa and Livorno and [?put them] into the hands of [Ꝭ = ?the Emperor], which is a thing greatly contrary to what the said [Ꝭ] has agreed by treaty with the [▯]. **f. 47v.** And I believe he has learned of it, for yesterday evening he let me know how he had begun to play the sick man while waiting for news of Monsieur the Admiral, and that if, at his departure from this city, he was in good will, he was at this hour in [?] good will. **Clear close.** Monseigneur, I commend myself very humbly to your good grace, and pray God to give you [in good] health a long life. At Rome, the 11th day of October. Your humble servant, G. de Gramont, b[ishop] of Tarbes. Key: BnF_fr3040_f16.png , decode.py , key.md

Harley MS 7001 f. 149r, the head of the page: the cipher continued from f. 148v, beginning “[as to] the one side, I am of opinion they have not enough against him to confiscate his fortune”. Image: British Library, Harley MS 7001 f. 149r, via DECODE R7766. The letter covers three pages (ff. 148r, 148v, 149r). The address leaf f. 149v carries the endorsement and “Given by Mr G. Holmes”. It answers the recipient’s letter of 1 April and follows Reade’s own letter of the 16th. The clear text covers: a malicious report that Reade had said, to two French gentlemen in a garden, that the Lords of the Parliament are fools. He denies it at length and asks the recipient to raise it with the Lord Chief Justice; the roads full of soldiers, which keep the household in its quarter of Paris for another month; “My Lo: Lieutenant”, Strafford, then on trial, “fallen into the hands of noblemen and persons of honor”; the King’s box of papers and a copy held by Mr Treasurer; the Queen’s business; Mr Montagu’s arrival, “very civilly” received; Sir William St Ravy leaving for England; a defence of Mr Forster, lodged with the household. The cipher begins where the letter turns to Windebank himself: “It is to be seriously considered what is to be done”.

March 1642”, the second “Windebank’s C[ipher] continued 1640”. The cipher has four parts: 1–50: single letters. Every odd number is marked + (a null). The even numbers are letters: 2 c, 4 f, 6 n, 8 h, 10 r, 12 t, 14 a, 16 g, 18 p, 20 b, 22 u, 24 o, 26 l, 28 e, 32 k, 34 m, 36 i, 40 s, 42 x, 44 d. 51–100: more letters and syllables: 51 r, 53 c, 54 l, 55 s, 56 a, 57 d, 58 m, 59 t, 60 e, 62 n, 64 i, 66 p, 68 o, 69 h, 72 u, 73 and, 74 am, 75 as, 93 again, 97 an. Symbol letters: m n, E o, ω m, Ǝ r, ⊔ i, + l, φ s, Δ t, * y, ⊕ a, π c, ɔ d, ∪ e, C p, and others. A code in alphabetical order from 100 to about 735: 128 be, 183 can, 202 do, 276 from, 323 him, 335 his, 362 King, 457 Parliament, 533 shall, 572 to, 574 the, 578 that, 636 will, 732 England, 735 France. Reade’s letter uses the same cipher. The most frequent code groups in it are the reconstruction’s the, to and that, and its symbol letters are the key’s. Several characters first transcribed as digits are the key’s symbol letters: φ looks like an 8, ɔ like a 2, and the looped n-sign like a D.

Passage A (f. 148v foot to f. 149r), after the clear “It is to be seriously considered what is to be done”: in case a proclamation shall goe out against my [455: patron?] as against the last [673], for as to the one side, I am of opinion they have not enough against him to confiscate his fortune, and they would be [willing] to take the advantage of his refusall to return upon the a summons. So on the other side, I do not find how his person can be strong if he shall return . The only [way] i[s] [conceived] to be that [His Majesty] will please to prevent that cause, if they purpose to take it, bu[t pres]sing that [Mr Forster] [should] give in his [90]; but God knows why that will suit. Passage B (f. 149r), after the clear “Sir William St Ravy (as I hear) parts this day for England, but I do but hear it from others, for he comes not at us”: I am [informed] he has done [Mr Forster] no good [offices] here, and that he will not do him the best in Court; they have an eye [over] him. The clear text goes straight on: “It may be that Mr Forster may have ill offices done him in England…”. This confirms the sense of the passage and supports the conjecture that 718 is Forster.

The passages have 254 groups, 215 of them after the nulls are dropped. Grades follow the README conventions: H a value on the key, C a rebuilt value with firm context, M a conjecture. Re-measured 5 October 2026. Key and rebuilt values together decipher 201 of 215 cipher groups (93.5%). The margin entry for 650 on the key sheet (R9115 f. 1) was read at full resolution: it is 650. w[r]it with an h above, not way , and none of the candidates fits the context, so 650 stays grade M. Neither key page has side notes for the other twelve open values. The fourteen single-occurrence blanks need key material: the Reade letters in TNA SP 16 (physical access). H, 193 groups (89.8%): deciphered from values on the key, including 203 done and 729 “ct.” (Court), which are side notes on the sheet. 562 is “strong” on the key, in the period sense of safe or secure (“how his person can be strong if he shall return”). Until 30 September 2026 this page printed a rebuilt “secure” there instead. C, 8 groups (3.7%): values rebuilt from the code’s alphabetical slot and the context. They are 100 advantage, 275 find, 437 one, 524 return (twice) and 573 they/the (three times). 573 fits “they” in two places. In “upon 573 a summons” “the” fits better, and there the 14 (a) is probably a slip. The key sheet has a partly legible entry at 573, “u. th…”: the word begins th, and the rest runs under a ruled line. It fits they or the but is too damaged to confirm either. M, 14 groups (6.5%): blank on the reconstruction and conjectured. 650 way, 160 conceived, 319 His Majesty, 539 should. 718 Forster (twice), 359 informed 444 offices, 452 over. 660, “they would be [willing] to take the advantage”: willing, glad or ready fit the sense. On the key 660 is blank among the y-words (652 you, 662 you, 664 your, 666 yet), where a w-word would not stand, and no y-word gives the sense. 487 (inside “bu…ing”), 90 (his answer or account), 455 (my patron?) and 673 (the last Lord Keeper? Finch fled in December 1640 as Windebank did). Only a fuller copy of the key would settle these. No other Windebank key is on DECODE, and no Windebank letter in this cipher was found there.

The images were fetched from DECODE and the two passages transcribed. The signature and endorsement gave the writer. The key of “Mr Browne” (R8694, Add MS 72438) was tried first and failed. Its code stops at 371, and its alphabet gives nothing. A search of the DECODE record list for Windebank found R9115 in Add MS 32256. Both of its pages were transcribed at full resolution and entered as a table. The table was applied to the passages, the doubtful glyphs were checked again against the key’s symbol list, and the result was measured. No printed edition or calendar of the letter was found. Harleian letters of this kind are outside the Calendars of State Papers Domestic.

Français 3669 is a recueil of originals: the King and Herbault writing to Béthune in Rome through the autumn and winter of 1625–26, most pieces catalogued “avec chiffre et déchiffrement” because the embassy’s clerk wrote the plaintext of each ciphered passage onto the sheet as he deciphered it. One piece breaks the pattern. The volume is digitised from a black-and-white microfilm of double-page openings; canvas equals folio plus five, fixed on the foliation of ff. 70 and 73. Piece Letter Leaves Cipher 24 Herbault → Béthune, 6 February 1626 ff. 67–68 none noted 25 Herbault → Béthune, 13 February 1626 ff. 69–71 cipher, no decipherment 26 the same letter, 13 February 1626 ff. 72–74 cipher with interlinear decipherment 27 Louis XIII → Béthune f. 75– cipher and decipherment Both copies are made up for sending, each with its own address leaf, wax seal and docket. Both open on the same words under the same marginal note, “Le roy fera responce” . And their clear text runs word for word: the same paragraphs on Rambouillet’s delayed departure for Spain, the promotion of cardinals and Marquemont’s hat, the courier sent on the 6th through the Venetian ambassador Contarini, the peace with the Huguenots, the prince of Piedmont’s arrival, down to the King’s sore toe, “quelque douleur à cause d’ung ongle qui luy entre dans la chair”, which kept him in bed and delayed Herbault’s report.

BnF Français 3669, f. 73r (no. 26): cipher with the 1626 decipherment written under each line: “vray que les affaires de cet estat avoyent besoing de ce” / cipher / “relasche et que le faix d’une double guerre ne se pouvoit” / cipher / “plus supporter. J’advoue que les affections”…. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3669 f. 73r, via Gallica btv1b9060205q canvas 78. Three things show that no. 26 is a copy of the same despatch as no. 25. The clear text is identical , paragraph by paragraph, including incidental matter no second letter would repeat verbatim: the memoir of Cardinal Bevilacqua for Horatio Giraldi, the naturalisation letters obtained through Cardinal de la Valette, the sore toe. The cipher runs fall at the same points , after the same clear words: “en laquelle il aura laissé”, “dont nous esperons estre bientost esclaircis”, “au nom de ce prétendu comte de”, “besoing de ce”, “Vous scaurez maintenant que”, “Toutes ces propositions”, “il nous faut continuer ceste mesme routte jusques”. The groups match where checked. No. 25’s first run opens to 92 … 17 … 43 and no. 26’s opens to 92 g 17 … 43 … ; the third run ends … 68 93 … in both, with the same short group after it. The two clerks’ hands differ enough that individual figures look different at this resolution, so the claim is limited to the runs corresponding; group-for-group identity is not claimed. The cipher itself is a nomenclator of one- to three-character groups mixing Arabic figures with letter-forms. The opening run, to 92 g 17 ẓ 43 x cu 4 7 ẓ p x 3 3 6 x , stands for “le Pape pour l’acheminement de ces troupes in la Valt(eline)”: about eighteen groups for some forty-eight letters, so most groups carry a syllable or a whole word. The table is not reconstructed here because the decipherment makes it unnecessary, and roughly thirty further glossed letters of 1625–26 in the same cipher sit in the same volume for anyone who wants it.

Herbault writes to the ambassador in Rome on the eve of the Treaty of Monzón. The ciphered passages concern the Valtelline, the Huguenot peace, the Dutch ships and Savoy. The Valtelline. Herbault waits on news of the papal Legate’s departure for Spain and of the last resolution in which he will have left “le Pape pour l’acheminement de ces troupes in la Valt(eline)” , an affair which deserves “l’envoy d’un courrier exprez” , and above all “principallement sy le Pape entroit dans la partialité” , the fear that Urban VIII would cease to mediate and take a side. Why the crown had just made peace with its Protestants. The peace “s’affermit de jour en jour” and is welcome even to those “qui ont tousjours le plus hautement conseillé le chastiment et la guerre contre les huguenots”, because, in cipher, “les affaires de cet estat avoyent besoing de ce relasche, et que le faix d’une double guerre ne se pouvoit plus supporter” , while “les affections de noz voysins qui font profession de ceste religion pretendue refformée estoyent grandement alterés” . In plain terms, France made peace at home because it could not afford two wars, and because the Protestant powers abroad were turning. The ships. Béthune has already been told of “la conduitte des Anglois envers nous, et comme une partye des vaisseaux hollandois s’estoyent retirez” . Now he is to know that the Huguenot admiral (Soubise, identified from context) “a suivy depuis sept ou huict jours avec le reste de sa flotte; la route des premiers par l’ordre des estatz et sans permission de Sa Ma(jes)té ny de Mons(ieu)r l’Admiral, et dans la conioncture de la conclusion de la paix” . The Dutch squadron lent to the King against La Rochelle had sailed home on its own States’ orders, while the peace was being concluded. And Savoy’s push for war. The prince of Piedmont reached Paris on Monday the 9th, surprising Longueville and the maréchal de Créquy who were to have met him, and saluted the King out hunting in the warren at Saint-Germain. Once the King is back he will begin to treat, and all his propositions “tendent à engager le Roy à la guerre avec l’Espagne, (et que) la Seig(neu)rie de Venize contribue comme faict l’Angleterre et Holande” . Herbault replies that Sa Majesté “escoutera tout ce qu’il luy sera representé, et scaura bien prendre la resolution convenable au bien de ses affaires” . Six weeks later the King did so, settling with Spain separately at Monzón and leaving Venice and Savoy out of it. A closing practical passage, also part-ciphered, weighs keeping the ordinary courier route against going by the Grisons, rejected for “d’autres longueurs et incommoditez, outre la despense”.

That correspondence, together with the word-for-word identity of the two copies' clear text, is what licenses reading no. 25 from no. 26. Deriving the key group by group would need the groups aligned to the glossed words, which the decipherer's placement only loosely indicates; that is left undone. It is not needed for the reading, and the volume holds some thirty further letters of 1625–26 in the same cipher, nearly all with decipherments, for anyone who wants the table.
