His Majesty awaits news from you on the departure of Monsieur the Legate to go to Spain, and on the last resolution in which he will have left **[cipher: the Pope as to the sending of these troops into the Valt(elline)]**, of which we hope soon to be enlightened, **[cipher: since this affair well deserves the sending of an express courier]** … **[cipher: principally if the Pope were to take sides]**. The King came back yesterday from Saint-Germain-en-Laye, where he has also been some days. His health is good, thank God, except for one foot, where he has felt some pain because of a nail growing into the flesh. This inconvenience obliged him yesterday to keep to his bed; what I have been able to do since his return has been to report to him the principal points of your despatches. Private matters have been put off, which prevents me from satisfying the memorandum of Monsieur the Cardinal Bevilacqua in favour of the Sieur Horatio Giraldi, for that gentleman of the house of Anguillara. He obtained some time ago the letters of naturalisation he desired, through the mediation of Monsieur the Cardinal de La Valette. As for the proposal made to you by the Sieur **[cipher: de Santriny ⟨?⟩]** in the name of that so-called count of **[cipher: Montembelans ⟨?⟩]**, I shall have [word] from you and shall reply by another particular letter before the ordinary post leaves. Monsieur the Marquis de Rambouillet has not left for Spain, and I think he will still delay some days. Care will be taken that the Spaniards cannot take any advantage of the office of compliment with which he is charged, and that nothing passes there to the prejudice of the King's dignity. The news of the promotion of cardinals has been well received here, and in particular the choice of Monsieur the Cardinal de Marquemont. His Majesty is replying to the letter he received from him on this subject, and testifies to him the consent he gives to his election. You will accompany this demonstration, if you please, with the customary offices fitting to the occasion. As for the other cardinals, writing to them will be deferred until they have informed the King of their new dignity, and until we have received an account of them all, of the weight and merit of their persons. I wrote to you on the 6th of this month under cover to Monsieur Marini, by an express courier whom Ambassador Contarini was sending to Venice, and gave you the news of the conclusion of the peace with those of the so-called reformed religion. I send you a duplicate of that despatch, with the copy of the act that binds them. This resolution grows firmer from day to day; it has public approval, even from those who have always most loudly advised chastisement and war against the Huguenots. It is true that the affairs of this state needed this **[cipher: respite, and that the burden of a double war could no longer be borne. I admit that the affections of our neighbours who profess this so-called reformed religion were greatly altered]**. You will have seen what I wrote to you before of the **[cipher: conduct of the English towards us, and how a part of the Dutch ships had withdrawn]**. You will now know that **[cipher: the admiral Soubise ⟨?⟩ has followed, seven or eight days since, with the rest of his fleet; the route of the first [ships] by order of the States, and without leave of His Majesty or of Monsieur the Admiral, and at the juncture of the conclusion of the peace]**. I even doubt, if the war had continued, whether the English and the others **[cipher: …]**. Monsieur the Prince of Piedmont arrived in this city last Monday, the 9th of this month, having surprised Monsieur de Longueville and Monsieur the Marshal de Créquy, who were appointed to go to meet him. The next day he went to greet the King, who was hunting in the warren of Saint-Germain. Now that His Majesty has returned, he will begin to treat of affairs. All these proposals **[cipher: tend to engage the King in war with Spain, (and that) the Signoria of Venice contribute as England and Holland do]**. But His Majesty **[cipher: will listen to all that is put to him, and will know well how to take the resolution fitting to the good of his affairs]**. I recognise the trouble that you and I suffer from the delay of our ordinary posts, the last bearer of your despatch of the 26th of last month having arrived only two days ago. It is also considered that, if we changed the old route and took that of the Grisons, other delays and inconveniences would be found there, besides the expense. That is why **[cipher: so that]** we must continue this same route until **[cipher: (the) affairs are further declared]**, and we shall be **[cipher: … rather by extraordinary couriers … (when the) affairs require it]**. I kiss your hands humbly, and beg you to believe me always, Monsieur, your humble and very [obedient] servant, **Phelippeaux** Paris, this 13th of February 1626

George Lasry’s plaintexts, on the DECODE records since 2020, are the decipherment of these letters. On 22 October 2026 each letter was decoded again with his key from the DECODE transcription, compared with his plaintext line by line, and written out in the figures’ own spelling ( texts/R785_reading.md and the others, with modern English). Two key values were corrected (292 = by , 435 = next ), 126 in R923 was read as 127 (the Queen), and 31 nomenclator numbers were given values from the alphabetical bands of the codebook ( texts/hm1645_codes.tsv ), shown in {braces}; [?word] is a doubtful word and a bracketed number an open code. R785 is signed “A Cowley”. In R923 the figures give “some forrain [?succour]”, checked on the image, where Lasry read “Lorrain support”. The openings of the three letters: I have very little to add to my last more than to tell you the {business} of the {ship}s [?doth] advance excellently, half the money being already givenn, and the [?remainder] will be got. A lettre also from the Duke of Orleans, writ as wee could have wished, is in the Queen's hands to return tomorrow (R785) I have received this week a large {dispatch} from {Sir} K Digby. The substance is that [?there] is no hope of money from thence but upon new termes proposed by [the] [?Pope] to {Sir} K D: a total takeing away of al the penall lawes (R790) and again the Duke of Lorrain puts us in some little remote hopes, but that ought not to be built upon yet. {Do} I beleive some forrain [?succour] is so like to be had that I already apprelend the comeing togethere of our forces for the releef of [85], least that draw on a battail (R923)

Of the 58 three-digit nomenclator numbers Lasry left in brackets, 31 were given values on 22 October 2026 from the codebook’s alphabetical bands and the context (for example {business}, {ship}, {dispatch}, {Sir}); about 30 stay open (120, 148, 208, 212, 228, 234, 237, 257, 300, 334, 344, 348, 350, 353, 424, 469, 486, 488, 489, 500, 507, 522, 525, 529, 535, 541, 543, 545, and the two-figure 85, a place, and 60). Eleven one- and two-digit figures (205 occurrences; 78 and 77 most often) that have no value in the key. Lasry writes them as “_”. They fall between words (“ST _ GERMAIN”), so they look like word dividers or nulls, although his key file says there are no nulls. This is not settled here. Who “120” is: a writer at St Germain, probably of the queen’s secretariat. R785 is signed “A Cowley”, and its f. 215 is a second letter in the same key. Measured on the words of the readings, R785 reads at 95.5%; R790 (93.0%) and R923 (93.8%) build coherent sentences but stay under the 95% bar, mostly for the open codes above. Tomokiyo’s list of ciphers with no known decipherment still carries these letters.

indus.html

Asko Parpola’s Dravidian readings checked on two independent corpora, then 2,364 hypotheses registered before testing (1,224 held, 1,140 failed), with Linear B and Ur III seal legends as controls. The grammar a reading must fit is set out: an ending slot chosen by the name’s last sign, line breaks that never split a word unit, numerals fixed with what they count. Seal names are individual compositions, as Linear B personal names are. No sign value is established. 4 · pot · 97 · 400 | 806 845 61 407 850 900 740 = the horned archer 255 435 690 740 · 705 33 520 · name + ending, never split by a line break Mohenjo-daro, Harappa and 50 other sites · logo-syllabic script, no accepted decipherment · c. 2600–1900 BCE · attempted, not read The Indus script: Parpola’s decipherment and 3,400 registered tests Parpola’s Dravidian readings checked, then about 640 sets of hypotheses registered before testing, on two independent corpora with Linear B and Ur III seals as controls: the grammar a reading must fit is set out, the Tamil Nadu graffiti are tested against it, and no sign value is established. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 24 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The text Some 4,500 Indus seals, tablets and sherds, most with fewer than five signs; about 400–600 signs, written mostly right to left, with no word dividers, no bilingual and no known language. How it was tried Every count in Parpola’s 2005 lecture and his 1994 readings was rerun on two independent transcriptions. Then hypotheses were written down and committed before the data were looked at, tested, and recorded as held or failed, with replications on held-out samples and controls on two readable scripts (Linear B, Ur III seals). What came of it A detailed grammar without sound values: names end in a slot whose form is chosen by the name’s last sign; line breaks respect word units; numerals are fixed with what they count. The kind of object shapes the text, and the size of a number decides what is counted. Parpola’s star readings rest on one or two seals each, and his later readings are not supported. The graffiti The Tamil Nadu graffiti resemble Indus signs one by one, about as often as simple marks resemble unrelated scripts; they do not combine signs the Indus way, and the Indus-like ones are not the oldest. Still open Everything phonetic, and the language. The tiers that decide a decipherment are near zero (section 9). Corrections and withdrawals are listed in section 10.
indus.html#method

Two transcriptions, tied sign by sign. A database derived from the Interactive Corpus of Indus Texts (ICIT; Wells and Fuls), published with the indus-website project (2,543 objects; a fuller export of 5,680 records with find spots, levels, sizes and materials), and Mahadevan’s 1977 concordance (M77, 2,906 texts). The ICIT signs are numbers only, so they were identified by drawing each in the database’s own font. Aligning the 991 lines the two share puts 96% of signs on a single counterpart; the 1,664 M77 texts missing from ICIT are the replication sample (‘B’) throughout. Parpola’s own transcription (the open digitisation of CISI vol. 1) agrees with ICIT on 92% of sign positions and 98% of last signs. Registered tests. For each set, hypotheses and thresholds were committed to targets/indus/PREDICTIONS.md before any script looked at the data, then run and recorded without moving the threshold; bugs and ill-posed tests are recorded with their corrections. Counts are over distinct texts, so mould copies and sealings of one seal count once. Readable controls: Linear B (DAMOS) and the Ur III seal legends (22,402 impressions, ORACC). The signs this page talks about, with their ICIT numbers and counts: the jar 740, the fish series (220 plain, 235 ‘roof’, 233, 231, 240), the crab 798, the fig 772–786, the fig + crab ligature 777, the eye, the double curve, the pot 700, the numerals, and the copper-tablet signs 806 845 61 407 850. Image: Drawn here in the indus-website font (ICIT sign numbers).
indus.html#parpola

The lecture’s counts mostly hold. The jar 740 is about 10% of all signs and never stands beside itself in South Asia (0 against 4.0 expected). Fish signs are 9.7% of seal signs; the crab stands beside the marked fish, not the plain one. The star names rest on one or two seals. ‘7 + fish’ (Ursa Major) occurs once, ‘fig + fish’ (the North Star) twice (M-172, M-414). The commonest numeral + fish is ‘2 + fish’ (113 texts), not ‘6 + fish’ (8), in three transcriptions and two ways of counting. The numbers before the fish are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 and 12, never 5, although Tamil has a star name for 5. The Tamil check is weak. For 98 picture concepts fixed in advance, some Tamil word begins one of Parpola’s star names 15% of the time (30% with the readings’ sound latitude). Sanskrit gives 19%, Sumerian 10%. Across 2,895 languages (CLICS4) the words for ‘fish’ and ‘star’ coincide in only three, Old Tamil mīn among them, so the first step of the fish readings is distinctive of Dravidian even though the compound check is not. The later readings are not supported. Sixteen readings from 1997, 2008 and 2010 were turned into predictions about how the signs are used. Two held, and both restate the positions the readings were built on (stroked jars open lines; 741 patterns with 740). The caged fish do not pattern with the ‘spear’ 520 they are said to be homophonous with, the two long strokes not with the fish, and ‘six + fish + yoke-carrier’ is not a unit. M-414, a bar seal from Mohenjo-daro, as impressed: an unclear crossed sign, the ‘fig’ and the plain ‘fish’, Parpola’s second ‘fig + fish’, vaṭa-mīn ‘north star’. Image: Corpus of Indus Seals and Inscriptions, vol. 1 (Joshi and Parpola 1987), p. 100, M-414 a.
indus.html#tablets

The copper tablets of Mohenjo-daro carry an inscription on one side and an animal or figure on the other; in some sets a single sign takes the place of the picture. Matching Parpola’s 46 sets to the transcriptions gives seven equations: the fig + crab ligature 777 = the markhor goat and the horned archer; 749 = the markhor goat; 341 = the rhinoceros; 753 = the hare; a lens-shaped sign = the long-horned bull; “3 700 900 165” = a spotted bull. These are the firmest meanings the script offers, and any reading must fit them. No published key gives values to 749, 341 or 753, and none of their glosses names the picture on any anchor text they cover, so every key so far is untested by this gate rather than passing it. The commonest copper-tablet inscriptions, as written (right to left), with the number of copies, the reading order and the picture on the other side. Image: Drawn here in the indus-website font from the ICIT-derived corpus.
indus.html#grammar

Four kinds of text, one vocabulary. A name with its ending, a line ending in a closer, a count, or a bare sequence: only 3 of 2,722 distinct lines fit none. The ending slot is chosen by the name’s last sign. 740, the ‘arrow’ 520, one of a dozen closers, then optionally 400 or 90. The last sign predicts the ending in 95% of Mahadevan’s separate lines; 30 of 30 signs that prefer one ending on ICIT keep it on M77. 740 is the open ending; the 520 names use 26 main words, mostly fish signs, and include the seal closing formula ‘705 / 706 + long 3 + 520’, the long form of the fish names. Names are head-final , grow at the front, and numerals stand before what they count. There is no number agreement and no chain of suffixes. Line breaks respect units. The 30 most tightly bound pairs are never split across a line (0 against about 5), and names are almost never split from their ending. Graphic marks. The cage of four strokes turns a fish into a closer that stands in place of the ending; strokes inside the jar or the U turn the ending into a name element. Other drawn marks (30 pairs from Parpola’s descriptions) keep the sign’s job: they differ from their base less than unrelated signs do. Substitution partners are a property of the sign. Texts identical except at one position put two signs in one slot; a sign’s set of such partners on the ICIT lines recurs on Mahadevan’s (p = 0.001). The method sorts Linear B signs into numerals, measures, ideograms and words (the positive control) and the ICIT signs into numerals, endings, markers and the rest, though not Mahadevan’s; the partner table is in results/substitution_classes.tsv , and a lexicon of 369 recurring units with their sites, object kinds, endings, counts and pictures in results/unit_lexicon.tsv . One system everywhere. Learned at Mohenjo-daro, the grammar parses Harappa almost as well as its own lines; learned on seals it parses tablets, and on late levels the early ones.
indus.html#texts

Seal texts are individual compositions. Capture–recapture across Mohenjo-daro and Harappa puts the population of names at roughly 3,000–5,500, with 92% on one seal, as Linear B personal names of the same length behave. On Ur III seals only the whole legend (name, title, father) is that individual. A name is not tied to its seal’s animal. The object shapes the text, the region does not. Sign context differs by kind of object (seals, tablets, pottery; copper, incised and moulded tablets; kinds of seal), and models that know the object kind predict unseen lines better (4.635 → 4.559 bits per sign, also on sign tokens alone, replicated). Within square seals no sign differs by region: apparent ‘northern’ signs (158, 400, 700) are moulded-tablet signs, and moulded tablets are mostly Harappan. Period, material, shape and workmanship add nothing beyond object kind. Seal size goes with content. Large seals carry 706 and the closing formula and more rare signs; small seals carry 156, 400, 590, doubled signs and repeated texts. Large seals look individual, small ones formulaic. Seals with the long closing formula are larger (30 against 27 mm), and where one name is written both ways the formula copy is the larger seal in 6 of 7, too few to claim. The size of a number decides what is counted. Numbers 1–3 count the fish signs and 803 / 806; numbers 4 and up count 390, 405, 407, 575, 585 and 900, and those large-number units stand at the end of the line (mean position 0.79–0.82 against 0.50–0.66), in every length band. Both hold on M77 and within one numeral series. They are not tied to one object kind (at Mohenjo-daro the large units sit on tablets, at Harappa the small ones do) and do not go with the picture on the object. A Linear B control shows the same split as ordinary bookkeeping: at Knossos sheep, grain, wool and olives take large counts, chariots, women, horses and months small ones, and 9 of 12 skews repeat at Pylos. By that analogy the large-number units are the better candidates for herds and bulk goods, the fish for persons or objects. Wells (2015, pp. 69–70) had noted part of the split. Both groups take endings alike; what sets the large-number units apart is that they stand bare at the line end (21–39% against 1–12%). The measure sign 700 takes a bounded set of values. Before 700 the long strokes read 2, 3 or 4 almost exclusively (1 once in 172 cases, 5 never), on moulded and incised tablets alike. A shortage of 1 is what Linear B measure sub-units show, but the Indus mode of 3–4 matches neither Linear B measures nor discrete counts: a graded unit, or a fixed set of denominations. The stroked jar and U ligatures do not stand where the written-out numeral + sign sequences stand (short-stroke sequences are never written; long-stroke ones share no contexts): a ligature is a form of its own, not an abbreviation. Short labels are different words. Two-sign ‘X + ending’ lines use different heads from texts of five or more signs, on both corpora and within square seals alone; their heads go with the seal’s picture only weakly (p = 0.02, mostly the default bull), unreplicated. Place and time. Within Mohenjo-daro, what a seal says does not depend on where it was found. Between early and late levels the ending slot does not change; the numerals and the way names begin do.
indus.html#type

Numerals before what they count, head-final names, a short class suffix fixed by the noun and no prefixes fit Dravidian and Indo-Aryan and count against Sumerian and Elamite. Against WALS and Grambank these features rule out 85% of language genera (77% of Grambank families); Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, Munda, Burushaski, Turkic, Mongolic, Japanese and Korean remain. Comparisons of name structure first leaned to early Prakrit donor names over Tamil-Brahmi ones; with genre matched, Japanese given names came out nearest, so those statistics cannot pick a language. The one class signal, fish-headed names taking 520, fits a Dravidian person / non-person split and a Sanskrit gender reading alike.
indus.html#claims

Mahadevan’s ‘merchant of the city’ (255 435 690 740) is a real unit in 22 texts at three sites, but it does not behave as a title qualifying nouns. ‘Too little repetition to be writing’ (Farmer, Sproat and Witzel 2004) fails on a genre-matched control: Indus seal lines repeat a sign about as rarely as Ur III seal legends repeat a word. Published keys. A character-model scorer that recovers Ventris’s Linear B key against all 100 shuffles finds no substantial published key reading its claimed language better than its shuffles (Fairservis, Yajnadevam, Parpola, Mahadevan). Fitting values freely picks the wrong language on Linear B (Sanskrit best, Greek last or third), so a free fit is no evidence for a language. Wells. His 1998 thesis lists the CISI objects each of his signs occurs on; 69 of 74 of his signs map cleanly to ICIT through those lists. His ‘dividers’ are mostly the heading recurring mid-line, and signs 1 and 2 do not divide words (as Fuls 2024 argues). His 2015 book proposes values for 13 signs and a volume system (700 + long strokes, one stroke about 40 litres from three measured jars); as predictions about use the values fail (032 is not an ending, 850 does not combine like a syllable sign, 752 + 820 never occurs), and the scribes’ line breaks do not fall at his initial-cluster boundary, though the opener and its marker 1 / 2 / 60 are never split. His 2011 book was not available.
indus.html#graffiti

The Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology and the Indus Research Centre have published 9,486 graffiti from 140 sites (Rajan and Sivanantham; tngraffiti.in), with an Indus parallel in Mahadevan’s numbering for 31 of their 42 base signs, sequences of signs written together, and find site and depth. Using their own parallels, so the tests are not shaped here: Composite marks do not combine signs the Indus way. The corpus’s multi-sign records are ligatured marks; of 193 adjacent component pairs, 62 are Indus neighbours, no more than with the parallels shuffled (p = 0.16) or the signs re-paired (p = 0.14), and their order does not follow Indus order (14 of 32). Graffiti order in general is looser (70.5% consistent against 88.0%), and the graffiti signs that most often enter composites do not correspond to the Indus signs that most often host marks (rho −0.05). The parallels are about what chance gives. The 42 base signs were matched, blind and under one strict standard, against 90 random signs from each of four scripts. Exact parallels: Indus 5–6, Cypro-Minoan 3–11, Linear B 2–4, Linear A 2. At the looser ‘exact or near’ level Indus reaches 57% and Cypro-Minoan 64%: the book’s “nearly 60%” is what simple marks (Y, U, circle, cross, hourglass, a stroke) find in any sign list. The Indus-like graffiti are not the oldest. Within 12 excavated sites they lie no deeper than the rest; at Keeladi, where layers are dated, 74% of the graffiti below 300 cm (5th–6th century BCE) have an Indus parallel against 82% above 200 cm. The book’s positional remarks do not carry over: the jar is the Indus line’s ending, leftmost only because the scripts run in opposite directions; the ladder is too rare to test; ‘the wavy line never stands alone’ is true of Indus but untestable there, and on the graffiti side the corpus’s own data show the wavy line alone 73 times and neither the jar nor the ladder mostly initial.
indus.html#prize

In January 2025 the Government of Tamil Nadu offered one million US dollars for a decipherment “to the satisfaction of archaeological experts”. The work was scored against what such a panel would need ( targets/indus/PROGRESS.md ): Meaning checked against outside evidence: 0.008% of sign tokens (the copper-tablet picture signs; numerals counted apart). One step short of reading, text units that go with one picture across distinct tablets cover about 5% of tokens, confirmed on held-out halves but right only about 5% of the time on unseen tablets: local labels, not portable meanings. The method passes the Linear B control (143 word–ideogram pairs against 2 by chance). Positive control: three of six methods recover Greek from Linear B; dictionary scores and free key fitting do not. Unseen texts: none read. The models are frozen for inscriptions published after the 2022 corpus, but none with sign numbers or usable photographs has been found online. Prediction: 4.559 bits per sign on held-out lines; a hidden sign is guessed first 40% of the time and in the top five 62% (9.6% and 22% by frequency). What would win: values for the seventy or so common signs, reading most tokens as phrases of one language, agreeing with outside evidence, passing the Linear B control and reading texts not used to set the values. The present work supplies the grammar and the tests such a claim must pass; it supplies no readings.
indus.html#open

Open. No sign has a sound value the evidence forces, and the language is not identified. Internal testing has largely run out: the last long runs ended after twenty loops in a row without progress. What is left needs new material: a bilingual, newly published inscriptions (the frozen models wait for them), CISI volumes 2 and 3, Wells 2015. Withdrawn or corrected by later tests (kept in the record): A shortlist of 46 ‘sound signs’ failed all its tests; ‘two numeral systems’ became one in several stroke forms. ‘Office + name’, ‘numeral compounds are local customs’, ‘Mohenjo-daro converges on Harappa’ and ‘Indus names are nearer Indo-Aryan’ were each narrowed or withdrawn by controls. ‘Indus names are personal names’ narrowed to ‘individual compositions’ by the Ur III control. ‘Shared phrases predict a tablet’s picture’ was a favourable split. ‘Regional signs’ were moulded-tablet signs; a ‘writing direction’ model had learned the source corpus; a context gain was the end-of-line token; long-distance sign pairs were repeated phrases; rare signs in long lines were a length effect.

A corrected key for the cipher of the 1573 Polish election embassy: Tomokiyo’s table had its first row displaced by one letter from m onward. The key was recovered from the Court decipherer’s marginal glosses, cut by the gutter on the microfilm, beside this letter and its siblings in BnF fr. 4735. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 4735: f. 124 (no. 51), ff. 154–157 (nos. 60–61), ff. 160, 164, 174, on the Gallica microfilm btv1b9060724s. Not on DECODE. The cipher A homophonic cipher of graphic signs, two or three per common letter, with a dozen signs for syllables and words ( et , car , pour , Allemagne , l’Empereur , me/nous ). How it was deciphered The key was recovered from the Court decipherer’s marginal glosses, cut by the gutter on the microfilm, and from a solver run with those values fixed, checked against shuffled and blind controls. It corrects S. Tomokiyo’s published table, whose first row is shifted by one letter. On 2 and 3 October 2026 the key was extended by about fifteen signs on ff. 154 and 156, and checked sign by sign against Tomokiyo’s current table, which supplied st , il , nous , par and a second t ; ff. 160, 164 and 174 were then transcribed again at full scale. What it says On 26 April, the dangers French travellers met in Germany. On 24 April, the Lithuanian lords’ promise of their vote, the Sultan’s recommendation made “avec ruse”, borrowed money, and to Catherine that by Monday she would be mere des deux plus grans roys du monde . In May, Polish venality and the powers ranged against the election. Measured Signs giving sense, per letter: f. 124 96/100 (96%); to Anjou, ff. 154r–v, 660/677 (97.5%); to Catherine, ff. 156r–v, 921/961 (95.8%); f. 160 91/91; f. 164 203/207 (98.1%); f. 174 123/123. The four letters of 9 May on ff. 182–189 turned out to be in clear. Still open 65 signs in all: line ends lost in the gutter of the microfilm or under the decipherer’s overwriting (Gallica has no other image of the volume), a few single signs, and one word sign on f. 164 that is in no key. Four signs of f. 124’s first passage carry a query.

BnF fr. 4735 is the second of the volumes of “pièces originales et de copies concernant l’histoire de France, 1569–1588” and, from no. 5 to no. 80, the Court’s file of the Polish election embassy: Monluc’s letters from Konin and Warsaw, the Polish memoranda on St Bartholomew, the King’s replies, and the letters of Lanssac and Gilles de Noailles from Warsaw and Płock in April and May 1573. The catalogue marks “avec chiffre et déchiffrement” against Lanssac’s letters of 24 April (nos. 60–61), 1 May (63, 65) and 9 May (70), and “avec chiffre” alone against no. 51 of 26 April. Gallica has the whole volume as a microfilm scan (btv1b9060724s, 614 unlabelled canvases); the folio of no. 51 is 124, canvas 242, not the 126 the catalogue entry here first gave. Fr. 4735 f. 124, upper half: the ciphered opening after “Sire”, the clear itinerary, and the second passage after “j’eusse sans doubte”. The decipherer’s gloss sits in the left margin, cut by the gutter. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 4735 f. 124, via Gallica btv1b9060724s canvas 242. What the catalogue calls the siblings’ decipherments is this same marginal gloss, line by line beside the cipher, on ff. 154, 154v, 156 and 157. The microfilm keeps only the last centimetre or two of each gloss line, but on f. 154v the first line of cipher stands beside “Car je n’ay pas cinquante escuz”, and the cipher line is exactly long enough for it.

Homophonic letters. Separate graphic signs (crosses, bars, figures, letter-like forms) written continuously, with points, commas and short bars as word separators. Common letters have two or three signs: e ✕ ✱ Γ Δ, a ⊤ π H, r ϕ ⊨, s 9 Lo IIII, i ⊢ ϙ, n ſ o-o, u/v o+ ff o+o, m 8 ᥙ, l 3 ⊥, o ꞔ L, t ʓ ттт, p y N, d ‡, c 7 ⋔, g ∞, f o-, h +, qu ꞗ. Syllable and word signs. et ♁, nt ꝸ, st 8 with a dot, de ᒐ, ou ᛏ, ns Λ, car Z, pour †, and Allemagne as a Z with a lower curl. Over the 741 signs transcribed from f. 124 and the first blocks of ff. 154 and 156, the merged frequencies are French: e-signs 17.6 %, then r, a, s, n, u, t, o. Tomokiyo’s table. His “Lansac’s Cipher” (cryptiana, French Ciphers during the Reigns of Charles IX and Henry III ) has the right signs but its first row is displaced by one letter from m onward (his ſ m, L n, б p, ⊨ q, 9 r, ʓ s, o+ t read n, o, qu, r, s, t, u ), his Γ = i is e , his ‡ = h is d , and the “pour” cross is the letter h in one of its two shapes. The corrected table with the evidence for each sign is targets/lanssac/key.tsv .

Each new sign was checked in the siblings before it was kept. Simulated annealing over the whole transcription (French 5-gram model, symbol to letter or short code, the crib letters held fixed). The free signs come out the same across seeds and give words in the siblings that the cribs never touched and the glosses confirm: les dangiers , causé , l’autre , beaucoup , grant seigniur , du monde , changement , sur la teste , recommandé , doubte ou vous mettre . Decoding of f. 124 : each sign was given its candidate values and the best-scoring sequence under the same model was kept. Passage one comes out as despuis les dangiers qu’encontrent en Allemagne les françois qui passent et vostre ser… , matching the three marginal fragments “…es dangier”, “…d’Allemagne”, “qui passent”. Controls. The key with the crib letters fixed scores −2193 to −2198 on the real sign order and −2924 to −3009 on three shufflings of the same signs. A blind run with nothing fixed reaches a higher score (−2033) but recovers only 6 of the 21 crib letters: on a transcription this noisy the language model alone does not find the key; the cribs and the glosses do, and the model then fills the rest consistently.

Cipher passages in brackets; sixteenth-century spelling kept; ? marks an uncertain sign, braces a run not deciphered Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573. Sire, [despuis? les dangiers qu’encontrent en Allemagne les françois qui passent, et vostre ser{o r h e}] Les empeschementz et les plus grandes causes qui ayent esté depuis deux {ans} … toute la Turinge, Misnie et Marche de Brandebourg m’ont tellement retardé que je n’arrivay en Polongne à Mezeritz que le vingt-cinquiesme de febvrier. Et sans la faveur que j’ay receue d’aulcuns des serviteurs et pensionnaires de vostre Majesté, principalement des Sieurs Alexandre de Militiz et George Luelz(?), qui me y ont accompagné avec bonne et forte troupe de leurs amis et assisté de leurs moyens, j’eusse sans doubte [pour le moins esté retenu ou empesché de passer oultre. Mais], la grace à Dieu, je me suis rendu il y a desjà long temps avec Monsieur de Valence, lequel m’a enseigné l’estat auquel estoient les affaires qu’il a bien et dignement commencées et continuées jusques icy, et dont j’ay faict ung recueil ensemble de ce que j’ay peu juger, lequel j’envoye à vostre Majesté. Et ne sçachant à présent rien digne d’escrire oultre le contenu audict recueil, sinon que j’ay receu la lettre qu’il a pleu à vostre Majesté m’escrire du xxiii(?) de febvrier, en obéissant à laquelle je me fauldray(?) à me comporter de sorte que j’espère que le bien de vostre service et les affaires qui sont à promouvoir par deçà en demeureront advancez. Je priray le Créateur vous donner, Sire, en très parfaicte santé très contente et longue vie. De Warsauvia, le xxvi e d’avril 1573. English translation Sire, [since the dangers that the French who pass through meet in Germany, and your ser{vice?}…] The hindrances, and the greatest causes there have been these two {years} … all through Thuringia, Meissen and the Mark of Brandenburg, delayed me so much that I did not reach Poland, at Mezeritz, until the twenty-fifth of February. And without the favour I received from some of your Majesty’s servants and pensioners, chiefly the Sieurs Alexander von Miltitz and Georg Luelz(?), who accompanied me there with a good strong troop of their friends and helped me with their means, I should without doubt [at the least have been detained or prevented from passing on. But], thank God, I joined Monsieur de Valence a good while ago, who has told me the state in which the affairs stood that he has so well and worthily begun and carried on until now, and of which I have made a summary, together with what I have been able to judge, which I send to your Majesty. And knowing nothing at present worth writing beyond what that summary contains, except that I have received the letter your Majesty was pleased to write me on the 23rd(?) of February, in obedience to which I shall not fail to conduct myself so that I hope your service and the affairs to be advanced here will profit by it, I pray the Creator to give you, Sire, in most perfect health a most contented and long life. From Warsaw, the 26th of April 1573. The Miltitz were Saxon nobles in French pay; Mezeritz (Międzyrzecz) is the first Polish town on the road from Frankfurt an der Oder to Poznań. The “dangers” are the hostility to Frenchmen in Protestant Germany after St Bartholomew’s Day, which is why this passage is in cipher and the itinerary is not. Lanssac reached Monluc at Warsaw in time for the election Diet, which had opened on 5 April; Anjou was elected on 11 May. The recueil he announces is no. 52 in the volume, “Estat des affaires de Pollongne selon que le Sr de Lanssac y a peu aprendre”, in clear.

The catalogue credits Lanssac’s letters of 24 April, 1 May and 9 May with a “déchiffrement”. It is the Court decipherer’s note in the outer margin, and the microfilm keeps only the last word or two of each of its lines; the cipher passages themselves cannot be recovered from the scan. With the key they decipher in full, but for one word sign. The first pass (17 September) left runs open; on 3 October 2026 the three letters were transcribed again from the full-size scans, with the sign groups aligned to the words ( ct_f160.txt , ct_f164.txt , ct_f174.txt , and read_f160_f174.md ). It found that the first cipher line of f. 164 had been skipped, read the four open runs of f. 164, and showed the open run of f. 174 to be a misdivision. Measured: f. 160 91 of 91 signs, f. 164 203 of 207 (98.1%), f. 174 123 of 123. Braces mark what is not deciphered. Fr. 4735 f. 174 (canvas 329): the six ciphered lines of the 9 May letter and the gloss beside them — “…la volunté et / …du Grand / …de l’Empereur / …de l’Empire / …de Spaigne / …et du / …Suède, qui tou[s] / …bandez contr[e] / …Majesté”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 4735 f. 174, via Gallica btv1b9060724s canvas 329. To Charles IX, Warsaw, 1 May 1573 (f. 160). … que pour en envoyer devant selon que les occasions des affaires premièrement surviennent. [Car je veoy que ceste nation est autant vénale et sujette à se laisser gaigner par argent comme sont les Alemans, leurs voisins.] Ce jourd’huy ilz mettent en délibération s’ilz doibvent prendre pour Roy ung Piaste ou ung prince estrangier, mais on sçait bien quelle en doibt estre la résolution. To the duc d’Anjou, Warsaw, 1 May 1573 (f. 164). … c’est de latin et d’argent, et à bonne quantité, car il y aura de quoy l’employer [en toutes sortes pour venir à vostre desir]. … les traverses de nos contraires qui n’y espargnent rien pour nous empescher, [car si jusques cy {word sign} a despendu trente mil escus en ceste negotiation, l’Empereur en y a despendu plus de trois cens mil, et n’y faict toutefois riens qui vaille pour soy; mais seulement il l[e] trouble vostre desseing, faisant le pis qu’il peult contre vous.] Encores ne veulx-je faillir, Monseigneur, de vous ramentevoir … que vous fassiez donner ordre que les navires soient prestz pour l’embarquement. To Charles IX, Płock, 9 May 1573 (f. 174). … ayant esté employé en un affaire de telle importance et qui est reüssy tant heureusement [contre la volunté et menées du Grant Seigneur, de l’Empereur, des princes de l’Empire, du Roy d’Espaigne, du Moscovite et du Roy de Suède, qui tous estoient bandez contre vostre Majesté]. Si est-ce que j’auray encores plus d’occasion de louer Dieu si je suis tant heureux que vostre Majesté me juge digne d’estre employé en ce second … English 1 May, to the King. For I see that this nation is as venal and as ready to let itself be won by money as are the Germans, their neighbours. — 1 May, to Anjou. … in every way, to come to what you desire. … For if until now {word sign} has spent thirty thousand écus in this negotiation, the Emperor has spent more than three hundred thousand in it, and yet does nothing in it worth anything for himself; he only troubles your design, doing the worst he can against you. — 9 May, to the King. … an affair of such weight, which has succeeded so happily against the will and the intrigues of the Grand Seigneur, of the Emperor, of the princes of the Empire, of the King of Spain, of the Muscovite and of the King of Sweden, who were all leagued against your Majesty. The 9 May list is the field of the 1573 election as the French embassy saw it: Archduke Ernest for the Emperor and Spain, Ivan IV, John III of Sweden, and a Habsburg-leaning party among the German princes. The “Grand Seigneur” (the Sultan) is the surprise, since the Porte was generally reckoned to favour the French candidate; every sign of the group now deciphers, with one irregularity forced by the gloss (Γ, elsewhere e , stands for the a of Grant ). On f. 164 the Habsburg outlay of 300,000 is set against 30,000 écus spent by a party written with a single word sign that is in no key and whose gloss the gutter has taken: the King’s side, or a Polish faction. New values from these leaves (4 = b, three strokes = z as well as t, the tailed 4 = p, Λ = ns, the hooked C = qu, the 6-like sign = o, Δ = g, the o with cross below = et) are listed in the notes; the last makes f. 124’s “retenu ou empesché” rather “retenu et empesché”.

Lanssac’s two long letters of 24 April 1573 (nos. 60 and 61) carry the most cipher in the file: 37 lines on f. 154 to the duc d’Anjou and two blocks on f. 156, with most of the verso, to Catherine de Médicis. Both have the decipherer’s running text in the margin. On the rectos it is in the inner margin and the microfilm keeps only its line ends; on the versos it is in the outer margin and survives nearly whole. On 2 October 2026 all four cipher pages were transcribed again from the full-size scans, with the sign groups aligned to the words so that each group could be scored as deciphered or not, and the key was applied and extended. On 3 October every open group was cut out at twice the scale and read again against Tomokiyo’s current table; both letters are now over 95%. Fr. 4735 f. 154v, the head of the verso of the letter to Anjou: the cipher with clear words written between its runs ( Aussi estois je party ), and the decipherer’s gloss in the margin, “Car je n’ay pas cinquante escuz / et y ay emprunté plus de xv c …”. The first cipher line was the crib that fixed eleven signs. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 4735 f. 154v, via Gallica btv1b9060724s canvas 297. Page Letter Signs deciphered f. 154r to Anjou, Warsaw, 24 April 439 of 454 (96.7%) f. 154v the same letter 221 of 223 (99.1%) Letter to Anjou 660 of 677 (97.5%) f. 156r to Catherine, Warsaw, 24 April 307 of 316 (97.2%) f. 156v the same letter 614 of 645 (95.2%) Letter to Catherine 921 of 961 (95.8%) Four pages 1,581 of 1,638 (96.5%) The counts are of cipher signs that give sense in the reading, measured with measure.py over the word-aligned transcriptions. A first pass over f. 156v at reduced scale gave 67.2%; the second, line by line at full scale (88.2%), found 130 signs the first had merged or skipped and drops the nine the writer struck through; the third, at twice the scale on every open group, gave 95.2%. f. 154v rose from 92.0% to 99.1% the same way: one “sign” of the first pass was not a sign, and the line past the end of the gloss reads le[s] nostre si inferieur . As a control, the raw decode of each page with no hand choices scores −1.93 to −2.49 per character on a French letter model of c. 1600, against −4.4 to −4.7 for the same signs shuffled. To Anjou (f. 154) [clear: … Depuis la conclusion desquelz] {…} j’ay aprins deux choses, l’une qui me donne gaing de cause, l’autre qui me trouble beaucoup. La premiere est que j’ay esté au devant des Lituans, les chefz desquelz m’ont promis ne donner leur voeu à aultre que à vous, [clear: qui sera de telle importance que] avec la bonne part que nous avons au royaume sans doubte ou vous mettre ceste grant couronne sur la teste, si la recommandation du Grant Seigneur, laquelle il a faicte de vous comme j’estime avec ruse par le vaivode qui(?) de la Valaquie, qui est(?) {5 signs} ameine quelque inespéré changement, qui est le second poinct qui me donne une traverse, de laquelle avec l’aide {4 signs} de Dieu nous esperons neaumoins sortir. [f. 154v] Car je n’ay pas cinquante e[sc]us, combien que j’en ay emprunté plus de quinze cens. [clear: Aussi estois je party] bien belistre pour venir si loing et demeurer si longtemps et faire contrecarre à celuy qui [par] beaucoup de grans dons ne sçauront vaincre le[s] nostre, si inferieur {2} … Et espere que dans peu de jours tous ceulx-là avec beaucoup d’autres seront vos subjectz. The Lithuanian lords have promised Anjou their vote, which with his party in the kingdom makes the crown certain, unless the Sultan’s recommendation of him, made (Lanssac thinks) with guile through the voivode of Wallachia, brings some unexpected change. Lanssac has not fifty écus left and has borrowed more than fifteen hundred; within days, he expects, the electors will all be Anjou’s subjects. Every surviving fragment of the recto gloss agrees with the decipherment (“…causé l’autre”, “…doubte ou vous”, “…sur la teste”, “…grand seigneur”, “…par le Vaynode de”), and the verso gloss gives the first block word for word. To Catherine de Médicis (f. 156) Fr. 4735 f. 156r, the first cipher block of the letter to Catherine, after the clear Vous advisant, Madame, que : “… vous serez mere des deux plus grans roys du monde …”. In the left margin, the ends of the gloss lines that the gutter has not taken. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 4735 f. 156r, via Gallica btv1b9060724s canvas 300. [clear: Vous advisant, Madame, que] {5 signs} les choses sont de present en telz termes que j’espere dedans lundi prochain vous serez mere des deux plus grans roys du monde, s’il n’advient quelque changement de voluntez pour quelque grande {1} inopinée occasion … il me semble que ce ne sera pas mal faict {2} vostre Majesté envoyast quelqu’ung {1} vers le roy de Dennemarc, non pour luy demander passage … mais bien pour luy faire entendre que les Imperiaulx, nos ennemis en ce faict … [f. 156v] Mais de crainte que l’Empereur {[cepen]dant} il n’y soit prevenu, et que l[e] {…} roy de Dennemarc [clear: ayant obtemperé à sa volunté, ne] nous donnast beaucoup d’affaires de ce costé-là, à cause d’estroit qui n’a pas demie lieue de {la(rge)}, {1} des fortz situez des deux costez de par terre. … de mectre à la mercy de ceulx {1} qui … Mais se monstrent estre ennemis jurez de {1} France, et specialement de Monseigneur, et lesquelz [so]nt extremement marrys s’il fault qu’il se voient enclos de deux si puissantz roys comme ilz seront. … {6} ces seigneurs demanderont qu’il ameine quatre mil gascons … recueilliez le plus d’argent querez(?) ensem{ble af}in que … ambassadeurs porter la couronne à {Monseigneur, et y ar}riveront vers luy, vous ne soiez lors empeschée d’en trouver. Ca[r] … aussi à commencer à faire estat que {[le]urs} navires seront propres à l’embarquement, et de faire mettre en ordre les galleres pour pouvoir servir. … {de ceste nation … servi}teurs, il n’y en a que quatre con[tr]e nous, et que toute la noblesse crie pour avoir ung roy, et nommement veule[nt Monseigneur]. By Monday next, Lanssac tells the Queen Mother, she will be “mother of the two greatest kings in the world” unless some sudden change of minds intervenes. He advises sending someone to the King of Denmark, not to ask passage but to tell him what the Imperialists are doing, because he fears the Emperor will forestall them and that Denmark, bending to the Emperor’s will, could make trouble at the Sound, less than half a league wide and fortified on both sides. Going by land would put Anjou at the mercy of the German princes, who “show themselves sworn enemies of France, and especially of Monseigneur”, and are “extremely sorry” to find themselves shut in between two such powerful kings; the road by Italy and Dalmatia is too long and costly. The Polish lords will ask him to bring four thousand Gascons; Catherine should gather all the money she can, so that she is not then hard put to find it when the embassy comes to bring the crown, and should reckon on the ships and have the galleys made ready. Of the Polish lords only four are against them, and the whole nobility cries out for a king, and namely for Anjou. Here the cipher corrects the decipherer, who wrote “si monsieur estoit ennemy d’icy de la France”: with the stacked 8 as st and the clover sign as -nt , the signs read se monstrent estre ennemis jurez , and the enemies are the German princes, not Monsieur. Anjou was elected on 11 May. The end of the letter, f. 157r, is in clear, with a postscript on the Diet (forty thousand horse, the great tent, the Emperor’s ambassadors). The new signs About fifteen signs were added to the key on these pages: a pronoun sign for me and nous (“qui me donne”, “que nous avons”, “ne nous donnast”), a barred N for il and a looped barred N for est , word signs for bien and par , the clover sign for -ment / -nt , a footed Π for t , further signs for qu and x , Tomokiyo’s u sign (confirmed), and 4 = b confirmed on eleven words. On 3 October the key was compared sign by sign with Tomokiyo’s current table: his st (stacked 8), il , nous , par , q and t agree and were adopted, and an f sign proposed on 2 October was withdrawn (it is the st ). The barred-N forms are now told apart on every page: the plain barred N is il throughout, the looped form on f. 124 stays p in despuis , and the “N = a ” of f. 160 was a misread tall T. The hand writes mectre , ameine , neaumoins , nommé . The full list is in key.tsv . The letters of 9 May are in clear The catalogue and the earlier notes here expected Lanssac’s four other letters of 9 May from Płock (ff. 182–189: to Anjou, now king-elect, to Catherine, to the secretary of state Pierre Brulart, and to his father Louis de Saint-Gelais) to be in the same key with a marginal decipherment. The images show all four written wholly in clear, with addresses on ff. 183v, 185v, 187v and 189v: the election, Balagny carrying the news, and requests for favour and for the costs Lanssac had borne. The cipher letter of that day is the one to Charles IX, f. 174, in section 05.
lanssac.html#residuals

Despuis rests on two signs read once each (ꝛ as de , the looped barred N as p , rechecked on the image on 3 October: read il , as the plain barred N is elsewhere, the word gives no French); the gloss fragment “…es dangier” is compatible with “…uis les dangiers” but the gutter takes the start of the line. François : the signs give fran-c-o-r-s ; the seventh sign must be the i sign ϙ, which this hand writes close to the r sign ϕ, or the word is another. Qui rests on the gloss; the cipher has ꟿ Γ, and ꟿ reads i in mais . Et vostre ser is followed by four signs that read o r h e under the key; service with one misread sign is the likely word and is left in braces. Two forms of the et sign ( et and nt ) and of the cross ( h and pour ) are told apart by context, not by shape, in the present transcription. The election letters of section 05: f. 164’s word sign before a despendu trente mil escus is in no key, Tomokiyo’s included, and the gloss beside it is cut (no key material); a stray c between pour and venir and the two signs of l[e] in il l[e] trouble , which give li , are single signs no value fits. On f. 174 two irregularities are forced by the gloss: Γ for the a of Grant , and Moscovite written without its second o . Tomokiyo’s “f. 331” is not a Lanssac item in the BnF notice. Gallica holds only this one microfilm of fr. 4735; a colour scan or the manuscript would be needed to go further. Simulated annealing of the remaining signs on a French 5-gram model with the crib letters fixed; blind and shuffled-order controls run on the same data. Third pass (3 October 2026): every open group of ff. 154–156 cut out at twice the scale and read again; the key compared sign by sign with Tomokiyo’s current table; ff. 160, 164 and 174 transcribed again at full scale with word-aligned groups; the share of signs giving sense measured per letter ( measure.py --letters ); controls rerun (−1.94 to −2.49 per character against −3.8 to −4.7 shuffled).

Ca[r] [ilz halteront sa venue par deça le plus qu'ilz pourront pour beaucoup de raisons. Il ne sera hors de > propos] aussi à commencer à faire estat que {[le]urs} navires seront propres à l'embarquement, et de faire mettre en > ordre les galleres pour pouvoir servir. [J'en ose parler avec telle asseurance, Madame, d'aultant que] {de ceste > nation … servi}teurs, il n'y en a que quatre con[tr]e nous, et que toute la noblesse crie pour avoir ung roy, et > nommement veule[nt Monseigneur]. Neaumoins [toutes choses sont en la main de Dieu …] Where pass 3 departs from the decipherer: he wrote "si monsieur estoit ennemy d'icy de la France"; the cipher, with the stacked 8 as *st* (Tomokiyo) and the clover as *-nt*, reads "se monstrent estre ennemis jurez de … France" — the German princes, not Monsieur. Pass 2's "mon frere" (from a supposed *f* value) is withdrawn. Sense: Lanssac fears that the Emperor will forestall them and that the King of Denmark, bending to the Emperor's will, could make trouble at the Sound, less than half a league wide and fortified on both sides; going by land would put Anjou at the mercy of the German princes, who show themselves sworn enemies of France and of Anjou and are extremely sorry to see themselves shut in between two such powerful kings; the road by Italy and Dalmatia is too long and costly; the Polish lords will ask him to bring 4,000 Gascons; Catherine should gather all the money she can so that when the embassy comes to bring the crown she is not then embarrassed to find it, should reckon on the ships being fit for embarking and have the galleys made ready. Of the Polish lords only four are against them; the whole nobility cries out for a king, and namely wants Anjou. ## Unread groups and why f. 156r: the 5-sign opening group (one sign struck through by the writer, the rest give *nt n c d ou*), one sign before *inopinée*, the 2-sign group *ff G* before *vostre Majesté* (gloss "…mal faict" ends the line), one sign after *quelqu'ung* (x5, a figure like "S" with bar: *homme*?). f. 156v: 31 tokens in 12 groups (listed in ct_f156v.txt with a note on each), all retried at 2x in pass 3. Three letters of Honoré Mauroy La Verrière in his own key sheet, Tomokiyo’s Nevers key no. 57, which setsunaatto matched to him. The letter of 9 July 1593 is deciphered in full; the key reproduces the office’s decipherment of the 13 July letter in a blind test; and it deciphers 94.8% of the Poissy letter of 12 August (fr. 3985 f. 58). 347 · 184Pn · 285 · 927# · 59 · ✗ vous estes necessaire pres du Roy 347 = vous · 285 = necessaire · ✗ = le Roy Châlons, Courgenay, Poissy → the duc de Nevers · Nevers key no. 57, a syllabic code of figures and signs · July–August 1593 Laurière to the duc de Nevers, July–August 1593 to Duke of Nevers Go to the full text ↓ Three letters written in the weeks around Henri IV’s abjuration, in the writer’s own key sheet, which an outside contributor matched to him: one deciphered group by group, one checked blind against the office’s decipherment, and one 94.8% deciphered. Measured on the words of the readings, f. 58 reads at 95.7%; no. 55 (93.3%) and no. 10 (90.4%) build coherent sentences but stay under the 95% bar. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read after matching with key from external sources · Extent: partial (96% of the cipher) With setsunaatto (solution, verification) · Also credited · Satoshi Tomokiyo (pointer to a source) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) At a glance External key matched · partial (96% of the cipher) The letters Honoré Mauroy La Verrière (catalogued as Laurière) to Louis de Gonzague, duc de Nevers: Châlons, 9 July 1593; Courgenay, 13 July 1593; Poissy, 12 August 1593. Where BnF français 3625 no. 55 (f. 66r) and no. 10 (f. 10r); français 3985 f. 58. Catalogue item 30, with the Champagne news-letters of 1590–91. The cipher Tomokiyo’s Nevers key no. 57 (fr. 3995 ff. 102–103), endorsed “Mons r de La Verriere”: two signs per letter, syllables, doubles, words in alphabetical order, places and name signs. How it was deciphered setsunaatto identified the key sheet as the writer’s and deciphered no. 55 with it; a blind test on no. 10 reproduces the office’s interlinear decipherment; f. 58 was then deciphered here with the key and checked against its interlinear. What it says Nevers must be with the King so that his assembly is not put off; Lorraine will treat only once the King is Catholic; the prince de Conty, the Montmorency house, La Trémoille, and papal letters against the Cardinal de Bourbon. Still open 13 tokens of f. 58: six illegible on the microfilm, seven with certain values that give no sense. These letters were filed with the Champagne news-letters of 1590–91 to Nevers, which use other ciphers and have their own pages: the two-digit alphabet of June 1590 and Bienvenut’s name code .

Fr. 3625 f. 66r, the first cipher run of no. 55, with “come” written over 347 (vous). Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3625 f. 66r, via Gallica (btv1b52511322v). The OAI item list of fr. 3625 places no. 55 at f. 66r (canvas 143): Laurière’s letter, “Chalons ce IX juillet 1593”, clear French with eight cipher runs (86 groups) in a mixed code of figures, letters and signs. The first pass (21 September) aligned the interlinear decipherment of his 13 July letter (no. 10, f. 10r) into a twelve-entry table and decoded 19 groups in fragments. That table turned out to be one group out of step: ✗ is le Roy , not que ; 335 is soit ; 141 is catholique ; “101 54y+” is au-ro-i-t , not Sa Majesté . The key (29 September 2026). setsunaatto (GitHub issue 13) identified the writer’s own key sheet: Tomokiyo’s Nevers key no. 57, BnF fr. 3995 ff. 102–103, endorsed “Mons r de La Verriere”, “Chartres 1593 fevrier” (Honoré Mauroy La Verrière, whom the catalogue calls Laurière). Each letter has two signs; the figures 1–72 are syllables, row + 14 × vowel (the sheet heads its grid “ba 1, be 15, bi 29, bo 43, bu 57”); 73–98 are double letters (92 = pr); 99–353 are words in alphabetical order (184 est, 285 necessaire, 347 vous); overbarred figures are provinces and towns; special signs stand for the Pope, the King, Lorraine, Gondi and the Grand Duke of Tuscany. Every entry used below was checked here on the sheet, and lines 1–2 of the issue’s transcription against the page and against the first pass’s transcription, group for group. The issue also tested the key blind on no. 10: 80% of the office’s glossed letters fall in matching runs of four or more, against a shuffle maximum of 30% (section 03). Run Deciphered 1, after “pour vous faire resouvenir” vous estes necessaire pres du Roy afin qu’il ne retarde d’ung jour son assemblée, ce que ses ennemys luy donne[r]ont tout l’empeschemen[t] qu’ilz pourront pour luy faire prandre autre dessein 2, after “Revenant a mon voiage” [le duc de Lorraine] montre desir de traiter, mais necessaire avant que [le Roy] soit catholique 2b, before “ce moquans de cela” quoy fait une election 3, after “francoir” s’il veult atandre la volonté du [Pape], non aussitost qu’il sera catholique, qui la traitera 3b, after “et en donne sa parolle” [le Cardinal de Gondy] pour [le grand duc de Toscane] The bracketed letters are missing in the cipher itself. The letter was written sixteen days before Henri IV’s abjuration at Saint-Denis: Laurière presses Nevers to be at the King’s side so that the assembly is not put off, reports that Lorraine will treat only once the King is Catholic, and that the Leaguers mock the idea of an election. He also asks whether the Pope’s consent is to be awaited.

Fr. 3625 f. 10r, run R3 of no. 10: “185 25 29̄ 18 12 344 234 …”, with the office’s decipherment written above it, “et qui ne se fera pour son effort maintenant”. Key no. 57 gives “et que [l’Espagne] fera tout hault effort maintenant”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3625 f. 10r, via Gallica (btv1b52511322v). No. 10, Laurière’s letter of four days later, has the office’s decipherment written between the lines, and it was not used to fit key no. 57. (Issue 13 used one of its runs to check which y-shaped sign is e and which is i; with the two swapped, the blind score below falls only from 157 to 152.) setsunaatto ( pull request 15 , 30 September 2026) transcribed five of its runs from crops that hide the glosses, fixed that transcription, and only then read the glosses. The other eight glossed runs were transcribed with the glosses in view. The score counts the gloss letters that fall in runs of four or more that the key reproduces; the control shuffles the signs of each run, 2000 times. Runs Gloss letters in matching runs of four or more Shuffled control 5 runs transcribed blind 157 of 196 (80%) 33.8 ± 6.3, at most 58 the same, without the run first seen with its gloss 121 of 160 (76%) 21.8 ± 5.0, at most 42 8 runs transcribed with the glosses in view 311 of 354 (88%) 97.7 ± 10.6, at most 129 Checked here before merging: the script reproduces these figures, and the first pass’s own transcription of three of the blind runs (21 September, before the key was known) agrees with the blind one on every figure group but one. Of the 21 word numbers the contributor added from the sheet, 18 were found on f. 103r exactly as given (100 aux, 122 bien, 150 congnoystre, 234 hault, 303 pouvoir, 307 quant and the rest); the other three were not viewed. The sheet’s alphabet rows also showed that our key file had c and h the wrong way round (μ stands under C, the c-shaped sign under H), as the contributor had pointed out. That is corrected. Apart from spelling and gaps in the gloss, key and office disagree in one run. Over “25 29”, where the 29 carries a bar with turned-down ends (the mark of a province number: 29 is “L’Espaigne ou Espagnols” on the sheet), the office wrote qui ne se ; the key gives que [l’Espagne] . Over “344 234” it wrote pour son . The figures are clear on the page and the sheet makes them tout hault , but the phrase is faire tout son effort , so Laurière probably meant 334 ( son ) and wrote 234. Among the other runs: ne pouvoir recongnoistre le Roy que premieremen ilz n’eusse eu la volonté du Pape, qui ne viendront jamais a c’est … que par force et que [l’Espagne] fera tout hault [son?] effort maintenant pour anpescher que le Pape ne le resoive, qui seroit tousjours une extreme longueur pour sortir du mal que nous tenons que [le marquis de Pont] suivra le duc de Lorraine (the marquis’s sign is close to the key’s, not identical: grade M) a l’assemblée ou elle sera tres necessaire One run has no gloss at all. After “que nous avions despesché” it reads: [le grand duc de Toscane] quant [le Roy] nous bailla par escrit (sa?) volonté. The barred 3 before volonté is not on the sheet, and sa is a guess from context.

Tomokiyo’s entry for key no. 57 says it is used in “a letter from Laveriere to the Duke of Nevers, Poissy, 12 August 1593 (BnF fr.3985 fol.58)”. That letter is f. 58r, canvas 114 of Gallica btv1b90606498 (the verso, canvas 115, is the address only: “Monseigneur le duc de Nivernois”), signed “Laverriere”, “A Poissy ce xij aoust 1593”. It is clear French with two cipher passages, run A in nine lines in the middle of the page and run B in brief pieces in lines 21–24, and the office’s decipherment is written over almost every cipher line in a lighter ink: the letter was deciphered at the time. To read it, the whole word list of the key sheet (words 99–353 and the province and town numbers) was transcribed from fr. 3995 f. 103r on 2 October 2026. Fr. 3985 f. 58r, the start of run A: over the figures the office wrote prince de Conty qui desire de retirer mais il ne sait a qui , then pour qui luy est de plus d’importance madame d’Angoulesme est a[…] du tout a and la maison de Montmorency et le principal appuy qu’il ait soit des catholiques soit . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3985 f. 58r, via Gallica (btv1b90606498, view 114). Key no. 57 as it stands on the sheet reads 235 of the 248 cipher tokens (94.8%) as sense ( fr3985_f58/decode58.py ; Laverrière’s own clear words inside the runs are not counted): run A 219 of 223 (98.2%), run B 16 of 25. The first pass of 2 October gave 222 (89.5%). For the second, on 3 October, the cipher block was fetched again as lossless image regions at Gallica’s maximum (the microfilm has no larger image) and read with contrast enhancement, and the name panel of the key, f. 103v, was examined at full resolution. The fr-1600-letters model gives −1.66 per character on run A, with French first among the languages. The last group of run A is the phrase Tomokiyo names as the one that let him identify the key, 17 9 70 26 17 32 ω q n s = de nature defians , and its first figure is his 304 = pour . [… ce qui l’empesche c’est] pour le fait du [prince de Conty], qui desire de ritirer, mais il ne sait a qui le confier, estant la personne qui luy est de plus d’importance. Madame d’Angoulesme est port[ée] du tout a la maison de [M. de Montmorency], et le principall appuy qu’il ait, soit des catholiques, soit de ceux de la religion, soit de ceste maison, qui s’acorderoit fort bien pour cela, s’il y avoit quelque remuement. Vola pourquoy il desire faire election d’ung fidelle serviteur et tabour le [lieu?], ou il le pourra mettre, et point, l’oter, instruire, gagner monsieur de la Trimouille, pour ne donner aucung soubs son[…] a ceux de la religion, estans tous de nature defians. … ny eust grand propos, et a [Espagnols] [?] [Pape] ce tiennent le plus empeschés [6 lam 340] … dict qu’il y a lettre[s] [du] [Pape] pour atanter a la personne du [Cardinal de Bourbon] , et disent avoir les lettres … Bold is cipher; the rest is clear. A fortnight after Henri IV’s abjuration, during the truce talks, La Verrière tells Nevers, who was preparing his embassy to Rome, that the young prince de Conty wants to withdraw someone but has no one to entrust it to; that Madame d’Angoulême (Diane de France) is wholly inclined to the house of M. de Montmorency, his main support among Catholics and Protestants alike; and that he therefore wants to choose a faithful servant and to win over La Trémoille, the Huguenot leader. Run B reports that there are letters of the Pope for an attempt on the person of the Cardinal de Bourbon. Key, slips and gloss. New word values used here include 160 desire , 183 estre , overbarred 200 plus , 243 importance , 245 instruire , 300 personne , 309 quoy , 327 serviteur , 340 tabour and 344 tout . 183 estre followed by n t stands for estant (grade I). The four name signs were first taken from the gloss; on 3 October all four were found on the key’s name panel, f. 103v, read at full resolution, and are now grade H: prince de Conty (an R crossed with an X), M. de Montmorency (singular on the panel), Cardinal de Bourbon (a hooked cross), and the duc de Lorraine at the end of B4. The writer’s caret ( p ) is a tall λ like his a ; with that, the word after est reads port[ée] (I), where the office wrote “a m…”. In run B the barred 29 is the province sign for the Spaniards and 252 is lettre (I). Six slips of the writer are forced by the context and agree with the gloss ( madame , princi- , soit , fidelle , vola , avoit ). Key and office differ in three places: the figures give a ceux where the office wrote a cause , and spell e-le-o-c-ti-o-n and ga-g-ne-t where it wrote election and gagner .

That, Monseigneur, is all I can send you, except that for the rest of the 1000 écus Monsieur de Sancy and [?Hombert], with Monsieur de Revol, will lend a hand and attend to it(?), so that you will be content, having found them all very devoted to your service; and I can assure you that Monsieur de Sancy forgets nothing and holds me for ever. Seventeen cipher telegrams between the Colombian Ministry of War and the military chief of the Amazonas in the first weeks after the Peruvian seizure of Leticia. Brice Dudout read all the alphabetic ones with the Ministry’s own weekday key (787 words, 99.5%); one numeric telegram stays open. afqiciñof · negemuppuf-yovcfulinh-ovigcifpqf … urgepedir · casabofformilproyectilesperfgrantes … Bogotá ↔ Puerto Asís · weekday alphabets · 9–27 September 1932 The Leticia cipher telegrams, September 1932 Go to the full text ↓ Telegrams from the first weeks of the Colombia–Peru crisis, on gunboats, ammunition and troops, read with a key issued by the Ministry of War itself in 1931. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 5 November 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (100% of the cipher) Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution, verification) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (100% of the cipher) The telegrams Seventeen cipher telegrams between the Ministry of War in Bogotá and Gen. Amadeo Rodríguez Vergara, civil and military chief of the Amazonas at Puerto Asís, 9–27 September 1932, after the Peruvian seizure of Leticia on 1 September. Where Archivo General de la Nación Colombia, Archivos Privados, Fondo General Amadeo Rodríguez Vergara, Asuntos militares, CO.AGN.AP.GARV..2.2.4, ff. 85–177 (on DataViva). The cipher Seven simple-substitution alphabets, one for each weekday, vowels to vowels, with the day name and D (forwards) or R (reversed) in clear at the head. All the telegrams seen are D. How it was deciphered With the Sección I key of 31 January 1931, kept in the same fonds (GARV..1.1.4 f. 44r). It scores 0.977 of characters on a held-out telegram against 0.381 for the best of 200 permuted keys. What it says Ammunition from Bofors, the gunboats Cartagena, Santa Marta and Barranquilla, the state of the troops (499 men, corrected to 599), the move to Caucaýa, the passage of Güepí, the Napo and the risk of a conflict with Ecuador, Peruvian reinforcements to Loreto, and the censorship of soldiers’ letters. Still open Telegram No. 143 (f. 151), about 160 numbers in a numeric system for which no key is in hand, and four unresolved words. Credit Daniel Bourdeau transcribed the key and read ff. 149 and 153 first; Brice Dudout (Europe chiffrée), working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents, transcribed and read the other telegrams.
leticia1932.html#the-telegrams

The Peruvian seizure of Leticia on 1 September 1932 opened the Colombia–Peru conflict. The telegrams are the traffic of the first weeks between the Ministry of War and the general at Puerto Asís on the Putumayo. Five of them have a contemporary clear text in the same file (ff. 117, 127, 137, 139 and 157), and f. 141 carries a pencil gloss of its last sentence; for these the reading is a verification of the period decipherment, not a new reading. The other eleven have no decipherment in the file. Copies are counted once (ff. 106 = 107, 132 = 125, 152 = 153, 154 = 158).
leticia1932.html#the-key

The Ministry’s key sheet (Sección I, “Criptografía”, 31 January 1931) gives the cipher letter of each plain letter for every weekday; its rules are on f. 43r. Daniel Bourdeau transcribed the table on 28 October 2026 and Brice Dudout transcribed it again independently on 4 November: the two tables are identical. Many slips of keying or transmission remain in the telegrams (b/h, i/e/a, dropped letters); f. 134 is headed “Martes D” but is enciphered with the Monday alphabet, and ff. 109, 141 and 170 have no heading. One pre-registered measurement was made on a held-out telegram (No. 82, 661 letters): 0.977 of characters and 0.854 of words, against 0.381 and 0.039 for the best of 200 permuted keys.
leticia1932.html#the-reading

The 787 cipher words give 759 certain, 24 probable and 4 unresolved: 99.5%. The clear words of most telegrams were left out of the transcriptions, so the reading gives the cipher parts. For the numeric telegram No. 143 (Lt-Col. Paz, 25 September) the weekday key does not apply; the Presidency key (GARV..2.2.1 ff. 6v, 8, 10) is a candidate and has not been tried. The Spanish and an English translation are under Full texts.
leticia1932.html#uncertain

Telegram No. 143 on f. 151: about 160 numbers from 1 to 181 in another system, with no key in hand. Four unresolved words (zeffe on f. 107, pascama on f. 153, hsla on f. 159, gixhtlo on f. 170). The sentence on f. 153 does not fully construe around “relator … yo”, and f. 159 should be re-read at full resolution. The historiography of the Colombia–Peru war was not searched beyond the catalogue’s searches of 3 November; no edition or study of these telegrams was found. Other files of the fonds (GARV..2.3.1, 2.3.2, 2.4.1, “con traducción”) were not opened. The DataViva images carry no explicit licence and are not reproduced here.

BL Add MS 4136 f. 172, upper half: the Forbes tracing of the four cipher passages of Percy’s letter of 23 July 1559, with his signature. Image: British Library, Add MS 4136 f. 172, via DECODE R9256. The heading reads “Sr Hen: Percy to Sr Wm Cecill from Norham 23 July 1559”. A second heading on the same page, “from Norham 22 July 1559 · A”, has only the signature under it. Below a rule is “Sturmius’s Cipher, 4 March 1562”, an alphabet with name codes and nulls. Its signs are Greek-like letters, not boxes, so it is not Percy’s key. The passages are transcribed one sign at a time. Each sign is a box shape (⅃ ⊔ L □ ⊏ 7 ⊓ Γ, and a barred I) with or without a mark beneath: an underline, one dot or two dots. Five other signs appear: a crossed 4, a boxed cross, a trident, a tailed 6 and a house. In all there are 13 words, 63 signs and 19 distinct sign-and-mark combinations. The transcription is in targets/percy1559/transcription.txt . Passages (3) and (4), on either side of the signature, begin with the same five signs and share their second word’s first three signs.
percy1559.html#context

Bain’s calendar (no. 501) summarises the letter. Percy has had Knox’s answer by word of mouth. Whytlaw is fully instructed, so his journey is at an end. Percy has conveyed a letter to the Lord Prior and encloses the Prior’s unsigned answer. Lord Hume has put off the border meeting at Lady Kirk. The Merse and Teviotdale go to the Dowager tomorrow, and the Congregation towards Haddington. The note on the manuscript is “A few words in cipher, deciphered by Cecill”. On 22 July Percy had written Knox’s name as a cipher sign (CSP Foreign I no. 1045). On 4 August he told Cecil he had sent the Lord Prior “a cipher” (Laing, Works of John Knox VI, p. 61). Percy’s cipher could spell out whole sentences as well as names. Bain (no. 480) records a postscript Percy added in cipher to Kirkcaldy’s letter of 1 July and deciphered himself. Laing (VI, pp. 33–35) prints it in clear: “The letter that Knoxe wrythe to you is by the meanes of the hole Congregatione, the names of whome I sende yowe here inclosed.” Its ciphered form is on the original only.
percy1559.html#tried

Word patterns. Each cipher word was matched against a vocabulary from Sadler’s State Papers and the Forbes volumes, with the calendar’s names added. Many words fit on their own. The repeated five-sign word fits prior or merse , for example. Rosicrucian pigpen. This tested each box shape as a cell of three consecutive letters, with the mark choosing among them. Every cell layout and mark order was tried, with 24- and 26-letter alphabets. None produces a single dictionary word, so this system is ruled out. One alphabet for all thirteen words. A constraint search looked for one alphabet that makes all thirteen words real words. It was run with the marks counted as distinct letters, with dots ignored, with underlines ignored, with all marks ignored, and with homophones allowed. It found no solution. The same search on the words read right to left also found none. A version that left up to six words free as name codes timed out without producing a candidate. Statistical search. The search scored letter triples, and then whole words from a vocabulary of the period. It gave only fluent-looking nonsense, as expected for 63 signs. Guessed names. Prior , Lord Prior , Knox , Whytlaw and Norham Castle were placed on the repeated words. None gives an alphabet that holds across all four passages.
percy1559.html#open

None of the four passages is deciphered. They may be name signs rather than spelled-out words, or the tracing may have miscopied some marks; a tracing cannot settle either question. Two documents would: the original of 23 July in TNA SP 52/1 with Cecil’s interlined decipherment, or the ciphered original of the 1 July postscript, which would give a sentence of known plaintext. Neither is online.

R1212 is two leaves, ff. 38–39, in the Vienna collection of cipher keys, a volume whose DECODE dates (1540–1774) are the span of the whole box. Pages 1–2 and 3–4 are two reports under the same head, “D[omi]no … Thur. Prim.” and “Practica Thur. Prim.”, each opening with the enciphered words horum omnium motuum , “of all these disturbances”. The foot of p. 4 carries two rows of signs with faint pencil letters over them: an inventory of the signs in the order they first occur in that heading. The key is on a separate leaf. The key is R1211, f. 37, the leaf filed just before the letter: A = Δ 3 5, B = L, C = 9, D = ꝛ, E = y M 2, F = o, G = B, H = #, I = Π Ꝛ ~ k, K = β, L = L 4, M = Ϙ Λ, N = P, O = φ x v, P = A, Q = Ҁ, R = Ɔ, S = σ, T = Ω, U = C Λ ɧ, X = π, and the codes 34 Transsylvania and 27 Petrovics. R1210 (f. 36), also labelled for Bornemisza, is an older numerical key of about 1540 (Rex Joannes, Frater Georgius, Verbőczy) and does not fit this letter. The writer is loose with the key: x and v stand for u as well as o, ~ for u and o as well as i, 9 (c) for t in prodicionem , nacionum , comiciis ; the barred Π is his h, and β serves for c and h as well as k. A pair of digits in a run usually stands for two letters (34 in alias , aliquando , alliciebat ).

The four DECODE images were transcribed in horizontal bands, first at half and then at full resolution, one pass per pair of pages. Each cipher run was deciphered from its signs with the R1211 key before the gloss was consulted, and every disagreement was settled on the image. The gloss is right in substance throughout; where the signs differ they give the better text ( ipse for the gloss’s apparent esse , nisi for nostri , maledictum for maledicti , evenisset for evenissent , inflammavit for inflamare , intellexerunt for intellexerat , perniciosarum for perniciosam , in celo for in celis , vexillum (?) for auxilium ). Apparent codes 0399, 134 and several 34s dissolved into letters. Counts: 288 cipher tokens (274 words and 14 codes); 257 words decrypted securely, 14 uncertain but in sense, 3 not decrypted; 5 codes in the key, 9 not.
