Prim.⟩ Of all these disturbances. ⟨I have hitherto always commended to Your Most Sacred Majesty a man in all good things, of which all […]; of signal⟩ perfidy I must deservedly accuse him. ⟨For no other⟩ is the cause of this uprising but Francis Kendi, three times a traitor; he himself ⟨to this end⟩ induced Antal Kendi and Menyhért Balassa ⟨and⟩ a few others of the nobles, ⟨and⟩ […]. But the treacherous man committed this treason ⟨out of⟩ his own cowardice and excessive despair. ⟨May the gods⟩ overwhelm this cursed traitor, who has lost this ⟨kingdom to Your Majesty⟩, no one else. {24} {15} ⟨and⟩ {10} ⟨beyond the gate⟩ are being solicited to come into this kingdom. ⟨I have written this to Your Most Sacred Majesty briefly but truly; there is no doubt in the matter.⟩ {41} {70} {55} {78} {18} ⟨[?have been killed]; still, to Your Sacred Majesty,⟩ they await help ⟨from⟩ the Sacred Majesty [?vestras], but not for long. If more troops were here now with a good captain, ⟨the wound would therefore still⟩ be curable. ### Page 2 I will say again that Francis Kendi alone has lost the kingdom to Your Majesty, no one else. This is as true as the Gospel of Christ. Without his counsel nothing is done in this kingdom; therefore he himself inflamed the others to stir up these disturbances; otherwise ⟨the manifest ruin⟩ would not have come about. Although there have been horrible complaints everywhere against the insolence of the voivodes' soldiers, about the deflowering of tender virgins, and this in the presence of the public assembly of the three nations, many violations of married women; besides many other plunderings, ⟨alas⟩, which no man could enumerate. ### Page 3 (Practica) Of all these disturbances and pernicious factions the sole and most certain author is Francis Kendi […], despairing of the defence of Your Sacred Majesty after they understood that the castles of Babolchia and others had been lost; who now hopes to have from {27} the [?banner] for the principality of {34}[?nie] [Transylvania]. And under a certain pretext he [?en]ticed me with his blandishments, saying that I ought to remain in this bishopric, but that I should cede Alba as a residence to the son of {52}, and I should [?reside] in the castle of Gialu, and sometimes at Alba in the Provost's house. These are the words of Francis Kendi to me at Vásárhely during the diet, in a private room, the two of us ⟨alone⟩ being present. If Francis ### Page 4 Kendi {34} had not [?made certain of] this defection, the king (sic) from Your Majesty, no such movement would now have occurred in this kingdom; this is as true as God in heaven.

The opening of R2232 (rotated): the clear “j’ai l’honneur de LUI exposer ce qui suit”, then the cipher, which starts “je suis l’auteur d’un plan”. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Wilhelmina Prinses van Pruisen (A32) inv. 192, first page (image P2), via DECODE R2232. The three DECODE images are out of order. The letter begins on image 2 (“Madame! Je demande Grace à Votre Altesse Royale, du mystérieux que je mets dans cette Correspondance”), continues on image 3 and ends on image 1 with the date “La Haye ce 25 juillet 1801” and a ciphered signature. The framing sentences, the forms of address and some whole sentences are in clear; the substance is in figures. DECODE R2233, the key sent with Wolff’s letter of 8 September 1801. Row 1 = 0 ⅛ ¼ ½, row 5 = 1 2 3 4, row 15 = a b c d, row 45 = i o u a. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Wilhelmina Prinses van Pruisen (A32) inv. 192, via DECODE R2233. The key lists one sequence, 0 ⅛ ¼ ½ 1 2 … 9 à a b c … n ô o p q r s t û u v w x y z a e i o u a , in overlapping windows of four: row N holds values N to N +3. The writer picks a row and marks the place in it with a superscript; a bare number means the first place. So a can be written 15, 14², 13³ or 12⁴, and the vowels at the end of the sequence give a, e, i, o more choices still. DECODE’s note on R2233 describes the system correctly, but neither record gives a decipherment.

Ciphered passages in brackets; spelling lightly modernised. Madame! Je demande grâce à Votre Altesse Royale du mystérieux que je mets dans cette correspondance; l’importance de sa matière m’y contraint. Je crois être sûr que ma lettre du 1er de juin est bien parvenue, et j’ai l’honneur de lui exposer ce qui suit. [Je suis l’auteur d’un plan qui a été envoyé à] Votre Altesse Royale et [au roi à Berlin en mars ou avril 1798, lorsque j’étais dans les villes anséatiques, d’un rassemblement … une descente au Havre de Grâce, et fait le bombardement de Paris; une autre en Hollande; un corps attaque l’Yssel et le reste opère sur le continent; de la pacification de ce pays-ci; d’un nouveau genre de commander des armées combinées], et d’autres choses trop longues pour être transcrites ici, et qui finit par le vœu de pouvoir faire comme [Coriolan]. Puisque cette pièce a été faite après [la paix] de [Campo Formio], et que les circonstances se ressemblent, je n’ai pas voulu manquer de me faire connaître, pour offrir très-humblement mes faibles services, pour co-opérer à son exécution en général, et spécialement dans l’endroit où j’aurais déjà alors voulu me voir employé … Outre cela j’ai [offert à feu le prince Frédéric de lui amener quelques milles hommes de la brigade suisse avec l’élite des officiers, par une lettre que j’ai expédiée le matin du 14 septembre 1795, jour que je fus arrêté; sans cet accident je serais entré alors à la solde de l’Angleterre, je n’aurais point soupiré 39 mois et 5 jours dans la prison, et je ne serais pas dans le besoin où je me trouve à présent. Je ne veux pas offusquer le mérite des autres]; mais s’il m’est permis de le dire, je crois pouvoir me flatter d’avoir aussi mérité en quelque façon [pour la bonne cause], que je ne suis pas indigne pour implorer la [générosité bienfaisante du gouvernement britannique] pour en obtenir la [demi-paye] depuis le jour de [mon arrestation; j’avais comme quartier-maître 50 florins] par [mois] courant, [ou un secours] conforme à sa [magnanimité] … … Daignez, Madame, m’accorder cette grâce avec la même bienveillance qu’il a plu à Votre Altesse Royale de s’intercéder pour moi, lorsque j’ai eu l’honneur de m’adresser à Elle en [1791, à Berlin] … et agréez [de disposer de moi …, lui fournir des occasions où je puisse donner des preuves de ma reconnaissance], ainsi que de [mon adhérence à la bonne cause], et de [mon attachement] aussi [sincère] que très [profondément respectueux à la personne et à la maison] de Votre Altesse Royale, dont [les ordres pourront me parvenir] par cette [même voie sans adresse], avec [3 marques ▽] … [Wolff]. La Haye ce 25 juillet 1801. A royalist who had been in the Hanseatic towns in 1798 claims authorship of a two-pronged invasion plan against France and the Batavian Republic sent to the Princess and to Frederick William III. With peace in the air again in 1801, he offers to help carry it out. He recalls an offer of Swiss troops to Prince Frederick of Orange (d. 1799), cut short by his arrest on 14 September 1795 and a 39-month imprisonment, and asks the Princess to get him British half-pay as a former quartermaster.

Translation reading_en.md # R2232, Wolff to Wilhelmina, Princess of Orange, The Hague, 25 July 1801: English translation Translated from `reading.md` (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026), the whole letter: clear text in plain type, the parts deciphered with the key in *italics*, as in the reading. `[?word]` = doubtful in the reading; … = unread. ## Translation Madam! I beg Your Royal Highness's pardon for the mystery I put into this correspondence; the importance of its matter forces me to it. I believe I can be sure that my letter of 1 June arrived safely, and I have the honour to set out to her what follows. *I am the author of a plan that was sent to* Your Royal Highness and *to the King in Berlin in March or April 1798, when I was in the Hanseatic towns: of an assembly … a landing at Le Havre de Grâce, and the bombardment of Paris; another in Holland; one corps attacks the IJssel and the rest operates on the continent; of the pacification of this country; of a new way of commanding combined armies*, and other things too long to be copied here, and which ends with the wish to be able to do as *Coriolanus* did. Since this piece was written after *the peace* of *Campo Formio*, and circumstances are alike, I did not wish to fail to make myself known, to offer most humbly my feeble services, to co-operate in its execution in general, and especially in the place where I should already then have wished to see myself employed, had the thing taken place in full and had I been at liberty to go there as I pleased. Besides that, I *offered the late Prince Frederick to bring him some thousands of men of the Swiss brigade with the pick of the officers, by a letter that I sent on the morning of 14 September 1795, the day I was arrested; but for that accident I should then have entered the pay of England, I should not have sighed 39 months and 5 days in prison, and I should not be in the need in which I find myself at present. I do not wish to cast a shadow on the merit of others*; but if I may be allowed to say so, I believe I may flatter myself that I too have in some way deserved well *of the good cause*, so that I am not unworthy to implore the *beneficent generosity of the British government* (at this point) to obtain from it *half-pay* from the day of *my arrest; as quartermaster I had 50 florins* a *month* current; *or relief* in keeping with its *magnanimity*; or else to receive from it such other *reward* as it may award me, and suited to *my need*, and proportioned [?to my services] … if I have the [?heart], and my *life*, which at all times has been and always will be *devoted to the old order*, depends on it. My *subsistence* … Deign, Madam, to grant me this favour with the same kindness with which it pleased Your Royal Highness to intercede for me when I had the honour of addressing myself to her in *1791, in Berlin; I in the …*, and be pleased *to dispose of me in the …; to furnish me with occasions where I may give* proofs of my gratitude, as also of *my adherence to the good cause*, and of *my attachment*, as *sincere* as it is most *deeply respectful, to the person and the house* of Your Royal Highness, whose *orders may reach me* by this *same way, without address*, with *3 marks ▽ in …*. I have the honour to be, with the deepest respect, Madam, Your Royal Highness's most humble and most submissive servant and valet, *Wolff*. The Hague, 25 July 1801.

DECODE R688 (three pages) is catalogue item 270, listed as a simple substitution in graphic signs. Why it was catalogued as a cipher Nothing on the images is enciphered. A Vienna clerk could not read Cyrillic, so the letter was bound with the ciphers and DECODE described it from the bundle heading. What it says Stojan greets aghas, knezes and his Vlachs by name and begs them to get him out of “the German prison”. The rest concerns money and pledges. Still open About a quarter of the words stay doubtful because of blots, deletions and the torn slip. The place names Z[?]vač and Bor[?] are uncertain. Why the plea sits among the conspiracy papers is not known.

Fascicle 327 of the Hungarian conspiracy files in the Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv holds a bundle headed Chiffres 1664–1668 . DECODE catalogued its items one by one, and dated each with the bundle's span. R688 is ff. 30–31. The nearest key record, R707 (ff. 60–61), is a Latin numeric nomenclator, and it has nothing to do with this letter. F. 30r, lines 2–10: ѿ града … поклонь и животе здравїе агамъ кнезїамь … , the greetings and the list of names. Image: Österreichisches Staatsarchiv, HHStA, Verschwörerakten Fasc. 327 Konv. D f. 30r, via DECODE R688 (image 1). Image 1 of the record is f. 30r. Image 2 shows an opening: f. 30v on the left, and on the right a small slip mounted on f. 31, with an endorsement in Latin on its edge that begins Epistola .
r688.html#the-letter

The opening, with doubtful words marked [?]: ✝ Сїи листь писа Стоянь … ѿ града З[?]вачь поклонь и животе здравїе агамъ, кнезїамь, ѿдабашамъ[?] и маламъ и великимъ. И пакъ посло и животе здравїе влахомъ моема: Вуку, Гаврилу, Радонѣци[?], Вучиту[?], куму Продану, Мирку, Павлу, Димитру, Марку с всемь христианомь. … Братїа, да ми се смилуете, можите мене извадить из немачкий тамнице а ваше душе из пакле. "This letter was written by Stojan from the town of Z[?]vač: greeting, life and health to the aghas, the knezes, the odabaše [company commanders], to small and great. And again I send life and health to my Vlachs: to Vuk, Gavrilo, Radonja, Vučeta, my kum Prodan, Mirko, Pavle, Dimitrije and Marko, with all the Christians. … Brothers, have mercy on me. You can get me out of the German prison, and your souls out of hell." The rest of f. 30r is about groschen, money he lacks, pledges and "what is needed". The last line is struck through and blotted. On f. 30v he says to bring the money to the town of Bor[?], and "I know horses and men, we can get [me] out, and all be glad, amen". The letter was written for him by someone else: Писа намъ Младь Бакиі[?] у градъ Бор[у] . A postscript sends greetings to his wife and asks kum Prodan to go himself to the Magyar[?]. Most of this postscript stays uncertain. The slip on f. 31 begins Сїи лисъ писа Х[?]саань[?] у Пет… and sends life and health to the writer's mother and brothers. It is too damaged to transcribe further.
r688.html#why

A letter in Cyrillic would have been as opaque to a Vienna chancery clerk as a cipher. It was bound in the Chiffres bundle, and DECODE described it from that bundle heading as a substitution in graphic signs. The same thing has happened to other items in this project. The DECODE record should read: not a cipher, cleartext Serbian (Cyrillic). This correction is queued with the transcription.
r688.html#open

The place names Z[?]vač and Bor[?] are uncertain readings. Settling them would help to place and date the letter. About a quarter of the words, mostly in the money passage and the postscript, are doubtful (grade M or I in the README Conventions scale). These are gaps in the transcription of a rough hand. A reader of early modern Serbian working from the original would close most of them. Why a Serb prisoner's plea sits among the conspiracy papers is not known. It may have been intercepted, or it may come from a prisoner held in the Habsburg border garrisons.

A later archival note at the foot reads “Legat … till L. Camerarius bref för 1628”: filed with the letters to Ludwig Camerarius for 1628. Where Riksarkivet, Stockholm, Chifferklaver låda II:114; DECODE R4284, undated (1600–1699), with no decipherment recorded. Formerly part of catalogue item 207. The cipher A homophonic alphabet of numbers 1–108, four for each letter, with larger numbers for words; Latin connectives in clear between the runs. This letter was filed on this site until 14 October 2026 with thirteen other Riksarkivet records of catalogue item 207. riksarkivet4284.html#letter

The first lines: comma-separated numbers, with the clear Latin Sequentes etiam , pro eo tempore , praeter omnia alia and et quorum between them. Image: Riksarkivet, Stockholm, Chifferklaver låda II:114, first page, via DECODE R4284. The letter fills two pages. The clear words are connectives ( Sed , Cum , Quo casu , Sed etiam tam pro ), so the matter itself is all in figures. The archival note ties it to Ludwig Camerarius, the Palatine diplomat who from 1626 served Sweden, and to the year 1628; it does not say who wrote it. A second leaf in the record holds four Latin phrases, effusorem sanguinis , pestem patriae , praeter naturalem and disturbatorem religionis , each written over equivalents in a letter cipher. It looks like a test of a key, perhaps of another cipher; it has not been used.
riksarkivet4284.html#tried

21 September 2026: the letter was transcribed from the DECODE images, about 750 numbers in the first count, with some twenty doubtful readings where two numbers may run together. Measured again on 14 October 2026, the file holds 822 groups and 170 different forms. Homophonic substitution was annealed against a Latin model, eight runs of 250,000 steps, and again on the guess that the numbers come in bands of four. The output was Latin-sounding nonsense. Seventy key records from the same Chifferklaver boxes (R4259–R4329) were fetched. Two were tested, the Transylvanian “Schauis” key (R4310) and a 1632 key in which 30 ends every word (R4296). Neither fits. The key, as it turned out, was among the other 68.
riksarkivet4284.html#key

In October 2026 Dolly Moulekhi tested the Chifferklaver key sheets against this site’s transcription and found that one fits: not the square grid on R4325 (Chifferklaver låda II:152), but the separate strip below it, a row of letters A to Ö with four numbers under each (a 5 29 55 102, e 9 37 57 104 …; Y and Z share a column; 22, 51, 74 and 89 are unused). Her reading of the strip was checked here on the DECODE image and agrees in all 104 values. Applied unchanged, it gives a letter to 729 of the 754 numbers, and they run as Swedish of the 1620s, with Latin enciphered as well as in clear: kunna giöra , orsak skull negociera , giorde ios der med een behageligt tienst och dette kunde skee på några … , media quae longum foret recensere , nobis et patriae securum , hafwa allaredan så många hamnar inne i Östersiön , det intet rådeligt ähr att öfwerlåta dem , sina barn och arfwingar som för sina wenner och förwanter . So the letter is mainly Swedish, not Latin as catalogued, and it concerns harbours on the Baltic. The project’s statistical test is underdetermined here: the decode scores −3.12 per letter, above every key fitted to the shuffled ciphertext (best −3.22) but not by the margin a pass needs. Some 750 numbers spread over 104 values are too few for a letter model, and the text mixes two languages. The case for the match is the archival key itself, applied unchanged, and the running Swedish it produces. The decoded text is not yet a reading: it still has to be divided into words and translated, and 23 larger numbers, probably word codes from the same sheet, are unresolved.
riksarkivet4284.html#gaps

A reading: the decode divided into Swedish and Latin words, the anomalous strings marked, and a translation. The 23 larger numbers (952, 347, 831 …), to be tried against the word lists on R4325, and the doubtful multi-digit readings, to be checked on the image.

Twenty-nine DECODE records catalogued as ciphertexts with no decipherment; most have a contemporary decipherment bound with them, and Satoshi Tomokiyo published the key in 2025. His key was applied to two letters outside his coverage, R9653 (the siege of Rhodes) and R9635, which were deciphered in part. The alphabetical order of the nomenclator predicted the missing numeral codes, three of them then found in the text, and the Lope Hurtado letters in the run use a different cipher. yeh s · xig · tom · xig · cef · y · cif · xel · mog vuc cartas · de · Francia · de · xxvi · y · xxvii · del · passado Venice → Charles V · homophonic alphabet with a three-letter nomenclator · 1522 Alonso Sánchez at Venice to Charles V, 1522 to Charles V Go to the full text ↓ Real Academia de la Historia, Salazar 9/23–9/26 · DECODE R9593–R9657 · the imperial ambassador at Venice reporting to the Emperor through the Italian War of 1521–26 Catalogued here as twenty-nine ciphertexts with no decipherment. Satoshi Tomokiyo reconstructed and published the key in September 2025. Three letters are now transcribed from contemporary decipherments filed on their DECODE records, checked against the cipher with his key (R9635, R9613, R9641); two more are decoded with the key but not read (R9653, R9593); 48 records have not been attempted. The work also corrected the catalogue entry, found the alphabetical ordering rule of the nomenclator and the numeral codes it predicts, and separated a second correspondent’s cipher. Where DECODE R9593–R9657, recorded as Non-decrypted ; almost every record has a contemporary decipherment bound with it. How it was read With Satoshi Tomokiyo’s key, published 6 September 2025; no cryptanalysis was needed. Here it was applied to R9653 and R9635, outside his coverage. What was added The catalogue entry corrected in three ways; the ordering rule, which fills the numeral run and was confirmed in the text ( cef = xxvi, cif = xxvii). sanchez1522.html#prior

Satoshi Tomokiyo, Correspondence in Cipher of Imperial Ambassadors Alonso Sanchez and Juan Manuel (1522) , posted on Cryptiana on 6 September 2025 and enlarged on 9 September, reconstructs the key. He worked from the contemporary decipherment attached to DECODE R9605, and describes how he began: browsing R9613 he noticed that vog and xig were frequent and so likely common monosyllables, and that a q with a double bar was often affixed to a code and might be the plural -s ; he was then stuck on the handwriting of the decipherment. Turning to R9605 he saw vog veg near the end, two codes close together in an alphabetical listing and both frequent, and matched them to en el in the plaintext. After that, as he puts it, there was no real difficulty. The article gives the substitution alphabet as a hand-drawn table, the nomenclature, and the deciphered first lines of R9593–R9632, plus the whole of R9621 and the last paragraph of R9623. It also reconstructs the parallel cipher of Juan Manuel , imperial ambassador at Rome (DECODE R9499–R9529), which is built to the same design with different values. For the prior-solution record: a published key and partial decipherment existed a year before this work, it was found before the attempt, and everything below uses it. Bergenroth’s Calendar (1866) also abstracts fourteen of these letters from the contemporary decipherings; that was found after R9635 had been deciphered in part.
sanchez1522.html#entry

The entry read “RAH, Signatura 9/24 (29 items)”, 1522–23, and justified its importance by the negotiation that brought Venice out of the French alliance and ended in the treaty of July 1523. The fifty-five DECODE record pages R9603–R9657, tabulated, contradict all three parts. The shelfmark. The run is spread over Salazar 9/23, 9/24, 9/25 and 9/26 . R9603–R9618 are in 9/24, R9619–R9632 in 9/25, R9633–R9657 in 9/26, and Tomokiyo’s list reaches back into 9/23. The dates. Every record carries a 1522 date, the last of them November 1522. Nothing in this group reaches 1523 , so the treaty of July 1523 is outside it. The letters belong to the year of La Bicocca, the loss of Genoa and the fall of Rhodes; the Venetian realignment came the year after. The authorship. Nine records are by Lope Hurtado de Mendoza , not Sánchez: R9634, R9644, R9645, R9646, R9648, R9649, R9650, R9652, R9656. A further correction matters more. DECODE marks almost every record in the group Inline Cleartext: Yes , meaning a contemporary decipherment is bound with the ciphertext, and the Calendar of State Papers Spain, vol. 2, calendars many of these same letters with the note “Autograph in cipher. Contemporary deciphering”. These letters were deciphered at the time. What they lack is an edition. DECODE’s Non-decrypted means that no decipherment is entered in the database; the catalogue entry took it to mean that none exists.
sanchez1522.html#system

The system is the 1496 Ferdinand-and-Isabella type: a homophonic substitution alphabet, three nulls that letters open with, a q with a double bar for the plural -s , and a nomenclator of three-letter codes for common words, names and places. Word division is kept. The vocabulary is large for the date. Tomokiyo’s table, set out as data, shows that the codes follow a pattern. They are consonant–vowel–consonant over first position, sixteen consonants z y x v t s r p n m l h g f d c b , running backwards through the alphabet as the plaintext runs forwards; middle, the five vowels a e i o u ; third position, nine consonants b c d f g h l m n . That is 720 slots, of which about 177 were recovered. Sorting by (first consonant, third consonant, vowel) puts the plaintext in alphabetical order: zid zod zud | zef zif | zog zug | zel | zem zom | zen zun gives a(h)un, ahun, al, allende, algun, alla, alli, antes, aqui, aquell, arma, assi . The alphabetisation is the clerk’s own and is loose at the edges ( allende before algun , cosa before concorda ), so what the rule gives for an unassigned code is a range, not a point. Where the plaintext is a numeral series, the range collapses to a value.
sanchez1522.html#numerals

Tomokiyo has cob xviii, cub xix, cad xx through cud xxiv, and caf xxv, and leaves the rest of the block blank, with a query on cud and an uncertain “[xxviii?]” in his reading of R9598. The ordering rule fills the run: code cab ceb cib cob cub cad ced cid cod cud caf cef cif cof cuf value xv xvi xvii xviii xix xx xxi xxii xxiii xxiv xxv xxvi xxvii xxviii xxix The two in bold were predicted before they were seen, and then met in the foot paragraph of R9653 in a context that can only be a pair of dates (next section). That in turn resolves the uncertain “[xxviii?]” of R9598 as cof . The predicted values are carried in key_codes.tsv flagged as this project’s, separately from Tomokiyo’s.
sanchez1522.html#r9653

R9653 is Sánchez to Charles V, Venice, 20 November 1522, Salazar 9/26 f. 299–301. It is beyond the end of Tomokiyo’s list and is not calendared in CSP Spain 2. Folio 299r is a mixed leaf: six lines of cipher at the head, some thirty lines in clear, two lines of cipher at the foot, then the signature. RAH, Salazar 9/26, f. 299r. The clear middle carries the news of Rhodes; what could not be said openly went into the cipher above and below it. Image: Real Academia de la Historia, Madrid, Salazar 9/26 f. 299r, via DECODE R9653. The clear middle, transcribed from the image: A xiij del presente fue la postrera que escreui a v[uest]ra m[agesta]d y dixe las nueuas de Rodas que aqui hauia dicho vn patron de vn nauio; despues [vinie]ron cartas y los d’esta republica me embiaron vn sumario, cuyo traslado sera con esta. Esta manyana han houido otras cartas y son de Candia de su general de xx del passado, y las tenia el de Rodas de x del mismo. … Lo que dizen es que hasta x de octubre hauian dado los turquos cinco conbates muy rezios a Rodas por diuersos lugares, y baterias, y por debaxo de tierra por las minas y por debaxo de la agua, y siempre los hauian rebotado y muerto gran numero dellos — dizen xx mil. Pero vn secretario de la Señoria me ha dicho a mi que despues que el turquo esta sobre Rodas se le han muerto cinquenta mil hombres en las batallas y de dolencia; su armada de mar estaua muy mal en horden, y algunos hauisos hai que la persona del turquo se ha retirado y passado en tierra firme. … Dizen que los de Rodas esperan socorro con desseo, y que si les llegasen mil infantes ternian por muy cierta la victoria. No hai duda sino que ahora hauria buena disposicion de hazer muy gran daño al turquo y a su armada. Rhodes capitulated a month after this was written, on 22 December 1522. The cipher, 23 October 2026. The images were reopened: f. 299v carries more cipher, and the cipher of the foot of f. 299r and of f. 299v was deciphered sign by sign with Tomokiyo’s key ( R9653_reading.md , R9653_cipher.txt ). The first paragraph builds a sentence (“[?Este] embaxador y ahun la señoria tienen cartas de Francia de xxvi y xxvii del passado de [?Sangerman]”), but the second, on f. 299v ll. 7–12 (Adorno, the protonotary, Juan Manuel), does not: its code groups xug , zi , tac , lud , qef , sob , ca and nu are absent from Tomokiyo’s table and met once here. No decipherment of R9653 is bound or imaged, so it stays decoded, not read . Its second copy (f. 300v) is seen only as bleed-through, and R9654, of the same date, has no images on DECODE. The foot paragraph. It opens with the three nulls every letter in this cipher opens with; the second line decodes completely. Image: Real Academia de la Historia, Madrid, Salazar 9/26 f. 299r (foot), via DECODE R9653. The second line runs yeh +plural xig tom xig cef y cif xel mog vuc xig …: “cartas de Francia de xxvi y xxvii del passado de …” : letters out of France of 26 and 27 October, the month in which Francis I’s position in Lombardy collapsed. It is this pair of dates that confirms cef and cif . The first line gives ta es , vam embaxa(dor) , vuc +plural, zid a(h)un , rug la , gub señor , vog en , around spelled-out letters not yet settled. A small corroboration from the other end of the group: Lope Hurtado’s letter of 9 November (R9648) opens in clear “La carta de V. M[agestad] recebi de xxvj de octubre”, the same post that Sánchez reports reaching Venice.
sanchez1522.html#r9635

R9635 is Sánchez to Charles V, Venice, 16 September 1522, Salazar 9/26 f. 20–22, calendared in CSP Spain vol. 2 p. 482 and also beyond Tomokiyo’s list. Folio 20r is the best ciphertext page in the group: about twenty-five lines of cipher, whole-page, in a clean well-spaced hand , with a contemporary decipherment written between the lines in lighter ink. The decipherment covers only patches, so most lines have to be decrypted with the key. RAH, Salazar 9/26, f. 20r. Each paragraph opens with three nulls, padded out with the meaningless clear words como and quien . This is what Tomokiyo’s “como quierr” note under the nulls column of his alphabet means. Image: Real Academia de la Historia, Madrid, Salazar 9/26 f. 20r, via DECODE R9635. cipher reading xof +s yeh +s xig dom pud das cartas de vuestra magestad pac +s xig vum gɣ lal los de esta republica xel gub rac del señor infante vud +s zef xig pac +s mud +s cob pol9 ducados allende de los otros xviii mil ped xig cab pol9 vud +s mas de xv mil ducados faf +s pac +s … pol9 vud +s pic xig vom todos los … mil ducados luego de esto interlinear gloss obligados … fuessen restituydas sus bienes The subject is money and reprisals: the sums owed by the Signoria under the capitulation (eighteen thousand ducats outstanding from a previous year, more than fifteen thousand in another reckoning) and, in the glossed lines, goods seized that were to be restored to their owners . That is the same business as the sequestrations of imperial vassals’ goods at Venice which fill R9638 (11 October 1522) entirely in clear, and the same reckoning of xx mil ducados allende de xviii mil that Tomokiyo deciphered in the last paragraph of R9623. Two points of notation, which the page settles: pol9 is pol ( mi ) followed by the letter sign for l , giving mil ; that sign is easily taken for a g in this hand; and gɣ lal is the spelled letters r-e followed by lal ( publica ), giving republica , the word these despatches turn on. This page also attests cab = xv , in mas de xv mil ducados , the third of the numerals predicted from the ordering rule, after cef and cif in R9653. None of the seven is contradicted. The decipherment of the time, found 23 October 2026. Besides the interlinear patches, the DECODE record holds a full contemporary decipherment of the letter: a clear court-hand copy on f. 22r (image P3, right page). The reading now follows it, checked against the cipher of ff. 20r–20v with the key ( R9635_reading.md , English R9635_en.md ). A tear across f. 22r ll. 9–11 was filled from the cipher of f. 20r ll. 11–14, read sign by sign ( hec = quiera , vac = dicha , gta = l + es , which settles the token that had resisted). It opens: Visto que [?ya] tanto tardavan cartas de vuestra magestad, pues en esto no se puede perder nada, fuy con los desta republica y dixeles que ya sabian que por la capitulacion de la tregua que con vuestra magestad tienen assentada, el primero deste mes havian de pagar otros xx mil ducados, allende de los otros xviij mil que deven del otro año; que les rogava quisiessen pagarlos y cumplir con lo que son obligados. Four words of the decipherment stay uncertain in the cramped hand ([?bastar], [?tenido], [?Menorami], [?Lucerna]). The decipherment makes hec quiera where f. 20r had suggested Inglaterra above. Three more letters, 23 October 2026 R9613 , Venice, 18 June 1522 (Salazar 9/24 ff. 203–207): read from its contemporary decipherment, a clear copy on ff. 206r–207v of the same DECODE record, never opened before ( R9613_reading.md ); its first sentence checked word for word against the cipher of f. 203r ( hug = recebi ). “Recebi la carta de vuestra magestad del postrero del passado, y fuy con los desta republica …”: Charles V is well disposed to peace with Venice on honest and reasonable terms. CSP Spain 2 no. 429 abstracts the same letter. R9641 (with its duplicate R9642), Venice, 27 October 1522 (Salazar 9/26 ff. 173–188): read from its contemporary decipherment on ff. 187r–188r, filed on DECODE under R9642 as “Sánchez?” ( R9641_reading.md ); checked against the cipher of ff. 173r and 174r (“de todo esto tengo dado aviso al duque de Sessa”; new value vad = duque ). The Venetians are content with the Pope’s answer to their complaint about the imperial army’s quarters in the Ghiara d’Adda. R9593 , Venice, 5 March 1522 (Salazar 9/23 f. 27): read sign by sign with the key on the two DECODE images ( R9593_reading.md ): letters of Don Juan Manuel and Geronimo Adorno sent on, the lansquenets’ passage of Val Camonica, the French taking Caravaggio, the Swiss at Monza. Two values adopted ( gim = suyos , fef = toda ), but about twenty groups stay open and the end of f. 27r and lines of f. 27v do not build: decoded, not read . CSP Spain 2 does not calendar it; the next letter, R9594 (15 March), is CSP no. 396, which Bergenroth abstracted from a contemporary decipherment while calling the cipher “not extant”.
sanchez1522.html#alphabet

Tomokiyo gives the substitution alphabet only as a hand-drawn table. Measured off the table at high zoom, it has about thirty signs over twenty-two letters (a b c d e f g h i l m n o p q r s t u x y z), most of them with two or three homophones: a = n , ʒf ; d = ∞ , 3 , ɸ ; g = bold ∞ , L ; n = ᶻ , ℞₄ ; and so on. Two results follow. The “q with a double bar” is the letter s , and there is no separate plural marker. The plural ending is the letter s written after a code group, so Tomokiyo’s guess that it “may well be the plural ending -s” is right, for a different reason. And r is a different sign , a q with a loop, easily confused with it in this hand. The map is carried in alpha.py and checks out on spelled runs taken from R9635 f. 20r: nx#gn = ahora , ttn#n = nada . At this stage it did not yet give the spelled runs continuously, for the following reason. Tomokiyo transliterates the code groups with latin labels drawn from a set that includes v , which is not one of the twenty-two plaintext letters; the code labels and the alphabet therefore do not share one transliteration, and every sign has to be matched to both by eye. So the runs are left marked rather than filled in. The remedy is in the glosses: collate the patchy interlinear decipherment on R9635 f. 20r word by word against the signs beneath it, which fixes each homophone in this scribe’s hand; the unglossed lines and the rest of the group then follow. R9605 (9/24 f. 39–44, 7 May 1522) is the record from which Tomokiyo recovered the key, and its images show why: the cipher and the clerk’s full contemporary decipherment sit on facing leaves . Aligned at the end of the letter, where the clear reads Plegue a Dios no lo yerre en el camino. Code groups stand for syllables as well as whole words : nuf is no the adverb in one place and the final syllable of cami-no in the next, so a decryption that treats every group as a word will divide the text wrongly. And the lookalike signs are distinct : camino needs β = m , ahora ( nx#Ɋn , R9635 f. 20r) needs Ɋ = r , and the bold ∞ is g . All three are a “g”-shape at the resolution DECODE serves, and they are the single largest source of error in the spelled runs. Continuing the same passage against the clear “la venida del visorey con todas las postas , que despacho y escrivo” gives three more results. xel def = del visorey and ded + xof = veni + da = venida , verbatim. The spelled run for escrivo is seven signs for seven letters, fixing z = c, ɡ = r, aɤ = i, m = v , # = o with the known plaintext above them. The clear at “que fue a …” stands over the group cud , which Tomokiyo gives as “xxiv?”; had the clear read xxv , the whole c-block series would shift by one and the values predicted here would be wrong. It does not settle the question: the date is written over a correction and reads as something like xxv y xxvij , two dates rather than one, so it cannot be matched to a single group. cab , cef and cif do not depend on it: each was confirmed in its own context, independently of where the run starts. The same alignment runs from the very first word of the letter. Clear (f. 42): “Ya dixe a V. Mag. que el embaxador de Hungria fue respondido de los desta republica con buenas palabras…” ; cipher (f. 39r ll. 1–2): cig = ya ; vu ·o·ɣ = di +x+e = dixe ; dom pud ho veg = vuestra magestad que el; vam vuc ·ɡ = embaxa + do +r = embaxador ; n·℞·∞ ɡ·aɤ = Hun-gria, spelled across the line break; sa = fue ; ɡ·ɣ·q·ao·#·& vu vuc = r-e-s-p-o-n + di + do = respondido ; xig vum ɡ·ɣ lal = desta republica ; xa yuc ·n+s = con buenas . It fixes the sign table against a known plaintext instead of by eye: n =a, ɣ =e, ɡ =r, aɤ =i, o =x, # =o, q =s, ao =p, & =n, m =v, z =c, β =m, and the q-with-double-bar = s. ( q =s here against Tomokiyo’s alphabet column q =t: two similar glyphs, and the pair to watch next.) Applied to R9635, which has only patchy glosses, the table alone does not decrypt it, which corrects the diagnosis above. On R9635 f. 20r the first line is ‖ como ‖ quien ‖ deg ho feb ʒnɡ xof +s yeh +s xig dom pud . The tail is secure ( das cartas de vuestra magestad ), and the null padding matches R9605 exactly. Sense wants recebi in that slot, whose code is hug , unlike anything written there. So the obstacle lies in the step before the sign table: turning the cursive shapes into labels. R9605’s hand and R9635’s differ enough that a shape read confidently as d in one is something else in the other, and a wrong label yields a code group that either does not exist or exists with the wrong value. The alignment has to be done on the image , glyph against the clerk’s word above it, building a reference set of each sign as this scribe forms it, instead of transcribing to labels first and resolving afterwards. That is slower and more reliable. R9605 and R9613 are therefore not counted as results here: the Emperor’s clerk deciphered them in 1522, on the facing leaves. The failure reported above came from a wrong assumption about how the page is written; correcting it made the page decipherable. Everything here is written in ordinary latin-looking cursive. The two systems are told apart by shape-length and context: three-letter latin trigrams are nomenclator codes ( xig , vog , dom , pud , lig , nuc ), looked up in Tomokiyo’s table; single letters and short runs between them are the substitution alphabet , where the letterform and the value differ: n =a, y =e, g =r, o / ✗ =x, # =o, ao =p, m =u/v, z =c, β =m, 9 =l, q-with-double-bar = s. Three nulls open each paragraph, padded with the clear words como and quien . Verified on R9605 f. 39r l. 1 against the clerk’s plaintext on the facing leaf: cig vu·o·y n dom pud ho veg = “Ya dixe a vuestra magestad que el” , with vu (di)+ o (x)+ y (e) = dixe . With that, the page can be deciphered. R9635 f. 20r ll. 2–3 give continuous text: lig vog vom nuf gad lel ao-y-g- xig -g nuc … xa pac +s xig vum g-y- lal = “pues en esto no se puede perder nada … con los de esta republica” Two things in that sentence are new. lel = puede , a code Tomokiyo did not recover: it falls between lal publica and lol pudi , and the sense fixes it. And perder is written p-e-r + xig ( de ) + r: a code group used inside a word for a syllable , the same pattern R9605 showed with cami + nuf ( no ) = camino . Line 9 gives an independent check: nul ( obliga ) + vuc ( do ) + s = obligados , the word the 1522 decipherer wrote in the gloss above that stretch. Key, alphabet and gloss agree without being fitted to each other. Further down the page: pef pac ho zel xig a-h-o | r-a = me lo que antes de ahora ; yig ( capitula ) + c-i-o-n = capitulacion ; and ho hob hec ho pac +s = que quien Inglaterra que los , with hec = Inglaterra ; the English ambassador at Venice is a running subject of these months. Lower on the page: vom +s cad pol-9 xig a-h-o-r-a = estos xx mil de ahora ; ao-# xig g pac suf -z-e-r lu - ho = poderlo hazer, porque ; and rug +s lul ta = las quales . The last examples show the converse of the stem-plus-ending pattern, codes run together to make one word : lu ( por )+ ho ( que ) = porque , lul ( qual )+ ta ( es ) = quales , suf ( ha )+z-e-r = hazer . The page closes with darian todos los …, no pude …, si no se … en …, and then opens a fresh paragraph with the same three nulls and pac +s xig vum r-e- lal = los de esta republica . One code there, cag , is unassigned in Tomokiyo’s table and sits at the end of the numeral run immediately before cig ( ya ); cag = xxx is the natural continuation and suits the sense, but it is one slot past where the run is attested and is left probable, not certain. Line 5 gives xof veg + p-r-i-m-e-r-o + xig ta = da el primero de es [te], which fixes β = m on this page independently of camino in R9605; and at high zoom the ending of capitulacion is the curly second form of c that Tomokiyo draws as a backwards 3, so that word is settled rather than inferred. Every line of f. 20r now has at least a partial decipherment. Continuous or substantial: ll. 2–6, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15, 17, 18, 20, 22, 23, 25, with the passages at ll. 7 and 14; partial, with runs still unresolved: ll. 1, 8, 12, 16, 19, 21, 24. The subject, the sums, the parties and the drift of the argument are deciphered throughout the page , while a scatter of spelled runs inside partially deciphered lines stays open. It is not a word-perfect diplomatic edition and is not offered as one. (The crops were cut by dividing the written area into twenty-five equal bands, so the line numbers are approximate; each decipherment is tied to its own words.) The remaining runs need the same transcription work and no cryptanalysis; they are left untranscribed rather than filled in by inference. One token resists: gta , a dozen occurrences, cannot be a code (its middle position is not a vowel) and is most likely g ( y ) + ta ( es ), but that does not sit well everywhere and is left unresolved. The nine Lope Hurtado records bound in the same volumes look at first like more of the same: the same period, the same recipient, cipher mixed with clear inside the sentence, code groups of the same shape. They are not in Sánchez’s cipher. The test is the third position. Sánchez’s codes end strictly in b c d f g h l m n . Folio 260v of R9648 gives tep , tap , and groups ending in z , finals that Sánchez’s key does not contain. Juan Manuel’s Rome cipher, by contrast, does use p r s t z as finals ( jap papa , jir , jus , boz , qat ). So Lope Hurtado’s key is a third member of the family. Whether it is Juan Manuel’s own key is not settled here. None of the groups legible on that leaf ( ton , tep , tap , xul , xild , zar , xurzun ) has a value in Tomokiyo’s Juan Manuel table either, but that table is itself a partial recovery, so their absence decides nothing. Several of these records carry contemporary decipherments, so the key is recoverable by the same route Tomokiyo took; they need a separate target.

The page is not written in exotic symbols: **everything is written in ordinary latin-looking cursive**, and the two systems are told apart by shape-length and context — - **three-letter latin trigrams are nomenclator codes** (`xig`, `vog`, `dom`, `pud`, `lig`, `nuc` …), read straight off Tomokiyo's table; - **single letters and short runs between them are the substitution alphabet**, where the letterform and the plaintext value differ: `n`=a, `y`=e, `g`=r, `o`/`✗`=x, `#`=o, `ao`=p, `m`=u/v, `z`=c, `β`=m, `q`-with-double-bar = s, `9`=l; - the three nulls `ℋ`, `℈#`, `ℍO` open each paragraph, padded with the meaningless clear words *como* and *quien*. Confirmed on R9605 f. 39r l. 1, where the clerk's plaintext stands on the facing leaf: `cig vu·o·y n dom pud ho veg` = **"Ya dixe a vuestra magestad que el"**, with `vu`(di)+`o`(x)+`y`(e) = *dixe*. ## Lines read continuously Codes in `code`, spelled letters hyphenated, *italic* = written in the clear on the page. **l. 1** ‖ *como* ‖ *quien* ‖ `deg` `ho` `feb` `ʒong` `xof`+s `yeh`+s `xig` `dom` `pud` > … que … **das cartas de vuestra magestad** `deg`, `feb` and `ʒong` are codes Tomokiyo never recovered; bracketed, `deg` falls in the d-block between *visorey de Napoles* and *vimes*, `feb` in the f-block between *tene* and *tanta*. **ll. 2–3** `lig` `vog` `vom` `nuf` `gad` `lel` ao-y-g-`xig`-g `nuc` `Pmg` `xa` `pac`+s `xig` `vum` g-y-`lal` > **pues en esto no se puede perder nada … con los de esta republica** - **`lel` = *puede*** — a new code value. Respondieronme lo que antes de agora, que les fuessen restituydas sus tierras segun esta assentado en la dicha capitulacion. Repliqueles que las tierras estavan en poder del señor infante, y respondieron que quien quiera que los tuviese, vuestra magestad havia prometido restituyrlas. Dixeles que les [?…] [?bastar] tener los xviij mil ducados primeros hasta que fuessen restituydas las dichas tierras, y que pagassen estos xx mil de agora. Replicaronme no poderlo hazer, porque ellos havian pagado y pagavan cada año mas de seys mil ducados a sus subditos por las dichas tierras, las quales valian mas de xv mil ducados cada año; que en restituyendolas ellos pagarian todos los xx mil ducados luego. De esto no pude sacarlos, ni creo jamas los pagaran si no se les restituyen las dichas tierras. Los desta republica han [?tenido] estos dias cartas de [?Menorami] de xxviij del passado de [?Lucerna], y escrive que tenian todos los suyos que por agora yrian a servir en Francia a la parte de Picardia, y que por todo este mes no se podria mas campear en aquella parte y vernan a la empresa de Italia. Tambien tienen estos cartas de su embaxador que esta en Francia de xxvj del passado; dize que el rey de Francia yva de Bles a Paris y de alli a Picardia. Por dos vias me han certificado esto. ## Notes - **The decipherment against the figures.** Places where the cipher was read sign by sign (here or in `edition/r9635_f20r.md`) and the decipherment stands in the same order: *visto que … tanto* (`deg` `ho` `feb`, the last two unassigned in Tomokiyo, now *visto*, *tanto* by slot and this text); *cartas de vuestra magestad*; *pues en esto no se puede perder nada* (`lig vog vom nuf gad lel` p-e-r-`xig`-r `nuc`); *con los de esta republica*; *dixe(les) … que ya* (`vu`-x-e … `ho cig`); *capitulacion* (`yig`+c-i-o-n); *el primero deste mes* (`veg` p-r-i-m-e-r-o `xig ta`); *obligados* (`nul vuc`+s, under the 1522 gloss *obligados*); *allende de los otros xviii mil* (`zef xig pac`+s `mud`+s `cob pol`-l); *xviii mil ducados primeros*; *mas de xv mil ducados* (`ped xig cab pol`-l `vud`+s); *estos xx mil de agora* (`vom`+s `cad pol`-l `xig` a-h-o-r-a); *poderlo hazer, porque* (p-o `xig` r `pac` `suf`-z-e-r `lu`-`ho`); *las quales*; *todos los*; *no pude* (`nuf` p-u `xig`); *si no se*; on f. 20v *los suyos … en Francia la parte de* (`gim` = *suyos*: Tomokiyo's "suquos?") and *tambien … embaxador que esta en Francia … el rey de Francia … de alli … por dos … me*. - **Disagreements.** The earlier edition's *darian todos los* (f. 20r l. 22) is *pagarian todos los* here (the first sign was taken for `∞` d); `hec` = *Inglaterra* (f. 20r l. 13, "que quien Inglaterra que los") does not stand in the decipherment, whose text there is *en poder […] quien quiera q los*: r2i reads `hec` *quiera* (below). *ahora* of the cipher (a-h-o-r-a) is *agora* in the decipherment; the reading follows the decipherment's word, the figures give *ahora*. - **The tear (r2i, 23 Oct 2026).** f. 22r ll. 9-11 lose about ten words. Same holes. Seeing that letters from Your Majesty were so long [?already] in coming, and since nothing can be lost by it, I went to the lords of this Republic and told them that they knew well that by the capitulation of the truce which they have concluded with Your Majesty they were to pay, on the first of this month, another 20,000 ducats, besides the other 18,000 that they owe from last year; and that I asked them to be pleased to pay them and fulfil what they are bound to. They answered me what they had answered before: that their lands should be restored to them, as is agreed in the said capitulation. I replied to them that the lands were in the power of the lord Infante, and they answered that, whoever might hold them, Your Majesty had promised to restore them. I told them that it [?should be enough for them] to hold back the first 18,000 ducats until the said lands were restored, and that they should pay these 20,000 of now. They replied that they could not do it, because they had paid and were paying every year more than six thousand ducats to their subjects for the said lands, which were worth more than 15,000 ducats a year; that on their being restored they would pay all the 20,000 ducats at once. I could not get them off this, nor do I believe they will ever pay them unless the said lands are restored to them. The lords of this Republic have [?had] these days letters from [?Menorami] of the 28th of last month from [?Lucerne], and he writes that all their people [the Swiss] were holding that for now they would go to serve in France on the side of Picardy, and that after this whole month no more campaigning could be done in that region, and they will come to the enterprise of Italy. These lords also have letters from their ambassador in France of the 26th of last month; he says that the King of France was going from Blois to Paris and from there to Picardy. This has been confirmed to me by two ways. Transcription read_r9653.md # R9653 — Alonso Sánchez to Charles V, Venice, 20 November 1522 RAH Salazar 9/26, f. 299–301. Images `img/IMG_R9653_I45450_P1.jpg`, `_P2.jpg`. Not covered by Tomokiyo's article, which stops at R9632. ## Shape of the letter f. 299r is a mixed letter: a **cipher paragraph of six lines at the head**, then some thirty lines **in clear**, then a **cipher paragraph of two lines at the foot**, then the signature "El Alonso Sanchez". The clear middle is the news of the siege and fall of Rhodes; the cipher carries what could not be said openly. ## The clear middle (f. 299r), read from the image > A xiij del presente fue la postrera que escreui a v[uest]ra m[agesta]d y dixe las nueuas de Rodas que > aqui hauia dicho vn patron de vn nauio; despues [vinie]ron cartas y los d'esta republica me embiaron > vn sumario, cuyo traslado sera con esta. Esta manyana han houido otras cartas y son de Candia de su > general de xx del passado, y las tenia el de Rodas de x del mismo. Han me dicho me embiarian tambien > vn otro sumario de las nueuas que tienen, si lo hizieren a tiempo que pueda yr con esta, yra; sino, > embiarlo he a v[uest]ra m[agesta]d con otro. Lo que dizen es que hasta x de octubre hauian dado los > turquos cinco conbates muy rezios a Rodas por diversos lugares, y baterias, y por debaxo de tierra > por las minas y por debaxo de la agua, y siempre los hauian rebotado y muerto gran numero dellos — > dizen xx mil. Pero vn secretario de la Señoria me ha dicho a mi que despues que el turquo esta sobre > Rodas se le han muerto cinquenta mil hombres en las batallas y de dolencia; su armada de mar estaua > muy mal en horden, y algunos hauisos hai que la persona del turquo se ha retirado y passado en tierra > firme. Cartas de particulares no se dan, y de mi opinion [...] tienen ahun mejores nueuas de las que > publican. Dizen que los de Rodas esperan socorro con desseo, y que si les llegasen mil infantes > ternian por muy cierta la victoria. No hai duda sino que ahora hauria buena disposicion de hazer muy > gran danyo al turquo y a su armada. (Rhodes in fact capitulated a month later, 22 December 1522.) ## The foot cipher paragraph (f. 299r, last two lines) Transcribed sign by sign, then resolved against Tomokiyo's key plus the numerals established here. `‖` marks the three nulls the letters open with; `-s` is the plural sign (q with a double bar). ``` line 1 ‖ ‖ ‖ ta [xo]y vam vuc-s y zid rug gub a·u·n [xo·a·u·y] [tu] vog line 2 yeh-s xig tom xig cef y cif xel mog vuc xig [q·n·tu] ... ``` Resolved: - line 2 runs clean: **`yeh`+s `xig` `tom` `xig` `cef` y `cif` `xel` `mog`+`vuc` `xig` …** = "**cartas de Francia de xxvi y xxvii del passado de …**" - line 1 gives `ta` es, `vam` embaxa(dor), `vuc`+s = "dos"/"-dos", `zid` a(h)un, `rug` la, `gub` señor, `vog` en, around letters still to be settled. So the foot paragraph reports letters out of France of 26 and 27 October — the month in which Francis I's position in Lombardy collapsed after La Bicocca and the loss of Genoa. ## New code values `cef` = xxvi and `cif` = xxvii are **not in Tomokiyo's table**; they were predicted here by interpolating the numeral run and then confirmed by the sense of line 2. Han me dicho me embiarian tambien vn otro sumario de las nueuas que tienen; si lo hizieren a tiempo que pueda yr con esta, yra; sino, embiarlo he a vuestra magestad con otro. Pero vn secretario de la Señoria me ha dicho a mi que despues que el turquo esta sobre Rodas se le han muerto cinquenta mil hombres en las batallas y de dolencia; su armada de mar estaua muy mal en horden, y algunos hauisos hai que la persona del turquo se ha retirado y passado en tierra firme. Cartas de particulares no se dan, y de mi opinion […] tienen ahun mejores nueuas de las que publican. Dizen que los de Rodas esperan socorro con desseo, y que si les llegasen mil infantes ternian por muy cierta la victoria. Llegase en […sob] don Ioan Manuel, el qual pen[…] los […ca] alli en […sob]. Nuestro señor la imperial vida y estado de vuestra magestad guarde con el cumplimiento de la monarchia. Conventions: text carried by the decipherment; `[?word]` uncertain in the hand; struck words left out; spelling as written; *v. ma.* / *v. mad.* expanded to *vuestra magestad*; punctuation supplied. ## Reading Recebi la carta de vuestra magestad del postrero del passado, y fuy con los desta republica; dixeles que su embaxador havia assi platicado sobre la paz y dado una escritura, a la qual por parte de vuestra magestad fue respondido por otra escritura, que ternian por cierto de todo les havia su embaxador enbiado treslado; que les hazia saber vuestra magestad estava bien dispuesta, beniendo ellos a honestas y razonables condiciones, porque assi como vuestra magestad es emperador y cabeça de la republica christiana, assi desseava mas que otro establir y poner paz en ella, señaladamente en Italia, y unir las fuerças della contra los infieles y turcos; que yo estava bien instruydo de toda la negociacion y de la voluntad de vuestra magestad en ella; si querian platicar conmigo todos o diputar algunas personas para ello, que lo hiziessen, o que viessen que les parecia; si consultado entre ellos querian responder sin platicar otramente conmigo, sino hazerme saber lo que acordarian. Respondieronme que a su embaxador fue dicho que hiziesse una escritura como le parecia que se havia de assentar la paz, y que esto mostrava que parecia bien lo que dezia, pues le mandava hazer escritura; que parece que por parte de vuestra magestad se sale de aquella negociacion primera de paz y liga que ellos querian por mas vinculo, y se entrava en hazer tregua nueva; y que de otra parte se escrive que en la paz no puede prometer por el serenissimo señor Infante, y que en la tregua dize que su alteza tambien entrara. Tambien me dixeron que el cardenal de Inglaterra havia dicho a sus embaxadores queria ver las dichas escrituras y dezir su parecer. Yo repliqué que si consideravan bien todo lo que por parte de vuestra magestad se havia respondido, conocerian el buen animo y voluntad de vuestra magestad, y que debian bien considerar el postrero capitulo, que pide vuestra magestad al Rey de Inglaterra por conciliador; que ponderasse bien aquello, que vuestra magestad pedia lo que ellos havian de pedir, y verian si havia gana de tenerles lo que se assentava. Esto dixe porque se que uno de los fundamentos que hazen es que no havia de cumplirseles lo que se les prometeria. Y a lo del señor Infante dixe que vuestra magestad como havia de prometer lo que no estava en su mano ni era suyo; y tambien les dixe que yo [?nescia] vuestra magestad lo dezia, porque ya sabian lo que fue respondido a su embaxador quando propuso el volverse una parte a otra como antes de la guerra: que aquellas condiciones vuestra magestad no las havia acceptado, ni nescidad que era para las acceptar. Replicaron que no las havia vuestra magestad totalmente dessechado. A lo que me dezian del salir vuestra magestad de la primera negociacion, les dixe que no recibiessen engaño, que no se salia della, antes era entrar en ella con todo fundamento, y dezir y quitar las causas que lo podian destorvar; que si venian a las condiciones en la escritura de vuestra magestad contenidas, verian que no era desviarse nada de la primera negociacion de la paz; y que si ellos pedian liga para defension, que vuestra magestad pedia mas, liga que fuesse para offension, con la limitacion supuesta que se ponia; pero en caso que, por ser cosas de mucha importancia y qualidad, les pareciesse que havia necessidad de mas tiempo para assentarlas, que vuestra magestad dezia en este medio se podia hazer una tregua; que esto de la tregua les mostrava la buena voluntad de vuestra magestad, que no lo pedia sino en caso que les pareciesse no poder assi assentar la dicha paz; que veniendo a las condiciones en la escritura contenidas, vuestra magestad no hablava en tregua sino en la paz. Y porque conoci que se espinaron mucho que vuestra magestad offrecia que el señor Infante prometeria la tregua y dize que no puede prometer la paz, pareciendoles a ellos assi, aun no me lo dixeron, que aquello era de paz assi un gran postigo abierto para que en qualquier tiempo se les pudiesse dañar, les dixe que ellos podian venir a tales y tan honestas condiciones que vuestra magestad procuraria que el señor Infante entrasse en la paz. Quedaron que entre ellos consultarian y me responderian. Hame sido certificado que en Pregay, que pocos dias ha tovieron, platicaron mucho lo que devian de hazer en entregada que tuviessen Cremona, y que uno dellos dixo que Dios havia siempre ayudado a esta republica, que assi quedaria algunos dias por passar antes de entregarla, que verian lo que seria; que agora no estava en su libertad, que no podian ya bien hablar en lo que havia de hazer hasta que lo estuviesse, mostrando que entregarla [?nemora] era fuera de la obligacion de Francia; que muchos dellos tiene esta opinion. Yo tengo necessidad que no declararan ellos esto assi sino a mas no poder, y teniendo assentadas sus cosas con vuestra magestad. De Francia dizen tener cartas de tres, con las braburas acostumbradas. Dixeles su embaxador que el Rey de Francia le dixo que otras vezes Francia a resistido al imperio, a España y a Inglaterra, y que junta con esta señoria no solo resistiria, mas los offenderia. Mossen del Escut de Carmona fue enbiado treslado de una carta que tiene de vij deste de Turin, que eran alli llegadas seiscientas lanças y doze mil aventureros gascones, y que havian [?sus pagos]; e ya buelve Andrea Gritti a escrevirles confortandolos con Francia. A lo que siento, el turco no arma por mar este año, y estos lo dizen, y han licenciado las naos que tenia detenidas. Los de Rodas se defiende valientemente y con daño de los turcos. Pero estos continuan todavia su armar por la mar, de manera que se puede comprehender no arman por el turco; assi mismo me ha sydo referido que arman por su reputacion, y que su consul de Constantinoble les ha escrito que no deve dexar de armar por reputacion; pero yo no creo que por esto arme, que no son gente que gasten su dinero en el ayre. Tambien entiendo que quieren de aqui adelante dar todos sus officios por dineros, y que lo han acordado, que haziendolo sacaran mucho dinero en gran manera, y suele ser el postrimero esfuerço que ellos hazen quando tienen necessidad; y estos señales no me contentan para querer tomar concierto con vuestra magestad; antes entiendo que algunos no, pero gente del govierno, dizen que podria ser que no se concertassen con vuestra magestad, y otros dizen que no se puede concertar con vuestra magestad. El visorey de Napoles me escrivio de Mantua lo que passava; el rector de Verona y Prospero le escrivio que era bien resolverse con estos, e yo avise a vuestra magestad; no curare de dezirlo aqui. Assi me escrivio que solicitasse a estos le respondiessen a lo que su rector dixo, e yo ge les dixe quantos dias ha, y replicaronme que quando respondieran a vuestra magestad, que responderian al dicho visorrey, pues todo era una cosa; en especial que el dicho se deternia cinco dias en Mantua, y que luego se partio. En fin, este venir de franceses los tiene assi en sospecha, y mientra que tengan aquella esperança no pueden dexallos sino a mas no poder. Al señor Infante he escrito lo que vuestra magestad por la suya de xxx me tiene mandado, y continuamente escrevire y servire a su alteza con la mesma diligencia que vuestra magestad mando. De Venecia a xviij de junio. ## Notes - Uncertain in the hand: *[?nescia]* (f. 206v l. 32, a word before *v. mad.*, perhaps a slip for *necessitava*), *[?nemora]* (f. 207r l. 64, "entregarla nemora"; perhaps *Cremona* abbreviated), *[?sus pagos]* (l. 74). *Pregay* is the Venetian *Pregadi* (the Senate); *Mossen del Escut de Carmona* is written as read (Lescun, Thomas de Foix, the French commander at Cremona). - The decipherment was read on DECODE's images (3528 px across the opening); the secretary's cursive is fast, so a word here and there may be misread; the sentences hold throughout. Translation R9613_en.md # R9613: Alonso Sánchez to Charles V, Venice, 18 June 1522 — English Translation of `R9613_reading.md` (the contemporary decipherment, ff. 206r-207v). Same holes. I received Your Majesty's letter of the last of last month and went to the lords of this Republic. I told them that their ambassador had discussed the peace in this way and handed in a paper, to which a reply was given on Your Majesty's behalf in another paper, of all of which they would certainly have had a copy from their ambassador; that I informed them that Your Majesty was well disposed, provided they came to honest and reasonable conditions, because, as Your Majesty is emperor and head of the Christian commonwealth, so you desired more than anyone to establish and set peace in it, especially in Italy, and to unite its forces against the infidels and Turks; that I was well instructed in the whole negotiation and in Your Majesty's will in it; if they wished to discuss it with me, all of them or by deputing some persons for it, they should do so, or see what seemed good to them; or if, having consulted among themselves, they wished to answer without discussing it otherwise with me, only to let me know what they would decide. They answered that their ambassador had been told to draw up a paper on how he thought the peace should be settled, and that this showed that what he said was approved, since he was ordered to draw up a paper; that it seems that on Your Majesty's side one is leaving that first negotiation of peace and league, which they wanted as the stronger bond, and entering on making a new truce; and that, on the other hand, it is written that in the peace you cannot promise for the most serene lord Infante, while in the truce it says that His Highness would also enter. They also told me that the Cardinal of England had told their ambassadors he wished to see the said papers and give his opinion. I replied that if they considered well all that had been answered on Your Majesty's behalf they would recognise Your Majesty's good mind and will, and that they should consider well the last article, in which Your Majesty asks the King of England to be conciliator; that they should weigh well that Your Majesty was asking what they themselves ought to ask, and they would see whether there was a wish to keep for them what was agreed. I said this because I know that one of their grounds is that what was promised them would not be kept. On the lord Infante's matter I said: how was Your Majesty to promise what was not in your hand nor yours? And I also told them that I [?…] Your Majesty said it, because they already knew what was answered to their ambassador when he proposed that each side return to the other as before the war: that Your Majesty had not accepted those conditions, nor [?was there need] to accept them. They replied that Your Majesty had not rejected them altogether. To what they said about Your Majesty leaving the first negotiation, I told them not to be deceived: you were not leaving it, rather this was entering it on a sound footing, stating and removing the causes that could hinder it; that if they came to the conditions contained in Your Majesty's paper they would see that it was no departure at all from the first negotiation of the peace; and that if they asked for a league for defence, Your Majesty asked for more, a league for offence, with the limitation laid down; but in case, these being matters of great weight and quality, they thought more time was needed to settle them, Your Majesty said that a truce could be made meanwhile; that this of the truce showed them Your Majesty's good will, since you asked for it only in case they thought the said peace could not be settled so; that, coming to the conditions contained in the paper, Your Majesty spoke not of a truce but of the peace. And because I saw that they were much stung that Your Majesty offered that the lord Infante would promise the truce and says he cannot promise the peace, since it seemed to them, though they did not say so to me, that this left in the peace a great back door open by which they could be harmed at any time, I told them they could come to such and so honest conditions that Your Majesty would see to it that the lord Infante entered the peace. They left it that they would consult among themselves and answer me. I have been assured that in the Pregadi, which they held a few days ago, they discussed at length what they should do about the surrender of Cremona, should it come, and that one of them said God had always helped this Republic, that some days would thus pass before its surrender, and they would see what happened; that they were not now at liberty, so they could not well speak of what had to be done until they were, showing that surrendering it [?…] was outside the obligation to France; and many of them hold this opinion. I hold it needful that they should not declare this except when they can do no other, and when they have their affairs settled with Your Majesty. From France they say they have letters of three [days], with the usual boasting. Their ambassador was told by the King of France that France has at other times resisted the Empire, Spain and England, and that joined with this Signoria it would not only resist but attack them. Monsieur de Lescun at Cremona was sent a copy of a letter he has from Turin of the 7th of this month, that six hundred lances and twelve thousand Gascon adventurers had arrived there, and that they had [?their pay]; and Andrea Gritti is again writing to them, encouraging them towards France. As far as I can tell, the Turk is not arming at sea this year, and these men say so, and they have released the ships they had detained. Those of Rhodes defend themselves valiantly and with loss to the Turks. But these men still go on with their arming at sea, so that one can understand they are not arming because of the Turk; I have also been told they arm for their reputation, and that their consul at Constantinople has written to them that they must not leave off arming, for reputation's sake; but I do not believe they arm for that, for they are not people to spend their money on air. I also understand they mean from now on to sell all their offices for money, and have resolved on it, since by doing so they will raise a great deal of money; and that is usually the last effort they make when they are in need. And these signs do not please me as to their wishing to come to an agreement with Your Majesty; rather I understand that some, not however people of the government, say that it could be they would not come to terms with Your Majesty, and others say no agreement can be made with Your Majesty. The Viceroy of Naples wrote to me from Mantua what was happening; the rector of Verona and Prospero [Colonna] wrote to him that it was well to come to a resolution with these men, and I advised Your Majesty of it; I shall not trouble to repeat it here. He also wrote asking me to press these men to answer him on what their rector said, and I told them so some days ago, and they replied that when they answered Your Majesty they would answer the said Viceroy, since it was all one thing; especially as the said [Viceroy] would stay five days in Mantua, and he left at once. In short, this coming of the French keeps them in suspense, and while they have that hope they cannot leave them except when they can do no other. I have written to the lord Infante what Your Majesty commands me by yours of the 30th, and I will continually write to and serve His Highness with the same diligence that Your Majesty commanded. From Venice, 18 June. De Alonso Sanchez de xxvij de octubre*; transcription `R9641_decifrado_f187.txt`. The cipher stands twice: R9641 ff. 173r-174r (the letter, ending *en Venecia a xxvij de octubre*) and R9642 ff. 185r-186r (the same text, *Somos a xxviij del dicho y es treslado de otra enbiada por via de Genova; esta va por Roma*). Checked against the figures at the opening and the end with Tomokiyo's key: f. 173r l. 1 `cem` … `zud vad xig` L-e-L-a … `ho pac xig vum` g-4-`lal` `vec`+n `vum`+n = *yo … al duque de Sessa que los de esta republica dizen estan*; f. 174r l. 3-4 `xig faf vom fec xof vuc samg# zud vad xig` L-e-L-a = *de todo esto tengo dado aviso al duque de Sessa*; the postscript *Teniendo escrito hasta aqui recebi ayer* is written in clear on f. 174r and continues in cipher `dal yeh xig` ∞-4-ɡ-# … = *una carta de Jero[nimo] …*. New value: `vad` = **duque** (both places; v-block). DECODE gives R9641/R9642 as "Sánchez?" and R9642 as "N/A": both are Sánchez, and R9642 holds the decipherment. CSP Spain 2 no. 495? Conventions: text carried by the decipherment; `[?word]` uncertain in the hand; struck words left out; spelling as written, *v. mad.* expanded to *vuestra magestad*, *su sad.* to *su santidad*. ## Reading Yo he scrito al duque de Sessa que los de esta Republica dizen estan contentos de lo que el Papa respondio a su embaxador a la quexa que dieron de aposentar se la gente del exercito de vuestra magestad en Geradada, maravillando me que en cosa que toque a vuestra magestad responda el Papa bien a estos, y que esta manera de respuesta es que el Papa haze a estos daño para esta negociacion, y que si con su santidad se puede acabar seria cosa que esto viesse prevenido para siempre: que hablando le sus enbaxadores de estos sobre cosas que toquen a vuestra magestad, responda de manera que conozcan su santidad tiene no menos cuydado de las cosas de vuestra magestad que de las suyas proprias, y que llegando se ellos a vuestra magestad su santidad mirara por ellos, y haziendo lo contrario que lo miraran mal y no como les conviene. Y sepa vuestra magestad: este nuncio que aqui esta, al qual estos tienen credito porque es muy suyo, como tengo scrito, dize que si el Papa quisiesse, que estos se reduzirian a vuestra magestad con dezir a sus enbaxadores lo que arriba digo y que conosciessen en su santidad esta voluntad; y que las buenas respuestas que el Papa les da y la sperança de concertar a vuestra magestad y al Rey de Inglaterra con el de Francia los haze estar irresolutos con vuestra magestad, porque haziendo se el dicho concierto, como ellos lo tienen por cierto, piensan entraran en el con el medio de Francia sin haver se de dar con vuestra magestad ni dar le nada. Esto no me lo ha dicho a mi el nuncio, pero a lo dicho a persona cierta que me lo ha referido; y tanbien ha dicho que crehe estos dilataran quanto pudieren con buenas palabras de [?conversacion] con vuestra magestad. De todo esto tengo dado haviso al duque de Sessa. Teniendo escrita esta, recebi ayer una carta de Jeronimo Adorno, y [?vera] con esta el treslado; juntamente con ella me enbio una carta de vuestra magestad de xxvj del passado, por la qual me manda havisar de la venida del dicho Jeronimo Adorno y que traehe poder para el y para mi; y yo le scrivo con este mensajero e informo del estado en que esta la negociacion, como me lo pide; y llegado que fuere, con el ayuda de Dios, lo que en mi fuere procurare al servicio de vuestra magestad, como hasta aqui e echo. ## Notes - *Geradada* (l. 4, written *engeradada*): the Ghiara d'Adda (Gera d'Adda), the district on the Venetian-Milanese border where the imperial troops were to be quartered. - *[?conversacion]* (l. 25) is written *conversaçõn* with a superscript, uncertain. *[?vera]* (l. 28): "y vera con esta el treslado", one word uncertain. - The letter's cipher was not aligned word by word beyond the checks above; the reading follows the decipherment. Translation R9641_en.md # R9641 (R9642): Alonso Sánchez to Charles V, Venice, 27 October 1522 — English Translation of `R9641_reading.md` (the contemporary decipherment, ff. 187r-188r). Same holes. I have written to the Duke of Sessa that the lords of this Republic say they are content with what the Pope answered their ambassador on the complaint they made about the quartering of Your Majesty's army in the Ghiara d'Adda; I marvel that, in a matter touching Your Majesty, the Pope should answer these men favourably, and this manner of answer that the Pope gives them is harmful to this negotiation. If it could be obtained from His Holiness, it would be well that this were provided for once and for all: that when their ambassadors speak to him about matters touching Your Majesty, he should answer so that they know His Holiness has no less care for Your Majesty's affairs than for his own, and that if they draw close to Your Majesty His Holiness will look after them, and if they do the contrary he will look on it with disfavour, not as suits them. And Your Majesty should know: this nuncio who is here, whom these men trust because he is very much theirs, as I have written, says that if the Pope wished, these men would come round to Your Majesty, by his saying to their ambassadors what I say above and their seeing this will in His Holiness; and that the good answers the Pope gives them, and the hope of bringing Your Majesty and the King of England to an agreement with the King of France, keep them irresolute with Your Majesty, because if that agreement is made, as they hold for certain, they think they will enter it through France without having to come to terms with Your Majesty or give you anything. The nuncio has not said this to me himself, but he said it to a reliable person who reported it to me; and he has also said that he believes these men will delay as long as they can with fair words of [?conversation] with Your Majesty. Of all this I have informed the Duke of Sessa. Having written this, I received yesterday a letter from Girolamo Adorno, and [?Your Majesty will see] the copy with this; together with it he sent me a letter of Your Majesty's of the 26th of last month, in which you command me to be informed of the coming of the said Girolamo Adorno and that he brings powers for himself and for me; and I am writing to him by this messenger and informing him of the state of the negotiation, as he asks me; and when he has arrived, with God's help, I shall do what lies in me for Your Majesty's service, as I have done until now. R9593, Venice, 5 March 1522 (RAH Salazar 9/23 ff. 27r-27v) decoded, not read Sánchez to Charles V: letters of Don Juan Manuel and Geronimo Adorno sent on; his audience with the Signoria on the passage of the lansquenets through Val Camonica (he had not believed the reports until those conducting them wrote and signed them; Andrea Gritti's officer and the damage claimed); the French have taken Caravaggio, the Swiss at Monza said to be 16,000 and 4,000. A mechanical decode with holes in most sentences: shown so that the transcription and the key can be checked and improved, not as a reading. Five ciphered despatches of the nuncio in France, deciphered on arrival and printed deciphered by Lestocquoy in 1972. They were transcribed and checked with George Lasry’s key. The same key decrypts three cancelled cipher lines the edition omits: the clear postscript about the royal fleet bound for Corsica. 44 26 03 07 02 62 8 · 58 6 52 4 62 4 · 28 06 2 66 36 68 4 42 05 07 03 6 96 96 2 → fortuna · come ne · auiso del strozzi a = 28|38|8 · e = 24|34|4 · o = 26|36|6 · t = 07|76|86 · 1 = null France → Rome · homophonic cipher of one- and two-digit figures, with nomenclator · March–December 1553 Prospero Santa Croce to Cardinal del Monte, 1553: five ciphered despatches, deciphered on arrival and printed in 1972 from Prospero Santa Croce Go to the transcriptions ↓ ASV Segreteria di Stato, Nunziatura di Francia 3, ff. 117, 128, 230, 248, 263 (DECODE R6–R10; catalogue item 245). DECODE marks them "partially decrypted" and dates them 28 July 1552, the first date of the volume. All five were deciphered in Rome on arrival, and the decifrati are bound with them. Lestocquoy printed the letters in 1972 with the cipher passages deciphered. George Lasry’s key was applied to the transcriptions as a check. The one passage Lestocquoy left out, three struck-through cipher lines on R9, was decrypted with the same key. Lasry's reconstruction, as filed on the records, is a homophonic alphabet of one- and two-digit elements: a = 28, 38 or 8; e = 24, 34 or 4; i = 2, 22 or 32; o = 26, 36 or 6; t = 07, 76 or 86; u = 02, 04, 06 or 08; r = 03 or 56; s = 05 or 66; and single values for the other letters (b 48, c 58, d 68, f 44, g 54, h 64, l 42, m 52, n 62, p 46, z 96). The digit 1 is a null that mostly falls between words. Code groups for names and common words begin with a dotted digit. Element boundaries are not marked, so a run like 2 2 8 can be split in several ways. The decoder in the repository resolves the splits with a sixteenth-century Italian language model.
