For R6, R7, R8 and R10 the text is Lestocquoy's. The decrypts follow it where the volunteer transcription is clean, but on their own they have holes or garbled words in almost every clause: they are decoded, not read, and the reading is the print (reading audit, 22 October 2026). For example, Lestocquoy's p. 157 reads "ci è maneggio stretto col [duca di Ferrara], non so se sia per haver denari con promesse di mercanti et avvantaggio d’esso Duca o pur per qualche lega o per haver artigliaria con la scusa che ha usato il [duca di Firenze] a Siena". The R6 decode follows those words where it is clean. R8's "Il Re Chr.mo resta mal contento dell’impresa di Corsica … credo che si risolverà di mantenerla" agrees both with p. 218 and with the interlinear decipherment on the leaf. R7 (Ferrara as "generale supremo di Italia con vinti mila scudi", the Naples enterprise) and R10 ("Molti persuadeno S.M. di havere a far guerra in Italia") match pp. 162–163 and 244.

f. 248r (R9), Paris, 14 December 1553. Three lines of cipher struck through, and below them the same postscript in clear: "L’armata regia che partì per Corsica ha havuto fortuna et non si sa come né dove sia et non credo ci sia aviso del Strozzi". Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Nunziatura di Francia 3 f. 248r, via DECODE R9. Lestocquoy prints the letter of 14 December and its clear postscript (p. 240) but not the struck-through figures above the postscript. The figures were transcribed through the cancellation strokes and decrypted with the key. Long stretches match the postscript: line 1: 46 6 03 86 = port…, and 58 6 56 05 2 … 58 28 = Corsi…ca line 2: 44 26 03 [07] 02 62 8 = fortuna; 58 6 52 4 62 4 = come ne; 68 6 02 4 = dove line 3: 28 06 2 66 36 = auiso; 68 4 42 = del; 05 07 03 6 96 96 2 = strozzi So the cancelled cipher is the postscript itself: l’armata regia che partì per Corsica ha havuto fortuna et non si sa come né dove sia et non credo che ci sia aviso del Strozzi . In English: the royal fleet that left for Corsica has met a storm, no one knows how or where it is, and I do not think there is any news of Strozzi. The secretary began to encipher it, gave up, struck the figures out and wrote the sentence in clear. The cancelled lines themselves give only aligned words between illegible digits, so taken as cipher they are decoded, not read (reading audit, 22 October 2026): the sentence is known from the clear postscript, not from the figures. In this repository none of the five entries is therefore held as a reading: the reading is Lestocquoy’s printed decipherment of 1972, which is not copied here.

In the spring of 1516 Henry VIII was paying for Maximilian’s campaign to win back Milan from Francis I, and Cardinal Matthäus Schiner, bishop of Sion, led the Swiss who fought for it. The campaign failed. The Swiss mutinied at Bergamo for want of pay, Brescia surrendered to the French and Venetians on 23 May, and the English envoys Richard Pace and Sir Robert Wingfield blamed each other, Galeazzo Visconti and Schiner. In the middle of it Maximilian made Henry an extraordinary offer: the duchy of Milan, and the succession to the Empire itself. On 14 June, three days after reaching Verona, Schiner answered a letter of Henry’s from London of 8 May. He wrote it himself, four pages of dense Latin, and put the dangerous words into cipher. The letter is in the Cotton library, in a volume the fire of 1731 burnt at the edges, so every line has lost its ends. J. S. Brewer calendared it in 1864 as Letters and Papers II no. 2044, with a Latin extract full of gaps and the note “partly in cipher, not deciphered … Sense obscure.” The project’s catalogue took that at its word and listed the letter as not deciphered.
schiner1516.html#buchi

Albert Büchi, professor at Fribourg, collected Schiner’s correspondence for the Quellen zur Schweizer Geschichte . His second volume (Basel 1925, 1516–1527) prints the letter in full as no. 541, pp. 67–72. At the end he says where the cipher went: “Autograph. Badly damaged at the margin, partly in cipher, the cipher not resolved there and given here in italics.” There was no decipherment written on the original. The italics are Büchi’s. Image: A. Büchi (ed.), Korrespondenzen und Akten zur Geschichte des Kardinals Matth. Schiner II (Basel 1925), p. 72; scan: Swiss National Library, e-Helvetica nbdig-59316. His preface explains how. Twenty-nine letters of the volume are partly in cipher, most of them with the decipherment written over the lines, but seven had none. “Keys to them were found nowhere, and had first to be reconstructed.” He did it with the help of Traugott Schiess, the volume’s editor, and they recovered the keys of all but a single letter (no. 582). He names five kinds of cipher, used by Schiner and his agents “above all in dealings with England”. He printed no key and no facsimile. The letter was found by working through the sources that catalogue entry 290 had not checked. There is no DECODE record, and the British Library record says “Digitised Content: No”. Tomokiyo’s cryptiana item on Schiner is a different letter of 1520. HathiTrust holds Büchi’s volumes behind a bot check, but the Swiss National Library has both on e-Helvetica with a text layer. The text layer drops the italics, so the cipher passages were marked from the page images.

Büchi’s italics mark fourteen passages, 88 words in all, on pp. 67, 68 and 70. They are words and phrases set into clear Latin. Some are chosen for secrecy, and some seem to be ciphered for the practice of it. The opening of the letter in Büchi’s edition. Square brackets are Büchi’s restorations of the burnt margin. Image: A. Büchi (ed.), Korrespondenzen und Akten zur Geschichte des Kardinals Matth. Schiner II (Basel 1925), p. 68; scan: Swiss National Library, e-Helvetica nbdig-59316. Every one of the 88 words has a decipherment in Büchi’s text. 84 of them stand on surviving cipher. The other four, [quod omnia] and [regi Catholico] , fall in the burnt margin and are Büchi’s conjectures, and two more words are partly restored. The rest of the letter is clear Latin: Schiner’s defence against the men who blackened him to Henry, the welcome he says the Swiss gave him at Bergamo, the fall of Brescia, the lack of a month’s pay, and his view of the peace Wolsey had raised.

“Not deciphered” was never quite true. Brewer’s extract gives the words of passages 7 to 12: the duchy of Milan, the crown of the Empire, the Duke of Bari (“corrected from Mediolani”, his note says), and Galeazzo’s dealings. His footnote identifies “a monogram in cipher” for Vestrae Majestati inside passages 11 and 12. His marginal summary is the secret itself: “Maximilian’s offer of the Empire and duchy of Milan to Henry is known to Galeazzo and others.” What he left out are passages 1 to 6, 13 and 14. Without the leaf there is no telling whether the passages he gives were lightly disguised or whether he worked them out. The next leaf of the volume (L&P II 2045, Büchi no. 542) shows that London understood the letter in 1516. It is an abstract made in England of “the letters of the Cardinal of Sion, 14 June, from Trent”. It opens with his complaint that the Duke of Bari “knew everything”, as if he had read the instructions, and that Schiner believed Pace had told him. It then argues that the Roman Empire and the duchy of Milan were neither impossible nor unbecoming for the King. That is the ciphered content of the letter, summarised by its first readers, and it bears out Büchi’s passages 7 to 12.

Which indeed ⟦I regret; but with the utmost⟧ prayers I beg the same ⟦Majesty⟧ to deign to ⟦weigh⟧ the cause of this neglect. For from the day on which I set out from the Val di Sole to the Imperial Majesty's ⟦camp, to direct⟧ the armies and the affairs of war, I never [had the means of writing] to Your Majesty; [but, intent] on the remaining pending matters and on guarding against dangers, I at last reached [Verona] safe, and having now come as far as here, I have stayed three days to speed certain ex[peditions]. And since news of such [matters] does not come easily or safely either by letters or by messengers, it would [be] more right to confer and discuss everything by word of mouth [in person], which ought to be kept hidden under the veil of secrecy, since [minds of] good faith are strangers in these times. For in the past days, when I [noticed] that one of the [agents] was abounding in his own sense and proceeding by certain ways and means [against it, and I wished] to bring him onto the path that seemed to me both fitter and fairer for the business, having exacted an oath that he would not disclose to any creature, rational or irrational, by word [or] writing, the [secrets] I was to reveal to him, I showed him what the Imperial Majesty ⟦proposed to Your Royal Majesty⟧ and agreed, through my ministry, concerning ⟦the duchy of Milan and the crown⟧ ⟦of the Holy Empire to be conferred⟧ on a [friend], thinking them safely and faithfully hidden where h — —. [But while] talking ⟦with the lord Duke of Bari⟧, who [is] and always has been truly most devoted to me ⟦and has honoured me as a father⟧, he began to disclose to me how someone had told [him] that I had put forward dealings and ⟦had offered and promised Your Majesty [that I would do all] to have the duchy of Milan conferred on it⟧; and, as he [would] not [tell] me anything more, [I asked him to] trust me. But he would not reveal the person who had told him, and stead[fastly] refused to believe of me [what I had said]. Indeed I understand that such a word has already become known to the lord Galeazzo Visconti [and] those around him. I, however, more cautiously, wh[en] I knew the matter, dissembled and denied it, although I was greatly astonished, [since I knew that I] had revealed this matter to no one else; and I began to [think] various things within myself and to fear that perhaps, just as the teller himself did not keep quiet, so another(?), knowing something, might lightly taint it further, since it is most dangerous for such a thing to be heaped up among so many varieties of men, and each is drawn by his own pleasure: on this side the Swiss, [on that] the French [could] interpret most tortuously, forestall, taint or provoke what would not then be done fittingly after the fact or from the dealings already touched upon. [But lies] of whatever kind I do not fear, by the saying of Saint Jerome, and so much the more strongly because Galeazzo, [even now], as often, double, who ⟦had earlier usurped the duchy of Milan for himself, then offered it to [the Catholic King], that he might become its governor in it; and they say that the same Catholic King refused it on behalf of his nephew, and he is said to have offered it to Your Majesty⟧. The Emperor therefore walks with uncertain feet, and, placed [among such men], could neither hide it from them nor so taint matters greatly, that I believed it would be imputed to me as a crime to keep silent about [them towards] Your [Majesty] or not to reveal them, leaving [the judgement] of such hazards to Your Majesty's discretion, unless I have erred in this, that I dared to disclose it to him whom, had I not known him to be Your Royal Majesty's ambassador and most trusted, I would have kept silent [until] death. As for the rest that pertains to what is to be conferred and negotiated with the Imperial Majesty, [although I was not with] him, I have nevertheless striven by letters and other means so much [that] I can promise, and on his behalf I promise, that in all things and for all things he will act, proceed and persevere most fairly and most confidently [in what has been said] and promised, with a marvellous [advance] and increase of ardour, love and [fervour], so that after the divine goodness sor — — (one line illegible). [Nevertheless I had wished,] to obey Your Majesty's command and to satisfy the duty I owe, to make known to it the [reasons for my] departure from there. But being compelled, as circumstances required, to [take part in] the articles [of peace] and to be busy in those places and to stay in the face of the enemy, who were [unused] to messengers, there was less opportunity. And since in all these things that have been done [so far] other agents of Your Royal Majesty have intervened, and nothing has been committed worthy of honour or [praise], but rather much worthy of reproach, both in hiring [soldiers and] in proceeding in the matter and in laying out and pouring out money, [I feared] that if I wrote the truth — since I have never been used to do otherwise — I would have had to reproach what was done. [Therefore, lest, wishing] to recount it, I should rather seem to judge it, I thought I should abstain; and [I grieve] at this the more strongly [because] I have learned that some pursue me with bites and hatred, and tear me to pieces before the Royal Majesty in writing and in words; who, would that they had lent their ears to my warnings and their steps to my directions! — unless it had pleased God, best of all, otherwise — they would have made the Royal Majesty master of all its wishes, and themselves loaded with merit and praise before it. For I have never been found, over a long time, to deceive anyone with the French, since I have been used to have neither dealings nor practices with them, nor subjection, nor wife, nor children, nor gifts from them; nor prodigal, nor to have ill administered the money and the province entrusted to me; on the contrary, to spend my own, not to ruin what belongs to others; and as such I have been held also by the Roman pontiffs and others for whom I have administered. I also have twenty years' continuous practice, knowledge and exercise with the Swiss, and speech without an interpreter. To them, if they judge rightly, I have been for the heaping up and restoring of much honour and advantage; and when they followed my warnings they abounded in honours; but when they did otherwise, it went otherwise with them. But those among them who favour the French, and they are countless, and others, wherever anything adverse and contrary befalls them and their fortune, like the French themselves, strive to derive the origin and cause from me and to turn vengeance back on me, as though they thought that every straw of opposition would be rooted out once I was trodden down. And if they redouble their darts against me everywhere, I have also scented from afar that some rivals have reported even to Your Royal Majesty and elsewhere that the Swiss, out of the hatred with which they were moved against me, made dissension, tumult and withdrawal at Bergamo, so as not to serve with me. A marvellous thing: when they heard and saw me coming to them, all of them, suddenly moved with joy and immense applause, ran to meet me, filling the roads, gates and windows, so that even the stones and everything seemed to resound with joy at my coming, and many were wet with tears; who, if they had burned with hatred or envy against me, since it has been known of old to every judge and to men that those whom they hate ⟦they cannot look upon with glad eyes or a cheerful face⟧. But as the light is hateful to owls and to sick eyes, so certain directors, the royal agents and captains of troops, and the business, ⟦which they took care should succeed otherwise than rightly⟧ (!), envying my honour, when they saw that by it the things they had ill done and their frauds were being repaired and recognised, began from then on to grumble and to say that the business was not going according to my view, but otherwise; and so much that for two days and nights [they tried] to stamp the distrust of a third pay, and to sow evil and tumult among the Swiss, so that it is most notorious to all where they led matters. From then on everything began to be in danger and to go [backwards]; and if I had not repaired it by promises and by the pledge of my own person, they [themselves] would have gone off together with the Swiss, so that in one and the same course both the troops and the engines [called] blidin of the Imperial army would have been the prey of the French, and whatever the Emperor [had] in Italy would have come to the enemy. And the evil grew so far that, before fittingly — — — Brescia, whose revenues are 100,000 ducats, was surrendered to the enemy, [unless] 60,000 florins had been applied. And they were already losing Verona, [and some of the French] began, having laid waste the fields and burnt [the villages, to besiege the city], garrisoned with soldiers; then, because they [heard] that 4,000 Swiss were to come down from here, [they not only fled], but [left behind] also some boats thrown across as a bridge, anchors and other things, so much that from Brescia, as the scouts report, they strove both [to sally out and to snatch the citadel from the enemy], having left 300 peasants as a garrison there — — the hope certainly hangs on the forces, the city and citadel having been recovered by them — — were shaken. For the soldiers are not [inferior] in strength, experience and up[rightness, but] the want of gold and of one whole month's pay has hindered us, with which we could sufficiently both increase the infantry and [hire] the horsemen, whom we greatly need, drive the French from Italy and shake the Venetians. [All of which] could now be readily achieved and had at once and together. Other — — and other things are lacking, which, had together, would bestow the whole victory, after — — from now on will be recovered in the lands, that not only not further other pet — — restore, and we would be able to pursue the whole war even into France. The [Bishop] of York, in his letter to me, speaks of a peace to be negotiated sufficiently by the Imperial Majesty. In truth there is no one, nor the Emperor, who has not long wished for it; for [whose restoration] two Roman pontiffs, kings and princes have done much. But they [never] wished to play except with wrappings, nor ever to come to fitting articles. [Which was] the greatest cause, for so many years, of the [cavilling] not only of Italy but of all Christendom. If they had been content with just pacts, peace would long since have been restored, and to the Teucri(?) too, and France would have been [conquered] by Your Royal Majesty while the Imperial Majesty was coming down to visit it. Then they pressed the Imperial Majesty with new and most bitter wars [to adhere], and so all wishes on both sides came to nothing. And n[ow the French], after taking Brescia, are so puffed up that they would not [yet] entertain any conditions of pe[ace]. They also claim — and so they have pacts with the French — that everything long [usurped by others], which the Roman Church and every other have recovered, should come into their p[ower]; and the Frenchman is already said to have ced[ed] Crema [to the French] on the pretext of having recovered Brescia, which [I take as a sign] not only of such ambition and greed but truly of their ruin, [nay rather] that Brescia can be recovered, if a few aids are not lacking to the Emperor, and, [once Brescia is taken and the French] driven out, Crema with the duchy would be recovered. And if the Venetians held Crema, there would [never be peace]. I fear indeed, and I have heard the Pope judge, that the Venetians will never be quiet unless they have usurped Italy, nor can any rest be promised to Italy unless they are [driven back] to their usual marshes. When this is rightly understood, there will be no need to argue it. Yet I do not believe that the Imperial Majesty rejects a fitting peace, nor shall I [ever] fail to persuade His Majesty of it lawfully, so that I [may] serve Your Royal Majesty. If at last there were any other things concerning the earlier expedition and [to be reported] about it, I have taken care to make them known point by point to Your Majesty's ambassadors and agents, [and I do not doubt] that they will have fulfilled their duty and mine towards Your same Majesty by informing Your Majesty. I for my part abstained from letters, so as not to heap the troubles of a troublesome business on Your Royal Majesty by letters; but if the same [Majesty] wishes to know every particular, I shall fulfil its wishes as it commands, who also these s — — — except too much then of my honour, which, as I have kept it unstained, [I shall keep], because with all the strength of soul and body heaped together, understanding above — — I have consecrated my devotion to Your Most Sacred Majesty, to have [increased] whose [praise] I shall rejoice in more than to have gained all the treasures of the world, — — fearing the loss of these, unwillingly to preserve with — — — to be taken away and the Royal favour — — — I communicate my mind, although the Archdeacon, my servant, [left] Your Majesty not long ago, who [reported] one by one every piece of news here and what continually [happened]. May it deign to hear them, and to number me among [all] its perpetual and most faithful little servants and hold me commended, remembering at some time my help — — most [—] and of the sacred faith and of the Christian commonwealth, for increasing honours — — — and advantages, as it is believed to be decreed in heaven, to be accomplished on earth. Safe — — — Trent, 14 June. Address: To the most Christian and most sacred lord, the lord King of England and France, his most dread lord.

The volume is the first of Ségur’s négociation for the king of Navarre with the German princes. Three of its ciphered letters, of 1585–86, are Navarre’s in a key recovered here from the ciphertext alone ( key A ); two more, of 1586, are in the key Tomokiyo rebuilt from f. 321 ( f. 333 ). This 1583 letter is in neither: a different cipher, with its own page since 14 October 2026. It is not from the king. Its clear text speaks of the cipher itself: “Il me semble qu’il n’est point besoin d’autre alphabet, vous y avez toutes choses tellement dispersées en lettres, syllabes, doubles, nulles et tout le reste qu’il est impossible de le descouvrir … Les noms sont en lettres et syllabes.” That is the design both later keys turn out to have. The clear passages also carry the name numbers 156, 134 and 136, and a short run of figures before la marks a place name.
segur1583.html#cipher

Three lines and a fragment of a fourth, 58 numeric figures with 42 distinct values, plus the letter-written signs Pa , a , H , L and I : 133 21 73 39 43 111 118 84 24 26 5 62 3 4 30 65 13 70 22 39 14 123 45 121 40 81 42 14 48 15 63 122 35 29 41 Pa 26 6 119 38 81 40 a 2 13 41 14 30 H L I [Ha grand faute des] 156 […] The f. 321 key (letters 12–62, syllables from 63) gives nothing: the figures below 12 that it treats as doubles and nulls are frequent here. Key A (letters 1–53, syllables 54–123) gives scattered French-looking fragments ( …ande efeire… , …faisi… ) inside runs that are not French ( hfurtsitumailaco ), so if the two keys are related they are not the same. The structured annealer that recovered key A needed about 460 figures; on f. 333 (108 figures) it failed, and so did a matched control of that size. A run that builds in the alphabetical design would also need this table’s offsets, which 58 figures cannot fix.

S. Ill.ma” (a lord or ambassador), c. 1527–1529 from its content; ten lines of cipher with ten clear stretches. Where Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308, fasc. 2: the cipher is no. 13 (DECODE R4801), its clear copy no. 16 (DECODE R4804); both catalogued “1500–1599” with no status. The cipher Homophonic substitution, 37 signs, many shaped like numerals: one or two signs per letter, four signs for the doubled letters ll, gg, ss, cc, one null, no code words. How it was deciphered George Lasry transcribed the cipher and built an initial key in CTTS; Claude Fable 5.1 finalised the key and the transcription from the plaintext of no. 16 (17–18 October 2026). What it says The Pope’s agreements and his delay in coming to Bologna have left “qualche ruggine”; the writer would claim some castle, as Lautrec took Modena and Reggio, “perché al peggio non si ha sinon a rendere”. V. S. Ill[ustrissi]ma His translation: “baca(?) because the Pope, in these agreements, with per accordato and the delay of his coming to Bologna, it seems that some rust remains, so that their investigations and advice will be very necessary, especially as the greater part of the principal men of the court do not seem to speak of him except ill … and therefore we shall have judged it fitting, in this doubt and occasion, to spend everything for the abasement of the neighbours and, claiming some castle or other, to do our business as he did non sabbatte(?) when Lautrec passed, who at his own expense took Modena and Reggio; and this because at the worst there is nothing to do but give back; and all is left to the most discreet consideration of Your Most Illustrious Lordship.” The papal journey to Bologna after agreements and Lautrec’s seizure of Modena and Reggio (1527) point to the years between the sack of Rome and Clement VII’s coming to Bologna in the autumn of 1529, 1527–1529. George Lasry marked the date as unverified in his report and confirmed 1527–1529 on 18 October 2026.

Two Italian letters written half in clear and half in a three-figure syllabic code (DECODE R664, R660), which the English codebreaker who intercepted them called the Venetian Cifer. His interlinear glosses and his own grid of the code (R658) rebuild it as a systematic syllabary of 117 values, checked on his glossed strings (46 of 46 groups). Phrases are deciphered; the letters are not yet decoded through. The file’s other ciphers have their own pages. 211 433 436 154 253 319 152 560 · 240 · 468 434 516 146 456 461 252 359 del la lo ro si cu re za · et · quel le de nu o ve se n “della loro sicurezza” · “et … quelle de nuovo senza” London, intercepted Italian letters · three-figure syllabic code · c. 1623–24 · code rebuilt from the codebreaker’s own grid; decoded, not read The “Venetian Cifer” of a Jacobean codebreaker’s file, TNA SP 106/10 Go to the transcriptions ↓ Two intercepted Italian letters in a three-figure syllabic code, rebuilt from the English codebreaker’s own glosses and grid; phrases are deciphered, but the letters are not yet decoded through, so nothing reads as text yet. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 20 September 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · none (key obtained, text not read) The letters Two Italian letters, sender and recipient unknown, written half in clear and half in code, intercepted in London. They sit in a file dated 1623–24. Where The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 ff. 167–169 and 139–140 (DECODE R664, R660); the codebreaker’s grid f. 125 (R658) and glossed strings f. 182 (R702 p. 2). DECODE lists them as anonymous ciphertexts, “1558/1625”. The cipher One three-figure group per syllable. Each consonant takes five groups in a row, one per vowel a e i o u ; a few groups are whole words, with a superscript letter for the ending. How it was deciphered About 45 values were aligned from the codebreaker’s syllables written above the groups. His own grid of the code then gave 117 values and corrected four of them. What it says Fragments: della loro sicurezza , et hoggi terzo giorno quelle de nuovo senza , and on his sheet i colonelli , che possiamo prometter , di 24 di maggio . Still open Neither letter has been transcribed group by group and decoded through with the table; the writers are not identified. Checked on 23 October 2026: R664’s file holds two decoded phrases and one clear line, not the letter, so R664 is decoded, not read; R658 (the codebreaker’s grid), R702 p. 2 (his worksheet of glossed strings) and R701 p. 1 (his heading and word list) are working papers, not prose. No document of this entry reads yet. The way on is to transcribe R664 and R660 group by group and decode them with the rebuilt code. Credit The values are the contemporary codebreaker’s. These letters were one part of a single codebreaker’s working file, which this site first treated as one entry. The file holds several different ciphers, and each now has its own page: the two-figure nomenclator of his key sheet R725 ( sp106r725 , which also dates the file), a second three-figure code used in a Venetian secretary’s letter of 1625 ( sp106r722 ), a letter-and-figure syllabary ( sp106r704 ), and a 1645 royalist letter that only shares the box ( sp106r931 ).

R660 and R664 are letters written half in cleartext and half in code. The writer enciphered the words that mattered and left the Italian connecting phrases in clear, which gave the English codebreaker his cribs, and gives them now. One whole line of R664 stands in the clear, and it is about the cipher itself: “potrete continuare nel modo cominciato, osservando però il [mutamento … alle volte … col … numeri suppositi]” The codebreaker wrote his solutions above the groups, syllable by syllable. Aligning those syllables against the figures gives the code back. About forty-five values were fixed this way, each by a word that admits no other division (260, 262, 263 and 459 as corrected by his grid, section 04): 111 al · 145 nume · 146 nu · 151 ra · 152 re · 153 tri · 154 ro · 165 che · 211 del · 240 et · 245 si 252 se · 253 si · 254 so · 260 ta · 261 te · 262 ti · 263 to · 316 ta? · 319 cu · 320 in · 340 lettere 344 el · 356 i · 357 l · 359 n · 366 col · 411 qui · 430 a · 433 la · 434 le · 436 lo · 456 o · 459 r 461 ve · 463 volte · 468 quello · 515 da · 516 de · 518 do · 535 mi · 536 mol · 537 mu · 542 quan · 544 gua · 560 za · 568 vostre R664 f. 1, line 38: 211 433 436 154 253 319 152 560 … with del·la·lo·ro·si·cu·re·za written above: “della loro sicurezza”. Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 f. 167, via DECODE R664 (p. 1). With these values line 38 decrypts as follows: 211 433 436 154 253 319 152 560 ·312· 359 518 ·367· 433 del la lo ro si cu re za ? n do ? la and lines 41–42, with a word running over the line break: 240 | hoggi terzo giorno | 468 434 516 146 456 461 252 359 → 560 et (in the clear) quel le de nu o ve se n za “et hoggi terzo giorno quelle de nuovo senza…”
sp106box10.html#method

All of this depends on matching the codebreaker’s interlinear syllables to the right groups, and a one-group drift would produce plausible nonsense. The alignment produced one apparent contradiction, and its resolution supports the rest: group 252 was glossed sen in one line and se in another, and 359 za in one line and n in two others. Both resolve if the word senza runs over the end of line 41 ( 252 se + 359 n closing the line, 560 za opening line 42), which is what the manuscript shows. After that correction no value conflicts with any other across lines 34–45. The images came from DECODE with the project’s login and had to be rotated before transcription. The codebreaker did the cryptanalysis four hundred years ago; the work here was to find the sheets on which he wrote it down, transcribe them and apply them.
sp106box10.html#grid

Seven more records of the box, which DECODE lists as another set of anonymous ciphertexts (catalogue item 62), are his worksheets. On R701 he heads a list of word groups “Wordes marked with letters in the Venetian Cifer” : 369° nostro , 467° questo , 430 a passata . The same words stand in the side column of R658, and R658 is his table of the code of R660 and R664: every group from 136 to 565, with a count of its occurrences below it and his value above it. R658 (SP 106/10 f. 125, turned the right way up), groups 251–565: sa sca stra sta over 251–551, se sce stre ste over 252–552; te ti to tu over 261–264, tre tri tro tru , ve vi vo , ze zi zo zu ; 165 che , 465 quel ; at the right 467 questo , 568 vostro , 440 Spagn… Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 f. 125, via DECODE R658 (rotated here). The grid shows how the code was made. Each consonant takes five consecutive rows in the order a e i o u , and each hundreds column a different consonant: 151–155 ra…ru , 251–255 sa…su , 351–355 sca…scu , 551–555 sta…stu ; 260–264 ta…tu , 360–364 tra…tru , 460–463 va…vo , 560–564 za…zu ; 433–437 la…lu , 142–146 na…nu , 242–246 pa…pu , 442–446 pra…pru , 542–545 qua…quo ; the row x56 holds the bare vowels, x57–x59 single consonants (357 l , 359 n , 459 r ), and a handful of groups are whole words (339 liga , 340 lettere , 439 per , 165 che , 465 quel ), their ending given by a superscript letter. With the table, the code has 117 values, 102 of them written by the codebreaker and 15 predicted by the pattern. The check is R702, where he wrote out group strings with his own glosses. Every one of its 46 groups is in the table, and every string decodes to his gloss: 356 318 436 143 435 → i·co·lo·ne·li “i colonelli” · 341 433 436 154 → del·la·lo·ro 252 359 518 253 → se·n·do·si “sendosi” · 167 252 459 253 → con·se·r·si “conservarsi” 165 245 556 253 156 526 445 534 261 459 → che·po·s·si·a·mo·pro·me·te·r “che possiamo prometter” The same sheet glosses di 24 di maggio , del campo , per nome suo , sono capitate and efficacia : the letter he was working on was written in late May and spoke of a camp and of colonels. The table also corrects four values first aligned on R664 alone: 260 is ta , 262 ti , 263 to and 459 r (they had been taken as mento , to , ti and v ), and 316 ta does not fit the ca…cu run it stands in. The 1625 letter of the same file ( sp106r722 ) is in a code built the same way but with another table (R701 p. 3: 244 ra , 245 re , 366–370 la…lu ; here 244 is pi , 245 po , 433–437 la…lu ). The words R701 lists under “the Venetian Cifer” are the words of R658’s side column, so on the sheets’ own evidence the name belongs to this code.

No date has been found in these two letters. The file they sit in is dated to 1623–24 by the vocabulary of the codebreaker’s other key, R725 ( Marques Inichiosa , the Spanish ambassador of 1623–24; C. Barberino , cardinal from October 1623; Palatinato ; see sp106r725 ), and R702 adds a 24 May and colonels, which would fit 1624. The date is taken as c. 1623–24, not proved for these letters.

The grid table is H for the 102 values the codebreaker wrote and M for the 15 predicted from the pattern; 440 Spagn… and 556 ( s on R702, unclear on the grid) are M . Groups seen but not valued on R664 f. 1: 233, 312, 367, 439, 477, 534, 551, 556, 566. Several dozen more stand on ff. 2–3. walsingham1572.html#the-record

Harley MS 260 is a fair-copy letter-book of Walsingham’s embassy in France, 1570–73, the book Digges printed. DECODE R8363 has three images: f. 398r, top: the end of a letter signed Frauncis Walsingham, “At Paris the 21 th of Januarie 1572”. It covers the Cardinal of Lorraine bringing a dispensation from Rome for Monsieur to marry his niece, and Marshal Tavannes’s hope of recovery. CSP Foreign x calendars it between nos. 726 and 727 as “a copy of Mr. Secretary’s letter”. DECODE’s date and its blank recipient come from this tail. f. 398r–399v: “To the right hono[ra]ble and my verie good Lord the Lord Treasurer”, dated 20 January 1572/3 and signed. It concerns the Vidame’s man, who has not delivered two letters and some books; “Steward” (Colonel Stewart), gone to La Rochelle, who sent “a fond cipher” that Walsingham found “not for the purpose”; letters from Davison he cannot forward safely; and Walsingham’s reluctance to carry on as “a distributer of letters” for young and inexperienced parties.
walsingham1572.html#the-cipher

The whole of the cipher is the last two lines of f. 398r: The matter of most importance conteyned in the same was touchinge a Gentleman of [9] departed hence to 2 1 ⌘ ε 9 4 w th intention to imbarke there yf the barke were not departed. F. 398r, last lines: “… a Gentleman of [9] departed hence to 2 1 ⌘ ε 9 4 w th intention to imbarke there”. The bracketed [9] stands for a name the copyist left out (in R8364 it reads as Alençon, so probably a gentleman of the Duke; see R8364 ); the six symbols, a port, are not deciphered. Image: British Library, Harley MS 260 f. 398r, via DECODE R8363. The copyist writes [9] , a bracketed flourish, wherever the original had a cipher name he did not copy. It stands for other names in R8362 (“longeth to heare from Lyons [9]”) and R8364, and Digges prints it as “[7]” or “[s]”. The six symbols 2 1 ⌘ ε 9 4 were copied, and Digges set them as “2 ) ⌘ 6·) 4”. Burghley’s answer in the same book (f. 419r, DECODE R8364, February 1572/3) has one group in the same system: “a Shipp sent to 2 0 ⌘ H 6 1 tt ymagined that Ball there had a meaninge to provoke Glasco [9] to come hither”. Both groups start with 2 and have ⌘ third.
walsingham1572.html#what-was-tried

Print. Digges 1655 pp. 312–313: the cipher printed as cipher. CSP Foreign x, January 1573: no. 725 (Walsingham to Burghley, 20 Jan) opens with the Vidame’s servant but goes on to a book defending the Queen of Scots and to Dr Dale, and does not include the passage. The signed original in SP 70 was not seen. Keys. DECODE has no key record from Harley 260 and no Walsingham key before 1577. Tomokiyo’s survey of Elizabethan ciphers has none for Walsingham’s Paris embassy. The Cecil–Norris table of 1567–68 (see norreys1567 ) turns the group into “r a ? ? i p”. Siblings. The nine Harley 260 records on DECODE (R8356–R8364) were fetched. The two from the same weeks were examined: R8362 has placeholders only, and R8364 has the one group above. Ciphertext only. Twelve symbols of nine kinds. Under a homophonic alphabet of digits and signs, Dieppe, Calais, Nantes, Brest(e) and Rouen(s) can each be made to fit both groups. A gentleman leaving Paris to catch a ship points to a Channel port, Dieppe likeliest, but that is a guess (grade I).
walsingham1572.html#what-remains-open

The port “2 1 ⌘ ε 9 4” is not deciphered. It is too short, and no key survives. The name behind “[9]” was never copied into the book. Only Walsingham’s signed original in SP 70, if it survives, could show it.
